en: The Śrī Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, Part One: The Section on Devotion (Upāsanākhaṇḍa).
Now begins the Śrī Gaṇeśa Purāṇa;
the opening salutations.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Salutations to Śrī Svānandeśa, the Lord of Brahmā.
Salutations to Śrī Mahāsiddhi.
Homage to Śrī Mahābuddhi.
Homage to Śrī Lakṣa. Homage to Śrī Lābha.
Salutation to the illustrious King Nagnabhairava. Salutation to the illustrious Gaṇaka, the teacher of the Supreme Brahman.
Salutation to the illustrious Mudgala, the supreme preceptor.
Salutations to Śrī Bhṛśuṇḍī, Gārgya, Gṛtsamada, Bhṛgu, and Vyāsa.
Salutations again and again to the venerable Gurus of all the Gaṇeśas and to the Ācāryas.
Salutations to the Lord of the Seat of Great Siddhi, Śrī Brahmabhūya, the venerable Yogīndra, the son of Girijā.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa, the teacher of the world, the venerable Gaṇeśa Yogīndrācārya.
Salutations to the illustrious bearer of the goad, the true guru, the lord of yogis.
Salutations to the illustrious true guru Herambārāja.
Table of Contents for the First Half:
Section on Meditation (Upāsanākhaṇḍa) Chapters and Subjects: [List of chapters and subjects]
1. The Story of King Somakānta; 2. The Origin of Somakānta’s Leprosy Falling from His Limbs and His Resolve to Go to the Forest;
3. Instruction to Somakānta’s Sons and the Description of Proper Conduct.
4. The king entered the forest.
5. He approached together with Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu.
6. The one who loves Soma resided in the hermitage of Bhṛgu.
7. The story of Somakānta’s previous birth;
8. The warding off of various doubts by Bhṛgu’s utterance of "Huṃ";
9. Bhṛgu’s instruction to the king.
10. Vyāsa’s confusion due to the absence of Gaṇeśa Maṅgala, and his journey to the presence of Brahmā;
11. The instruction of the Gaṇeśa mantra to Vyāsa by Brahmā; 12. The manifestation of Gajānana to the gods.
13. The praise of Lord Brahmā by the god Brahmā, who was born from the belly of the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa).
14. Distressed by obstacles, Lord Brahmā hears a voice from the sky saying, "Perform penance.
15. The penance of Lord Brahmā, his vision of Gaṇeśa, and the procedure for his worship.
16. The origin of the Daityas Madhu and Kaiṭabha; Brahmā, the god, entreats the Goddess.
17. Mahāviṣṇu’s instruction of the six-syllable mantra to Śaṅkara regarding Gajānana. 18.
Mahāviṣṇu’s vision of Gaṇeśa and the granting of boons; the origin of Siddhakṣetra.
19. King Abhīma obtains a son through Queen Kamalā; description of the son. 20. Dakṣa, the son of Kamalā, has a vision of Gaṇeśa.
21. Mudgala-Dakṣa performs the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra of Gaṇeśa.
22. Ballāla, a devotee of Gaṇeśa, beholds Gaṇeśa; 23. The condition of Vaiśyakalyāṇa; 24. The performance of rites by Dakṣa and his auspicious dream.
25. The death of King Candrasena and the grief of Queen Sulabhā; 26. Dakṣa’s accession to the kingdom and the expansion of his lineage; 27. A description of the consecration of Rukmāṅgada.
28. Mukunda’s curse upon Rukmāṅgada and the vision of Nārada;
29. The instruction given by Nārada to Rukmāṅgada; 30. The violation of Ahalyā’s chastity.
31. Gautama’s curse directed at Indra;
32. Gautama’s praise of the gods by means of the six-syllabled mantra;
33. Indra’s assumption of a divine body through the power of the six-syllabled mantra.
34. Indra’s performance of penance, the vision of Gaṇeśa, and the description of the Cintāmaṇi Tīrtha. 35. Rukmāṅgada’s attainment of a divine body and his departure for the world of Gajānana.
36. The birth of Gṛtsamada through the union of Mukunda and Indrāṇī, the destruction of his pride and arrogance, and the mutual exchange of curses between mother and son.

37. Gṛtsamada performs penance; the vision of Gajānana and the attainment of the boon. 38. The wondrous penance of Gṛtsamada [and that of the Tripura Asura]; the granting of the boon by Gaṇeśa. 39. The defeat of Indra by the Tripura Asura.
40. The defeat of the god Brahmā by the Asura Tripura, and the penance performed by the gods; 41. The surrender of Tripura before him by Gajānana in the form of a Brāhmaṇa;
42. The battle between Śaṅkara and Tripura.
43. The defeat of Śaṅkara and Pārvatī’s departure to the vicinity of Himālaya; 44. Śaṅkara’s penance, the appearance of Gajānana, and Śaṅkara’s receipt of boons;
45. Gaṇeśa instructing Śaṅkara on how to perform the hymn of praise known as the *Gaṇeśasahasranāma*.
46. The Thousand Names of Gaṇeśa;
47. The battle between Śaṅkara and Tripura, and the burning of Tripura;
48. The arrival of Pārvatī, the worship of the earthen image (up to the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada), and its greatness.
49. Description of the earthen worship (pārthivapūjā) of Gaṇeśa; 50. The earthen worship and the dialogue between Pārvatī and Himālaya;
51. Himālaya’s departure with Pārvatī for the vow of the earthen Gaṇeśa.
52. The story of King Candrāṅgada regarding the Pārthiva Gaṇeśa vow. 53. The story of King Candrāṅgada regarding the Pārthiva Gaṇeśa vow.
54. Instruction by Nārada for Queen Indumatī to perform the Pārthiva Gaṇeśa vow. Pakoṭā.
55. Through the power of the worship and vow during the Gaṇeśa-vrata, the union of Pārvatī and Śaṅkara occurred.
56. By the power of remembering the names of Gaṇeśa, the sinful weaver assumed the form of Bhr̥guśuṇḍi.
57. Through the Saṅkaṣṭa-caturthī-vrata, Kṛtavīrya attained his goal.
58. The fall of Indra’s celestial chariot upon the capital city of Śūrasena;
59. The greatness of the Saṅkaṣṭa-Caturthī vow, and the story of Kṛtavīrya; 60. The majesty of the Aṅgāraka-Caturthī vow.
61. The greatness of the Saṅkaṣṭacaturthī vow; the curse and the grace bestowed upon the Moon; the majesty of Dūrvā grass.
62. The mutual exchange of curses between the Kṣatriya wife Sulabhā and the Brāhmaṇa Madhusūdana.
63. The praise of Dūrvā grass; the story of the Asura Kālānasa.
64. The narrative of the sage Kauṇḍinya; 65. King Janaka’s abduction of Sītā; 66. The satisfaction of Gajānana by means of the two horses given by Virocana and Triśiras.
67. The power [of the Lord] to provide shelter even for a single blade of dūrvā grass to the wife of Kauṇḍinya. 68. The observance of the Saṅkaṣṭa-caturthī vow by Kṛtavīrya.
69. The greatness of the Saṅkaṣṭa-caturthī vow, including its primary and secondary components.
70. By whom and by whom was the Saṅkaṣṭacaturthī vow performed in former times?
71. The procedure for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the Saṅkaṣṭacaturthī vow. 72. Kṛtavīrya’s obtaining of a son who was devoid of limbs.

73. The performance of the Pravāla-kṣetra ritual by the son of Kṛtavīrya, the vision of Gaṇeśa, and the attainment of a thousand arms by Kṛtavīrya; 74. The story of the Cāṇḍāla who taught the Saṅkaṣṭa-caturthī vow; 75. King Śūrasena’s observance of the Caturthī vow and its fruit.
76. The story of Dūrvāputraṣudha, and the greatness of the fourth-day vow named Dūrvā.
77. The arrival of Sahasrārjuna at the hermitage of Jamadagni, and the occasion of the meal. 78. The effort made by Kārtavīrya (Sahasrārjuna) to take away the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu).
79. The defeat of Kārtavīrya by the army produced from the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and the killing of Jamadagni. 80. The abandonment of the body by Reṇukā.
81. The elevation of the ancestors to heaven through the praise of Dattātreya.
82. Rāma’s penance at Mayūreśa-kṣetra, the vision of Mayūreśa, and the acquisition of the axe (paraśu).
83. The birth of the demon Tāraka. 84. The reduction of Kāmadeva to ashes in the presence of Śaṅkara.
85. The history of Skanda’s birth; 86. Śaṅkara’s narration of the Gaṇeśa-vrata to Skanda;
87. Skanda’s penance at the sacred site of Elāpura, the granting of boons by the Lord Lakṣavināyaka, and the slaying of the demon Tāraka.
88. Śeṣa performs penance and propitiates Gaṇeśa according to the instruction of Nārada; 89. Kāma performs penance; Gaṇeśa grants him a boon; 90. The rebirth of Kāma and the narrative of Śeṣa.
91. Praise of Gajānana;
92. The Greatness of the Twelve Names of Gajānana beginning with "Sumukha. Chapter One: Named "Description of Somakānta."
Oṃ, salutations to that Gaṇeśa, the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman,
whose name alone acts like Agastya in drying up the ocean of obstacles.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O one of great wisdom! O you who are proficient in the Vedas and Shastras!
O treasury of all sciences, no other speaker can be found besides you. (1)
The exceedingly great merit accumulated by us through birth after birth has resulted in this vision of you, who are truly omniscient. (2)
We are the most fortunate in the world; our life is well-lived, for we have our fathers, the Vedic scriptures, ascetic penances, and the stages of life.
The eighteen Purāṇas have been recited to us in detail;
O best of the twice-born, we also desire to hear other [works]. 4.
Engaged in the great twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, we have no other cause for rest than drinking the nectar of your stories. (5)
Sūta said:
Well asked, O highly fortunate ones, by you whose deeds are meritorious!
The intellect of the virtuous, who possess equanimity of mind, is intent upon the welfare of the world.
O twice-born ones, I too take great pleasure in recounting these stories;
therefore, I shall relate them especially to those of virtuous conduct.
There are eighteen other Upapurāṇas as well:
the Gāṇeśa, the Nāradīya, and likewise the Nṛsiṃha, and others.
Of that Purāṇa concerning Gaṇeśa, I shall first relate the beginning, the hearing of which is especially difficult to obtain in the world of mortals. (9)
Merely by remembering him, a person becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done;
even Śeṣa and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) are not able to describe his power.
Nevertheless, at your command, I shall speak this in brief; however, its hearing can only occur through the merit accumulated over many lifetimes. (11)
It does not belong to heretics, to nihilists, nor to those who perform evil deeds;
for it is, in reality, eternal, devoid of qualities, and without beginning.
The true nature of Gaṇeśa cannot be described by anyone;
nevertheless, for those devoted to his worship, he who is beyond all attributes (nirguṇa) is thus described.
The Blessed One, whose form is the syllable Oṃ, who is established at the beginning of the Vedas, whom the sages and the gods, Indra and the others, always remember within their hearts. 14.
He whom Brahmā, Īśāna, Indra, and Viṣṇu constantly worship;
he who is the cause of all worlds, the cause of all causes. 15.
By whose command Brahmā creates, and by whose command Viṣṇu performs protection;
by whose command even Hara destroys, and by whose command the Sun-god moves through the day. 16.

By whose command even the wind blows, by whose command the waters flow in all directions, by whose command the stars fall to the earth, and by whose command the fire blazes throughout the three worlds. || 17 ||
O twice-born ones, I shall relate to you that secret deed of his which has not been disclosed to anyone; listen with respect. 18.
This was formerly told by Brahmā to Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor;
he told it to Bhṛgu, and he in turn told it to Somakānta.
The wisdom that arises belongs to those who possess millions of merits acquired through vows, sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and pilgrimages. || 20 ||
O best of the twice-born, for those who listen to this Purāṇa called Gaṇeśa,
there is no delusion regarding worldly existence, nor among wives, children, or lands.
O best of sages, you are full of reverence for the story of Mayūreśa;
let his greatness be heard now in connection with Somakānta. 22.
In the city of Devanagara in Saurāṣṭra, there was a king named Somakānta;
he was a knower of the true meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras, and was devoted to the principles of the Dharmaśāstras. || 23 ||
Ten thousand elephants and twice as many horses,
along with six thousand chariot-warriors, followed him as he set forth.
There were also innumerable foot-soldiers likewise bearing fire-arms and weapons;
others carried bows, and still others carried two quivers.
He surpassed Bṛhaspati in intellect, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) in prosperity,
the Earth in forbearance, and the great ocean in profundity.
That king surpassed the sun and the moon in brilliance and luster;
he surpassed fire in majesty and the god of love in beauty.
In that [kingdom], there were five powerful ministers of firm prowess, who understood the true meaning of the treatises on policy and were capable of crushing enemy kingdoms. || 28 ||
Among them, the first is Rūpavān, and the next is Vidyādheśa; Kṣemaṅkara is attainable through knowledge, and Subala is remembered as the fifth. || 29 ||
By their own prowess, they have conquered various lands;
these regions are exceedingly beautiful and adorned with diverse ornaments and garments. || 30 ||
Constantly performing the king's business and being exceedingly dear to the monarch,
he had a wife named Sudharmā, who was endowed with virtuous qualities.
Upon merely beholding his form, Rati, Rambhā, and Tilottamā were overcome with shame; they found no pleasure anywhere and could not even think of themselves.
She wore on her ears two beautiful golden earrings set with many jewels, and around her neck she bore a golden chain and pearls.
There was a girdle made of precious gems at her waist, and similar anklets on her feet; and there were excellent rings upon the fingers of her hands and feet.
She was devoted to the service of the Blessed One, to giving, and to honoring guests, providing thousands of costly garments of many colors.
Constantly devoted to the service of her husband and always intent on his word,
these two had an auspicious son known as Hemakaṇṭha.
Possessing the strength of ten thousand elephants, wise, valiant, and a scorcher of his enemies—
such was that best of kings, Somaka, on this earth.
Having brought all [kings] under his control, he ruled the kingdom upon the earth;
O best of the twice-born, he was constantly devoted to dharma, a performer of sacrifices, a giver, and one of great renunciation.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of Somakānta," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 0 + 38 = 38.
Chapter Two.
The Sages said:
O Sage, please tell me quickly, out of compassion, what kind of greatness belongs to the Śrī Gaṇeśa Purāṇa in connection with Somakānta.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to the misdeed of Somakānta;
suddenly, a most painful case of oozing leprosy befell him. 1.
Then, due to the ripening of his former karma, neither auspicious nor inauspicious action ever leaves King Dharmaśīla. ||2||
In whatever state a deed is performed,
in that very same state it is certainly experienced by living beings.
He became submerged in an ocean of suffering like one without a raft in the sea;
he experienced intense pain as if bitten by a serpent. || 4 ||
Strewn with various grains of rice, with blood flowing here and there,
filled with pus and gore, the king was overwhelmed by worms;
he became nothing but skin and bone, as if seized by consumption.
Agitated by anxiety and afflicted with pain in all his senses,
the king then spoke to his ministers, having restrained his mind with great effort.
The king said:
"Fie on my kingdom, and fie on my beauty! Fie on my strength, my life, and my wealth! By what seed of action has this calamity befallen me? (7)
Because I surpassed the Moon in beauty, I became known as Somakānta.

By me, the virtuous, the distressed, the learned in the Vedas, and even the hermitages—(as well as the holy ascetics)—and likewise the people of the countryside were protected like my own children. 8.
By means of which my enemies of terrible form were conquered by my arrows. || 9 ||
By him the entire earth was brought under his own control;
he had perfectly propitiated the God, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva.
By that body of mine, which was formerly devoid of association with the wicked and which practiced the restraint of the mind, fragrant objects of desire were enjoyed. (11)
Therefore, my life now seems foul-smelling and in vain;
hence, with the permission of you all, I shall go to the forest of self-restraint (the forest of asceticism).
Let all of you sprinkle my son Hemakaṇṭha, who is endowed with wisdom and valor, for the sake of the kingdom, and let them protect him with their prowess. || 13 ||
Now I shall not show my face to the world in any way whatsoever—
not for kingdoms, nor for wives, nor for life, nor even for prosperity.
"O great ministers, I shall accomplish my purpose for my own welfare in the forest.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, he fell to the earth like a tree struck down by the wind. 15.
O best of the twice-born, that place was filled with floods of pus and blood;
there arose a great clamor from the ministers and the women. (16)
And for a moment, there was a most terrible cry of "Alas! Alas! among the people;
then, by means of fans made from the waving of garments and other swift-acting medicinal remedies, [the situation was addressed]. || 17 ||
By means of the application of ministerial spells, they restored him to consciousness;
when the king had become healthy, the ministers spoke as follows.
The ministers said:
"By your grace, we have enjoyed happiness equal to that of the lord of the gods, which is unattainable for all other people.
But now, how shall we live without you, and how shall we survive like mere cattle-slaughterers? (19)
"Let your son alone rule the kingdom—he who possesses abundant treasure, is powerful, and is a slayer of enemies.
O King, abandoning all worldly pleasures, let us go together this very day to dwell in the forest. (20)
Sūta said:
Then Sudharmā, the foremost of the distinguished ones, spoke these words to the king in the forest: "O sole hero, let us go to Vraja to serve him; with my son, rule the kingdom together. (21)
There is no other who experiences the suffering or the happiness of a living being created by its own prior actions;
in whatever way the fruit of karma has accrued, that very same result must be experienced by the individual himself.
By me as well, who possess various kinds of enjoyments, this kingdom has been enjoyed in happiness;
for it has been declared by the sages that for women, the journey to the next world is indeed together with their husband. || 23 ||
Then his son Hemakaṇṭha, humble yet overwhelmed with grief, spoke these words to Somakānta at that time: || 24 ||
Hemakaṇṭha said:
"O tiger among kings, apart from you, I have no concern whatsoever for my kingdom, my wives, my life, or even my vast stores of wealth. (25)
O King, protector of righteousness, just as a lamp is without oil and a body is without life, so too is a kingdom in vain without you. 26.
Sūta said:
Having heard the nectar-like words of his son, the virtuous Sudharmā, the king’s mind was filled with joy, and he spoke to his son in accordance with dharma. 27.
The king said:
He who is ever devoted to his father’s word, who performs the śrāddha with faith, and who offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayā—he alone is called a son. 28.
Therefore, endowed with this policy and acting according to my command, rule the kingdom together with your ministers;
govern all your subjects as you would your own sons.
He who knows the true meaning of the treatises on Dharma, understands statesmanship, and commits no fault— such a son who delivers his ancestors is called a true son.
"I am going to the forest, afflicted with loathsome, oozing leprosy; together with my wife Sudharmā, grant me your permission, O you of noble vows. (31)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 38 + 31 = 69.
Chapter Three, titled "The Exposition of Conduct and Other Topics," ends here.
Sūta said:
Then, rising up and taking his son by the right hand, the king entered the upper chamber where he always held counsel.
There stood a divine golden throne, adorned with many jewels and set with pearls and corals, shining like the seat of Śakra himself.
There, both the father and son remained in many ways like two brothers, for they had entered into every jewel as if functioning as a collective whole.
Filled with compassion and desiring the glory of his own lineage, the king first taught his son proper conduct and various kinds of political ethics.
Somakānta said:
When only one watch of the night remains, a man who is awake should leave his bed, sit in a clean place, and remember the Guru. (5)
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity, one should bow down preceded by praise;
then, having requested the Earth, "Forgive me," one should touch her feet [in prostration] before that which pervades the universe.
At dawn, I bow to Gaṇanātha, the cause of all, the bestower of boons upon Brahmā and the other gods, enriched by all the Āgamas;
the giver of the fruits of dharma, artha, and kāma, the cause of liberation for living beings, beyond the reach of words, beginningless, and of infinite forms. (7)
In the morning, I bow to the Lord of Kamalā, of fierce valor, who delights in various incarnations for his own protection;
the Lord who dwells in the Ocean of Milk, the kinsman of the sovereign of the immortals, the remover of sin, the destroyer of enemies, and the cause of liberation. 8.
In the morning, I bow to the Lord of Girijā, who wears the moon upon his crest; who is clothed in a tiger skin and whose mind has cast away passion;
who grants boons to Nārāyaṇa and Indra; who is honored by gods and Siddhas; and who, O serpent-like one, wields the trident and the ḍamaru drum, the destroyer of the cities [of the demons].
At dawn, I bow to the Lord of Day, the remover of sins, the dispeller of dense darkness, worshipped by the highest worlds;
whose essence is the three Vedas, who has cast away the illusions of the enemies of the gods, the sole cause of knowledge, possessed of great power and noble nature. 10.

At dawn, I bow to the daughter of the Mountain, the cause of liberation from worldly existence, who carries one across to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra; she who has three eyes, who is the primordial cause of reality, who has cast aside the illusion of the enemies of the gods, who is composed of *māyā*, and who is the sovereign goddess praised by the lords of gods and sages. 11.
Having thus recollected other gods as well as hosts of sages,
and having worshipped them with mental offerings, one should ask for their forgiveness.
Then, carrying a water-pot, the Brāhmaṇa or the Kṣatriya should go to the south-western direction of the village and take very white earth. (13)
Likewise, a Vaiśya or a Śūdra shall not dig for black earth from the bank of a river,
nor from fertile soil, nor from an anthill, nor ever from the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
Having covered the ground with grass and other materials,
one should void urine and feces during the day or night, facing north or south.
First, having wiped the anus with grass, wood, or similar materials,
a man should thereafter wash it five times with earth and water.
One should touch the left hand ten times, both hands seven times,
the liṅga once, and the left hand three times.
After voiding urine, one should wash both hands twice;
the feet should be washed once. This is declared as the rule for a householder.
One who observes a vow should perform twice as much; one living in the forest, three times as much;
an ascetic, four times as much; and one observing silence at night, five times as much.
Half of the foot [of impurity] is for day and night, as is the case for women and Śūdras regarding purification;
then, having sipped water (ācamana), one should use a tooth-stick from either a milky or a thorny tree.
Having taken them with a prayer, one should cleanse the teeth and the tongue;
[this bestows] strength, vigor, fame, splendor, cattle, intelligence, and wealth. (21)
"O Lord of the Forest, grant me wisdom and the intellect for the Veda;
then, having first performed a bath with cool water that removes impurity. (22)
Then, with the mantras prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, he should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsanā),
as well as recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), Vedic study (svādhyāya), libation (tarpaṇa), and the worship of the gods.
The Vaiśvadeva offering, hospitality toward guests, eating in the presence of the twice-born, listening to the Purāṇas, giving gifts, and avoiding the censure of others. || 24 ||
One should perform service for others through the nectars of wealth, life, and speech;
yet one should not perform service for others while engaging in self-praise.
Betrayal of the guru, reviling the Vedas, atheism, the practice of sin,
eating forbidden food, and consorting with the wives of others— 26.
He should avoid the wives of others and approach his own wife only during her season;
he should always practice service toward his mother, father, teachers, and cows. 27.
One should give food along with clothing to the poor, the blind, and the wretched;
even at the risk of one's own life, one should never practice the abandonment of truth. 28.
The favor of the Lord and the protection of the virtuous, according to their offenses and having consulted the Dharmaśāstra; || 29 ||
Having consulted with wise men, one who is skilled in policy should administer punishment;
one in whom trust is not possible should never be trusted by him. 30.
One who desires prosperity should not place excessive trust in someone who has inspired confidence;
nor should one ever trust someone with whom enmity has been established, even if that person appears trustworthy.
By the employment of the six political measures, he should cause his own kingdom to prosper;
he should practice charity according to his capacity, otherwise it will fall into decay.
They declare that the lowest among those who cause others to be distressed is one whose vision is through spies, whose mouth is his messenger, and whose rod of punishment is ever-ready. 33.
Out of fear of punishment alone, people abide by their respective duties;
otherwise, there would be no restraint, and this distinction between "another's" and "one's own" would not exist.
If an inferior person should revile him, or if they should ever praise him, he should neither become angry nor feel pleased; for what is gained by that, and what is gained by that as well? 35.
Furthermore, even one who has previously committed an offense, if he should seek refuge, must always be protected;
likewise, one who was formerly a creditor is always to be maintained.
The concealment of counsel must always be practiced, for it is said that the kingdom is rooted in that;
having abandoned the six enemies beginning with lust, one should then conquer others.
An excellent king should not cause the destruction of livelihoods, the extermination of subjects, the displacement of deities, nor the destruction of groves and sacred shrines. || 38 ||
One should give gifts on auspicious occasions for the sake of fame and practice renunciation;
one should not deceive friends, nor should one speak of what ought to be kept secret from the three [classes of women]. 39.
One should rescue a Brahmin from debt and a cow from the mud;
one should never speak untruth, nor should one ever abandon the truth. 40.
He should win the hearts of his ministers, subjects, and servants;
he should always pay homage to the Brāhmaṇas and to the deities. 41.
Sūta said:
Having thus instructed his son Hemakaṇṭha in other matters as well,
as well as in conduct according to dharma and the science of polity (nītiśāstra) as he had heard it, the king—
Having observed an auspicious moment, he summoned his ministers— Kṣemaṅkara, Rūpavanta, and likewise Vidyādhiśa.
Having gathered together from various places the Brahmins who were learned in the Vedas and well-established in the performance of sacrificial rites, O King; 44.
The king summoned his high ministers, the queen, his own kinsmen, the leaders of the guilds, and the citizens.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and his chosen deity according to the prescribed rites for the sake of the investiture of his son, the slayer of enemies, [he performed the ceremony]. 46.
Having caused the recitation of benedictions preceded by the worship of the Mothers,
and having performed the *abhyudayika* śrāddha, he gratified the Brahmins with food.

Having caused the consecration of his son to be performed with the chanting of mantras, that beloved husband of Somakā addressed these words to his three chief ministers: 48. The king said: "This is my son"—such was the conviction held by my ministers;
yet this son has now been entrusted into your very hands. (49)
Just as my instruction was carried out by those expert in statecraft,
so too must his command be executed by you, together with the leaders of the guilds.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Conduct and Other Duties," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.

Chapter Four.
Sūta said:
Once the consecration was completed, that king performed the worship of the twice-born;
he bestowed jewels, pearls, and corals, along with cows accompanied by their calves.
He gratified them all with elephants, cattle, horses, wealth,
and garments— clothes from various countries interspersed with gold.
Of various colors, large in size, and produced in the land of Kaśmīra, [he gave them] to kings, to the wives of kings, and even to the heads of villages. || 3 ||
The king gave those [lands] to his virtuous servants according to their merit;
he gave other villages and much wealth to his ministers as well.
Then the king, overwhelmed by intense grief, went to the forest—
extremely defiled and impure due to the faults accumulated in his previous births.
As he departed, a great cry of "Alas! arose among the people;
abandoning each their own business, they rushed toward the lord of men.
The ministers, the king’s wives, and Hemakaṇṭha, who had gone to his friend,
rose up and fell down before him, stumbling, rushing, and even weeping.
The ministers and citizens, though themselves distressed, restrained him;
having traveled two leagues, the king stood there, overcome with fatigue.
Having seen the pond filled with cool water and surrounded by various trees,
he spoke to all the city-dwellers, the ministers, and his own kinsmen.
Whatever offense I have committed while governing the kingdom for so long, that must be forgiven; O people, I bow to you with my palms joined in reverence.
Out of compassion for my son, should he by chance arrive here, I entreat you all: let not your affection for me diminish.
"Let all those who have gathered here, including women and the elderly, go to the city;
let them remain there, free from anxiety, protected by my son."
"May you all grant me leave; with a pure heart, I am going to the forest.
Only when you have departed will my mind become steady."
May all of you, out of compassion, do me a great favor;
being distressed, I cannot bring myself to speak harshly, even though I am desirous of death. 14.
This great sin, accumulated by me alone through birth after birth, is indeed this separation from my kingdom and from those who act for the welfare of the world. 15.
"But what can I do, since I am afflicted with leprosy?
Everyone experiences the fruits of their own actions, both good and evil. (16)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, his friends likewise fainted;
some, overcome with intense grief, struck their heads with the palms of their hands.
Some who were wise and possessed of supernormal knowledge offered consolation to the king by recounting the conduct of kings born in former times.
Others, however, perceive that state as inexpressible,
just as yogis whose mental faculties are directed toward knowledge do when their own true nature has been realized.
Then some wise men, restraining their own grief with fortitude, spoke to that beloved of the Somakas, who was sorrowful and eager to go to the forest: || 20 ||
The people said:
"Having nourished and protected us, you ought not to abandon us, just as water does not abandon its coolness, nor fire its heat. (21)
Even the ocean its boundary, or the sun its radiance—how indeed shall we reach the city without you, O lover of mankind? 22.
O crusher of enemies, just as the sky, though filled with stars, does not shine when bereft of the moon, so too would this city not be beautiful without you, O King.
"Let us go together to two or three sacred fords;
O beloved, your form will become radiant through the service of those holy places. (24)
Then we shall go together to the city crowded with banners,
filled with great joy, preceded by musical instruments and bards.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the king, filled with anger and sorrow, bowed to them and said, "Do not speak thus, do not speak thus again! (26)
Then, filled with affection and compassion, and endowed with humility, the king together with his ministers spoke to the beloved Vemakaṇṭha.
The son said:
"I cannot bear to go without you, nor can I rule the kingdom or live.
I have never before seen you apart from me; how shall I endure this separation? (28)
The king said:
"For this very purpose, I previously taught you that auspicious treatise on dharma endowed with excellent policy; you ought not to let it be in vain. (29)
It is heard that in former times, the son of Jamadagni, who was wise and skilled in policy, slew his own mother in accordance with the command of his father. (30)
Rāma, however, abandoned the kingdom and went to the forest with his younger brother;
Lakṣmaṇa, moreover, abandoned Sītā in the forest without even asking for the reason.
"Hemakaṇṭha! Accompanied by three ministers, go quickly from here at my command to the city and rule the kingdom bestowed upon you by me. (32)
Just as the mind of a wise man who is capable of action is fixed upon the Supreme Self,
so does the mind of the world abide when its wealth is properly established.
Likewise, while I have gone to the forest, my heart remains fixed on you; by the turn of fate, O fortunate one, you have been born, and I shall return home again.
The Dharma will be fulfilled for you in that way if you act according to my words; it will not be so if you go with him. Therefore, go; I am departing.
Sūta said:
Then the ministers, the citizens, and the son, their minds resolved upon departing,
bowed to the king with great difficulty.
Then, having been permitted by him and greeted with blessings,
they circumambulated the king and returned toward the city.
Having assembled a great army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, the proud Agni,
adorned with a parasol and a banner and wearing a golden necklace, went to the city.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Journey to the Somakānta Hermitage," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 119 + 38 = 157.
Chapter Five, titled "The Dialogue between Sudharmā and Acyuta," Sūta said:
Then, approaching his mother with a mind distressed by affection, he said to her:
"O Mother, why do you abandon one who is innocent?"
The son said:
"You must say to my father, 'Let this son go along with you,' provided that he takes me with him in accordance with your word. (2)
Then I shall serve you both; my mind has no such inclination for sovereignty.
What happiness could that kingdom provide for me, deprived as I am of you two? (3)
Sudharma said:
"O mighty-armed one, the king, being so overwhelmed by suffering and grief, will not heed my words; therefore, go at my command."
"O child, by virtue of my devotion to my husband, I am dependent upon another;
for women, there is no deity other than their husband, and he alone is to be revered. (5)
Sūta said:
Having heard this, the son, together with his friends, paid homage to his mother;
then, having circumambulated her and received her permission, he went to the city.
Adorned with citizens wearing ornaments and decorated with banners, flags, and foliage,
its streets were sprinkled and rich with fragrance, just like the city of Indra.
Having given betel, perfumes, and garments, and having dismissed his kinsmen,
the king entered his magnificent palace, filled with both joy and sorrow.
He ruled the kingdom with righteousness, protecting his subjects like his own children;
he applied his mind to virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation according to his training.
The sages said:
"How did King Somaka come to the forest? With what companions did he go, and what deed did he perform? Tell us this in detail. (10)
Sūta said:
O sinless ones, I shall relate the reasons why Somaka’s beloved went to the forest and what deed he performed there with devotion; listen.
Accompanied by his two ministers, who were accessible through their subtle knowledge, and by his lawful wife Sudharmā, he entered the forest that was difficult to approach.
The queen went in front, the king followed in the middle,
and his lawful wife Sudharman followed behind him, just as Sītā followed behind Rāma.
Eating but once a day, with a single mind and a single dwelling place,
and sharing equally in both sorrow and joy, they went from forest to forest.
Exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, and by traveling over uneven paths, they sat down somewhere, taking refuge in the shade. || 15 ||
Having gone again to another forest, they beheld a great lake where crocodiles resembling elephants shone along with tortoises.
Tāla, astamāla, sarala, priyāla, and auspicious bakula trees;
sarala, panasa, jambu, nimba, aśvattha, vaṭa, and others. 17.
The trees, entwined on all sides by networks of various creepers, shone there where a dense darkness prevailed, like that within the interior of a mountain cave. 18.
There the breeze is pleasant to the touch, carrying the fragrance of lotuses and kādamba flowers,
and from which the sages gather flowers and fruits.
Where swans, cranes, hawks, auspicious crows, cuckoos,
sarikas, and ruddy geese utter their songs and cries.

O best of the twice-born, there is no conjunction of cold, heat, or the rays of the sun for those dwelling in bowers of various creepers and flowers; nor is there hunger, thirst, fear, or death there, just as it is in heaven for the meritorious.
Having gone there, they all drank the cool water that dispelled their fatigue;
and after bathing and performing their daily rites, they ate fruits.
And for a moment the king slept on the soft sand at the riverbank,
while his lawful wife Sudharmā remained standing, massaging his feet.
Having understood his consent, two ministers went forth to gather roots,
tubers, fruits, and lotus stalks.
There Sudharmā beheld a boy of fierce and wondrous form, blazing with radiance;
because of his preeminent beauty, he thought that this was Smara born again as a child in former times. || 25 ||
Upon seeing him, Sudharmā rejoiced and considered him a benefactor;
observing his heart to be both agitated and serene, she spoke of his service as one who had acted without seeking reward. (26)
He asked him: "Who are you? From where have you come? Whose sons are you, and who is your mother?
O friend, satisfy my ears quickly with a stream of the nectar of your words."
Sūta said:
Thus questioned, that boy spoke to the princess with words like nectar:
"O beautiful lady, my father is Bhṛgu and my mother is Pulomā; seeking water, I have come here from my own home. (28)
"O auspicious lady, I am indeed named Cyavana, an executor of my father's commands;
and who are you, and how have you come to this forest? (29)
How is it that his limbs ooze like a mountain during the rainy season?
And by what karma does he possess such extreme foulness? Tell me. (30)
How can you resort to this place, which is swarming with a multitude of worms, when you yourself are so exceedingly beautiful, delicate, and fair-eyed? (31)
O beautiful one with a serene countenance, gracing all your limbs with beauty, was she not previously presented to you by your father, your friends, your brothers, or the twice-born? (32)
"This man is known to be a leper, burdened by a multitude of worms; how did you, O lady of noble conduct, choose him and come to this inaccessible forest? (33)
Sūta said: Thus questioned by the wise son of the sage, Sudharmā,
filled with both grief and joy, explained everything to him.
Sudharma said: "In the country of Saurāṣṭra, there is a great and famous city named Devatā;
there my husband Somakānta indeed ruled his kingdom. (35)
He was arrogant, generous, brave, and possessed of firm prowess;
endowed with innumerable forces, he was the crusher of enemy kingdoms. || 36 ||
He was a performer of sacrifices, exceedingly handsome, illustrious, and a bringer of joy to his friends; he was a discerning judge of all affairs and an expert in the science of ethics.
O best of the twice-born, the king enjoyed his own kingdom for a long time, yet he has now reached this state as a result of the ripening of his past karma. || 38 ||
Accompanied by two ministers, he has come to this forest;
wandering behind him are those who say, "Give the kingdom to his son. (39)
Having come here from their two natures, which are accessible through subtle knowledge,
they both went to the forest with the king's permission for the sake of attaining the fruit.
"Here, rakshasas, pretas, spirits, beasts, and birds of various kinds terrify us; why do they not devour us? (41)
I do not know why they place me even at the forefront for the experience of suffering;
I see no end to this misery nor to the fruit of my evil deeds.
Though he partook of food that was pungent, bitter, sour, salty, sweet, and oily,
his relish for it was not as great as when he was surrounded by the twice-born.
Just as now, for the poor, even the digestion of what has been eaten— consisting of bulbs, roots, decoctions, sour fruits, and the like— is a great feast.
The power of the illustrious ones over food and its preparation was not such as it once was, for he used to lie upon a soft, divine, and delightful bed. 45.
Now, look at the reversal of time wherever you may be;
he whose auspicious and manifold fragrances once pervaded the quarters of the earth—(46)
Even the foul odor of one now smeared with pus and blood—who was once immersed in the ocean of bliss and surrounded by the wise—[is now perceived]. 47.
Now, surrounded by worms in this sea of suffering, how shall we cross this ocean of misery? I do not know, O descendant of Bhṛgu. 48.
Like a boat rescuing one sinking in the fathomless ocean, [it saves] one like a ship in the deep.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sudharmā and Acyavana," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 157 + 49 = 206.
Chapter Six, titled "Going to the Hermitage of Bhṛgu.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, Cyavana, the descendant of Bhrigu,
quickly took up his own water-filled jar.
Distressed by the suffering of another, he returned home in silence;
Bhrigu then questioned his son, who had been so long in returning.
Bhṛgu said:
"What unprecedented thing have you seen that you appear so startled? And why has this delay occurred? Tell me, my son, in my presence. (3)
The son said:
O sage, in the renowned country of Saurāṣṭra, in the city of Daivata,
there was a king known as Somakānta, whose eyes were like lotuses.
Having ruled for a long time, protecting his subjects with righteousness,
he, by the turn of fate, attained misfortune after having installed his son in the kingdom.
O father, accompanied by my wife Sudharmā, who carries out her husband’s commands,
I have come here along with these two ministers, Subala and Jñānagamya.
Afflicted with leprosy and infested with worms, wandering through an inaccessible lake,
he attained the state of having a thousand vaginas, just as Indra did before the sage Gautama.
"Where is that Sudharmā of beautiful limbs, and where is her husband, afflicted with wasting leprosy?"—
as I asked for his history, a moment passed.
My mind became deeply agitated by his compassionate words;
therefore, having filled my water-jar, I returned quickly. (9)
The son said:
He related to him everything that had been spoken by her;
and having heard that, Bhṛgu spoke again to his son Cyavana.
Bhṛgu said:
"O son! Go at my command and quickly bring them all here.
I shall witness their curiosity, or I shall show myself to them."
Sūta said:
Thus urged by his father, Cyavana, that ocean of compassion,
went to the region of the lake, eager to behold Sudharmā.
At that very moment, those two ministers, Subala and Jñānagamya, carrying loads of fruits and roots, arrived in the presence of the king.
Then that sage spoke to the beautiful-eyed Sudharmā:
"O lady of virtuous vows, my father summons you all to his hermitage."
Having heard those words, Sudharmā, overwhelmed with grief, immediately became alert, like a body when life returns. 15.
Having drunk that nectar of his words, the virtuous queen Sushila,
whose limbs were most beautiful and who possessed a twofold nature, departed.
Accompanied by her husband Somakānta and preceded by the sons of sages, she was like Śivā joined with Śiva, together with Gaṇeśa and Skanda. || 17 ||
Accompanied by Vācaspati at her head, she shone brightly in the middle of the path;
she reached the circle of Bhṛgu’s hermitage, which resounded with the chanting of mantras.
It was strewn with various flowering creepers and resounded with the cries of diverse birds;
there were cats, mongooses, hawks, elephants, cows, and peacocks.
Where serpents, birds, lions, and tigers sport together,
where the wind does not blow violently, and where the sun does not scorch intensely.
The cloud did not rain heavily, yet it rained according to his will;
filled with joy, they entered preceded by the son of the sage.
There, the king beheld that Bhṛgu, who was as resplendent as the sun and seated upon a tiger skin;
he bowed with joined palms to him, to his wife, and to the two attendants, and spoke.
The king said:
"O best of the twice-born! Today my blessings, as well as my accumulation of merit and my asceticism, have borne excellent fruit through the words uttered by you.
From birth, I have been completely purified; both my father and my mother have lived their lives well. (23)

O Lord of Sages! Even though this sight of you destroys the sins previously accumulated by me, it is nevertheless made to bear fruit through my stores of merit; it brings about future welfare and makes my birth pure throughout the three periods of time. 24.
O Lord of Sages, in the land of Saurāṣṭra, in the city named Devatā, you, whose gaze is never in vain, established a kingdom;
though afraid of sin, you, being wise in policy, performed worship of the twice-born, the gods, and others. (25)
"What is this sudden misfortune that has appeared before me—so fierce and so terrible—that it has brought me to such a wretched state? I know not even a single remedy for it. (26)
Stratagems employed by others lead to ruin, yet I seek the very stratagem devised by you;
for even innate enmities come to an end in the absence of hostility, and I have sought refuge at your hermitage.
Sūta said: Having heard these words of his, Bhṛgu, filled with compassion and firm in his vows, looked upon that beloved of Soma with meditation and spoke.
Bhṛgu said:
"O King, I shall tell you a remedy; you ought not to worry.
For living beings who come to my hermitage do not experience suffering. (29)
O best of kings, I shall also describe to you that evil deed committed in another birth by which you have reached this state; I will tell it to you now.
"Let all those who have been hungry for a long time take their meal;
they have gone from forest to forest, being exceedingly weary and with faces full of exhaustion. (31)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, he bathed him after first anointing him with excellent oil,
and fed him many times with foods possessing the six flavors.
Having rested, they too, well-adorned and having arrived by the command of the eminent sage Bhṛgu of immeasurable splendor, partook of the meal. || 33 ||
Having abandoned their insurmountable anxieties, they slept on a soft bed prepared by the sage,
as if they had already attained their own kingdom.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Bhṛgu’s Journey to the Hermitage," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 6 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 206 + 34 = 240.
Chapter Seven, titled "The Narration of the Previous Birth of Somakānta," ends here.
The Sages said:
Having gone there, what did King Somakānta do at that time?
Or what means was suggested by Bhṛgu, the knower of all things? || 1 ||
O best of the twice-born, tell us this story;
we do not reach satiety while listening, for we drink the nectar of your words.
Sūta said:
O highly fortunate ones, you have asked well; you are indeed oceans of knowledge.
O twice-born ones, neither a listener nor a speaker ever reaches the end of this narrative.
If a disciple reads a book while it is being written, or even steals it, or asks questions when the teacher has not been asked, [he incurs a fault]. (4)
Both of them are seen in the world as mute and deaf, O best of the twice-born.
Listen, for I shall now relate the story of the destruction of Somaka.
When that night had passed and the lord of day had thus risen,
that best of the Bhrigus performed his bath, the twilight rites, his recitations, and the fire-oblation.
When the king had bathed, performed his prayers, and was united with his wife in her natural state,
[the sage] began to relate to him the story of his previous birth.
Bhṛgu said:
In the beautiful city of Kolhāra, near the Vindhya mountains,
there lived a Vaiśya of great wealth who was renowned as Citrūpa.
His wife was renowned by the name Subhagā, Sulocanā;
she was virtuous, charitable, and a devoted woman who followed her husband’s word.
O best of kings, you attained the state of being her son in a previous birth;
those two, as prompted by the twice-born, gave you the name Kāmada.
Your parents, having reached the time of old age, showed you excessive affection and indulgence day and night while you were alone.
They performed the marriage ceremony with wealth, auspicious rites, and festive celebrations;
she was a deer-eyed woman of delicate limbs, renowned by the name Kuṭumbinī.
Always devoted to you, dear to the twice-born, the gods, and guests, she was a woman most beautiful among women, a jewel among womankind. (13)
She gave herself the meaningful name Kuṭumbinī;
with seven sons and five daughters, was she not indeed the beloved of the Five-Arrowed One? (14)
Then, after a long time had passed, your father met his death;
your virtuous mother was cremated with him and ascended to heaven.
Then you, along with your circle of friends, squandered that great wealth;
it was taken away, lost, consumed, and the fortune went to ruin.
Out of anxiety, your lawful wife rejected you most harshly;
yet her words were not heeded, and consequently, you sold the house.
She has gone with her children to her father's house, having been permitted by you—
though you are a thorn to the lineage— for the sake of nourishing her offspring, except for you.
Then, having become arrogant like a drunkard,
he became an evildoer in the city, like an elephant in rut.

A thief of others' property, a paramour among women, a robber in villages, a bringer of harm to the people, a hero in gambling, the very essence of a multitude of vices, one whose pastime is violence—a hero who is weak in strength. (20)

From whichever people were satisfied by their association with happiness, he took much wealth from them—from deposits made by his father, from friends, and from whatever was present in the city under some pretext. || 21 ||
"You have surely sworn false oaths, serving as witnesses for untruthful matters among women"—
thus did all the people become greatly terrified, as if from the serpent of fierce power dwelling within their own homes.
Having become like a *gokṣūraka* plant that has lost its companion when milk is poured upon it,
those people, having obtained the king's permission, extinguished you from that city.
Dwelling in the forest, you are a slayer of many creatures; you constantly slaughter women, children, and the elderly.
Yet, upon seeing a great crowd, you flee like a wolf or a deer at the sight of a lion.
Having killed fish, cranes, cranes, wild cocks, wolves, deer, monkeys, cuckoos, swords, lizards, and rabbits, you have needlessly nourished your own body with sin. 25.
Having driven out lions, tigers, and jackals from the mountain caves,
he gathered together various extremely formidable thieves scattered in many places.
With wood, clods of earth, and stones, you constructed an excellent house,
vast with an extent of one krośa, adorned with various wonders.
Terrified by his father, that wife was sent away along with the children to your home,
which is accessible from both the royal palace and the common folk.
Adorned with various ornaments and garments, even those children shone with splendor like celestial nymphs; and you, accompanied by your son, likewise shone brightly.
And you, having repeatedly struck down wretched people on the road, have returned home;
accompanied by thieves along with their children and women, you shine like a king who has gone there.
Perhaps that learned Brahmin, the famous Guṇavardhana,
was seen by you alone on the road at midday.
Having taken that brahmin’s right hand, you held him;
trembling, he recognized your intent because of that assault.
Thinking you were his own death, he fainted out of a desire for life; yet, awakening you with exceedingly compassionate words accompanied by reasoned arguments, he spoke to you.
Guṇavardhana said:
"Having become wealthy and fortunate, how can you wish to kill me—a twice-born man, the husband of a newlywed bride, peaceful and innocent? (34)
Abandoning the latent tendencies of a corrupt intellect, direct your mind toward the true dharmas;
my first beloved has departed, and another, even more lovely, has been attained. (35)
She was of noble conduct, most magnanimous, virtuous, and a mine of all good qualities;
she acted for the sake of discharging her debt to the ancestors and for the increase of the lineage of dharma.
It was performed with great effort by one desiring the dharma of the householder's life;
for without me, or without that [dharma], your births would indeed be in vain.
"Indeed, you are my father and I am your son;
for in the sacred scriptures, one who bestows life and protects from fear is declared to be a father."
For even bandits protect a twice-born man who has come to them for refuge;
you ought not to consume me, a worthy and protective twice-born man who has sought your shelter. 39.
Even if you were to enter the hells for a thousand eons, all these people—wives, sons, friends, and kinsmen—would still be the ones to enjoy [the fruits of your merit]. 40.
These are not partakers of evil; they are happy ones who have been deceived by you. I cannot conceive how many births it will take before you shall experience the fruit of your sin.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Previous Birth of Somakānta," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.

Chapter Eight, titled "The Warding Off of Various Birds," Bhṛgu said:
Having heard these words spoken by him, who was repeatedly succumbing to exhaustion,
your heart did not break, even though it was filled with compassion.
What indeed has Brahmā fashioned from you that is more solid than a diamond, since you slaughter many creatures and thousands of men? || 2 ||
Then you spoke those words, as cruel as Death itself, with a mind that had reached extreme harshness, like that of an ungrateful person.
The thief said:
"O Brahmin! What is the use of these multitudes of words directed at me in vain?
It is like pouring water into an inverted jar—there is no learning for one who does not listen."
O fool! Where is this mind of mine, and where is this instruction of yours?
Just as the contemplation of reality is of no use to a bee, it does not please me at present. || 5 ||
Attached to wealth, there is no consideration whatsoever for father or kinsmen;
even for one afflicted by lust, neither fear nor shame exists.
Have you seen purity in a crow, truth in a gambler, fortitude in a eunuch, the quelling of desire in a woman, or forbearance in a serpent? (7)
"By the decree of the Creator and through the turn of fate, you have been entrusted to me while I am free from worldly affairs; therefore, I shall never let you go."
Bhṛgu said:
Having spoken thus, he took a sharpened sword in his right hand and then severed his head,
as a cat seizes a mouse.
In this way, it is impossible for you to calculate the number of those killings of Brahmins, especially the killings of women, children, the elderly, and other living beings. 10.
"O Kāmandaka! Since you have become a distributor of the many sins of others, therefore, after a long time has passed, old age has come upon you. (11)
Then, as he sat down, there arose phlegm, exhaustion, perspiration, hiccup, or trembling; there was also drowsiness, yet it did not occur while he was fast asleep.
Then his sons, female slaves, servants, friends, children, grandsons, and even his kinsmen showed him disrespect. (13)
Only one trustworthy man, who was skilled in secrets and possessed irresistible movement, was seen there; and that brahmin too had been sent by you. (14)
In order to bring all those sages dwelling in the forest together,
they too have assembled at the word of the twice-born, solely out of fear of you.
Having paid them homage, he said to them, "Accept gifts from me.
They replied, "We do not accept gifts from one who has fallen."
Sin is transmitted from officiating at sacrifices, teaching, matrimonial alliance, social intercourse, conversation, as well as from traveling, sitting, and eating together with another. (17)
Having spoken thus and returned to their own hermitage,
they all bathed with their clothes on and then recited the Pāvamānī hymns.
Then, O Kāmandakī, a profound remorse arose in my mind because of this illness, the abandonment by my own kinsmen, and the desertion by the brahmins. (19)
Seeing his own vast wealth, consisting of gold, jewels, and other treasures, his mind became resolute regarding the restoration of the ruined temple. || 20 ||
Then, the auspicious, beginningless, and supreme form of Gaṇeśa was described by the twice-born as being situated in a small, dilapidated temple within the forest.
Then [he built] a very extensive and long [hall], endowed with four archways,
having four gates, most beautiful, and adorned with four pinnacles.
It was adorned with various pillars, surrounded by diverse altars,
and its beautiful courtyard was inlaid with pearls, corals, gems, and other precious things.
It was filled with various flowering trees and abounded with various fruit-bearing trees;
it was adorned on all four sides by beautiful water-filled ponds.
The wealth of one who has built a palace has been spent upon it;
moreover, some was taken away by his wife, his son, his friends, and his kinsmen.
Then, not long thereafter, you met your death;
bound by the messengers of Yama, you were severely beaten with lashes of the whip.
With his entire body pierced by thorns and even crushed upon a rock, he was submerged in a terrible hell, a mire of pus and blood. (27)
Thus led by those messengers into the presence of Citragupta and Yama, he is questioned by Yama: "What merit, or rather, what sin shall you experience?"
"You spoke of merit, O son of the Sun, saying, 'I shall enjoy it first.
Therefore, you have been appointed to the sovereignty over the land of Saurāṣṭra. (29)
Thus have I related to you my former birth, which was characterized by evil deeds, out of compassion for one who has sought refuge and by relying on the power of my asceticism. 30.
By building the Kāntaprāsāda, King Somaka became known as Kānta;
you shine with a lovelier splendor than your beloved wife, just as the moon shines with its radiance.
Sūta said:
Having heard what was spoken by Bhṛgu, that lowest of kings, the beloved of Soma, fell into doubt regarding those words and became as motionless as a stone. || 32 ||

Since he held a doubt regarding the words of Bhṛgu—who was an ascetic and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, and who knew the past, the future, and the present—[he questioned him]. || 33 ||
In a mere instant, birds of various colors and forms emerged violently from his body and then devoured the king.
Flying up again and again with their swift-moving beaks, they bit the royal beast with their firm jaws;
tearing off the flesh again and again, they devoured it in the presence of the sage.
Then, his body overcome with extreme grief, he returned once more for refuge and spoke in a piteous voice to Bhṛgu, the treasure-house of knowledge and austerity.
The king said:
"In your forest, there is indeed no mutual fear among those who are natural enemies;
how is it that these [beasts] are killing me, who am already dead, right before your eyes? (37)
O Sage, bestower of fearlessness upon all beings, now deliver me—who am devoted to your feet, wretched, afflicted by leprosy, and have come for refuge. 38.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed, Bhṛgu, who is compassionate toward the distressed, spoke to him again:
"O King! Because of doubt regarding my words, you have experienced this. (39)
"I shall tell you the remedy; be at ease for a moment, O King.
By my mere utterance of 'Hum', these twice-born ones will depart. (40)
Sūta said:
Having heard the twice-born man's sound of "huṃ," the other brahmins then vanished;
and the king, together with his wife and ministers, was filled with joy.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Warding Off of Various Birds," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.

Chapter Nine, titled "The Exposition of Advice to the King," ends.
Sūta said:
Then Bhṛgu, having meditated for a moment and seeing that [the king] was utterly overwhelmed by the suffering born of his own past karma, spoke again to that monarch.
Bhṛgu said:
Where indeed are those heaps of sins, and where are the means I have described? Nevertheless, I shall tell you one means for the destruction of evil.
If you listen to this Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa with haste, then at that very moment you shall be liberated from the ocean of suffering; there is no doubt about this.
Having spoken thus and having recited the excellent eight-hundred names of Gaṇeśa,
he then consecrated the water with mantras and sprinkled it upon the king.
As soon as that water was sprinkled by him, a small creature with a black face emerged from his nostril; it reached the ground and grew instantly.
He was seven palm trees in height, terrifying with his gaping mouth,
possessing a formidable tongue, blood-red eyes, long arms, and matted hair.
Vomiting fire from his mouth and, in an instant, pus and blood,
he brought blindness to eyes like another, second darkness.
Beholding that wondrous creature, who filled the ten directions with the sound of his snapping jaws, all the inhabitants of that hermitage fled.
That best of the twice-born, though he was himself learned, questioned that man in his presence: "Who are you? What is your name? Tell it to me. (9)
Being thus questioned by the twice-born, he replied to that sage:
"Residing within the bodies of all living beings, I am known by the name Pāpapuruṣa (the Man of Sin)."
"By the sprinkling of water with your mantra, I have emerged from the king's body;
tormented by hunger, I seek food—give it to me, for I am great, if not, [then I shall devour you]. (11)
"O Sage, O beloved of Soma, I shall devour the worlds before your very eyes!
Tell me of a delightful dwelling for one who has been expelled from here. (12)
Then, having come outside, the sage spoke to him again:
"Dwell in this hollow of the straight but tasteless mango tree."
"Eat the fallen leaves by my command;
otherwise, O lowest of men, I shall reduce you to ashes, for my word cannot be false."
Sūta said:
At the conclusion of those words of the sage, he touched that dry tree;
O twice-born ones, by the mere touch of him, the tree was reduced to ashes. 15.
Fearing the sight of the sage, he dissolved into those ashes;
once he had vanished therein, the sage spoke again to the moon.
Bhṛgu said:
"O best of kings, whatever merit has arisen for you from hearing the Purāṇas, let this fallen tree rise up again as soon as that [merit] is exhausted. (17)
Therefore, O King, perform that [rite] day by day upon these very ashes;
as this tree grows, you shall become free from sin.
The king said:
O Brahmin, where can that Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa be found, which has never been seen nor heard before? Or who, O Sage, is its expounder? (19)
The sage said: This Purāṇa, which destroys all sins, was formerly told by Brahmā to the wise Vedavyāsa, and from Vyāsa it has been learned by me.
"I shall tell you that; perform your bath at the sacred ford," and "I shall listen to the Purāṇa"—make such a formal resolve (saṅkalpa), O observer of noble vows. (21)
Sūta said: Having been urged by Bhṛgu, Somakānta bathed in the highly renowned Bhṛgutīrtha and,
filled with joy, then performed his formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
"From this day forward, I shall listen to that Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa.
As soon as this resolve was made, the king shone forth, free from all ailment.
By the grace of Bhṛgu, the king was freed from his blood and released from the wounds of the worms;
taking him with him, the astonished and joyful Bhṛgu departed.
Having sat upon his own seat, he caused a seat to be offered to him;
once seated, that best of kings, possessing divine luster, spoke to him.
The King said:
"By your grace, all my most grievous afflictions have vanished by mere thought.
Tell me this entire, wondrous ancient account of the elephant-faced one."
Bhagurū said:
Listen attentively; I shall relate that Purāṇa, by the mere range of whose hearing one attains an infinite accumulation of merit. 27.
Such an understanding arises in virtuous people, but not otherwise for evildoers;
by the mere hearing of which, even those [sins] acquired over seven lifetimes—28—
Whether small, dry, half-formed, or large, even great sins go to dissolution in that very instant through the grace of Gaṇeśa. || 29 ||
Of the immutable, the immeasurable, the devoid of qualities, the formless, who cannot be defined by mind or speech, and whose nature is absolute bliss. || 30 ||
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, do not know His true nature,
nor is the thousand-faced one capable of describing His majesty.
O best of kings, even though I am possessed of specialized knowledge, I shall speak as I have previously heard that most meritorious Purāṇa. 32.
Distressed by grief over the destruction of his sacrifice, Dakṣa heard from Mudgala about Vyāsa, who possessed knowledge beyond the senses and was endowed with immeasurable splendor.
O King, he whose devotion is firm toward Gaṇeśa, the bestower of all perfections, should hear this constantly; it must not be spoken to anyone other than such a person. 34.
If everyone were to practice the service of Vighnarāja, where then would the multitudes of obstacles sport at their ease? (35)
Who indeed would not experience various sorrows born of separation?
Vyāsa, the knower of the past, the present, and the future, spoke this long ago. (36)

Those devoid of knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, those who have abandoned the study of the Vedas, those lacking the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life, and those who cause the intermixture of castes; 37.
Having observed that people in the Kali age were crooked and doers of evil,

From those [Mahāpurāṇas], people understood the meanings of the Upapurāṇas;

Chapter Ten, titled "Description of Vyāsa’s Question," ends here.
Bhṛgu said:
The great sage Pārāśarya, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa, was a knower of the past and the future and a master of the true meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras. || 1 ||
Having divided the Veda into four parts for the sake of accomplishing the knowledge of its meaning, he,
out of pride in his learning, began to compose the Purāṇa.
In the beginning, he did not perform any means for the completion [of his work], nor did he offer obeisance to Gaṇeśa, nor even any praise of him anywhere. (3)
Then, being overwhelmed by obstacles, he could not remember any purpose whatsoever;
there was only delusion for him on both the worldly and the supra-worldly paths.
Even for one who is omniscient, and who explains the Vedic scriptures, regarding rites that are obligatory, occasional, or optional, whether they be Śrauta or Smārta; (5)
Like a king of serpents whose power has been neutralized by herbs and mantras,
he was utterly paralyzed within himself and could not perceive the cause of that state.
Then the sage Pārāśara, his heart overcome with wonder and filled with shame, went with reverence to Satyaloka to question Dhātṛ.
Having paid homage to the hosts of gods, the divine sages, and the lotus-seated Brahmā,
he sat upon a beautiful seat offered by Brahmā after having been honored by him.
The great sage Pārāśarya touched his feet with his hand,
and bowing down out of affection, he began to question Brahmā.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahmin, this is indeed a marvel; what has come upon me through destiny?
My intellect has been inspired to compose the Purāṇas, which contain the meaning of the Vedas.
He beheld all the worlds in the Kali age— devoid of knowledge and right conduct, paralyzed by ritualistic formalism, atheistic, and revilers of the Vedas.
"From my words they shall know both what is prescribed and what is forbidden;
yet my own knowledge has departed from me, and I have become as if deluded and intoxicated. (12)
I see no cause for that, nor does any manifestation arise;
I have come to you to ask about both its cause and the cause of its manifestation.
To whom else shall I go for refuge except you, O Four-faced One?
You are omniscient and the creator of all; dispel my delusion. 14.
O Brahmin, tell me the cause of my delusion, even though I am devoted to eternal conduct and am one whose nature is manifold like Nārāyaṇa, and who is indeed omniscient.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words and reflected upon them, the lotus-seated Brahmā,
smiling as if in wonder, spoke to the prostrate sage.
Brahmā said:
"Ah, I shall indeed tell you of the subtle course of actions;
having reflected thoroughly, one must perform that action which is either virtuous or otherwise. (17)
When a man acts in one way, the result turns out otherwise;
for through intellect, reasoning, and even sincerity, heavy matters may become light.
A wise person should accomplish his tasks neither out of pride nor out of envy;
for it was through pride that the Lord of Birds attained the state of being a vehicle. || 19 ||
Everything was destroyed by the son of Ambikā because of envy;
and in the past, the entire warrior class (kṣatra) was exterminated by Rāma for the very same reason—envy.
He who is the god without beginning or end, the creator of the world, composed of the world,
the supporter of the world, the sustainer of the world, both being and non-being, manifest and imperishable.
He who is able to act, to act otherwise, and to act at all times—
he whose command is eternally subject to the will of the gods, headed by Indra.
I, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Sūrya, Agni, Varuṇa, and the others—[he is] the remover of obstacles for his devotees and the creator of obstacles for others. 23.
In that situation, you displayed pride by relying on the power of your own learning;
out of the conceit of omniscience, you did not offer him honor. (24)
O Vyāsa, O sinless one, you did not perform the remembrance of Gaṇeśa at the beginning of this work, nor likewise that of another; therefore, this delusion has arisen in you.
At the commencement of all undertakings, or during entry and departure,
whether in matters pertaining to the Vedas, the Smṛtis, or worldly affairs, he who is remembered brings about the absence of obstacles.

Go with devotion, my child, for refuge to him whom those who perceive the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures call supreme bliss, whom they call the supreme goal, and whom they call the supreme Brahman— the one with the face of an elephant.
If the Blessed One is pleased, he will fulfill your desire;
if not, you shall not attain your wish even in a thousand years.
Vyāsa said: Who is this Gaṇeśa, what is his form to be known, and how is that [known]? To whom was he formerly pleased, O Four-faced One? (29)
How many incarnations are there, and what specific deeds were performed in each?
By whom was he worshipped previously, and at what time was he remembered? || 30 ||
O Great-grandfather, O ocean of compassion, explain all of this to me in great detail as I ask you with a distracted mind.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Questions," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.

Chapter Eleven, titled "The Discourse on Mantras," ends here.
Bhṛgu said:
Then the four-faced one, having been thus questioned and desiring to speak, replied to him:
"I shall tell you everything in due order after reflecting extensively upon the mantras of Gaṇeśa. || 1 ||
Brahmā said:
"O Sage, the mantras of the high-souled Gaṇeśa are indeed infinite;
nevertheless, I shall describe to you the worship of him who swiftly bestows success."
Seventy million great mantras reside in the scriptures of Gaṇeśa; O Sage, Śiva knows their secret, and I know it only in part. (3)
Among them, the excellence of the six-syllabled and the single-syllabled [mantras] is found;
by the mere remembrance of which, all accomplishment comes into one's hand. (4)
O Sage, those by whose worship one indeed becomes liberated while living are truly blessed;
they are worthy of honor and should be saluted even by the gods. 5.
Through worship of whom the Siddhas perform service,
they become omniscient, capable of moving according to their will, and assume various forms.
Those who perform devotion to Gaṇeśa with sincere feeling,
yet possess not even a fraction of such devotion, their birth is in vain.
O Gajanana, those who turn their faces away from you do not look upon your face;
by the mere sight of them, obstacles shall arise at every step. 8.
Obstacles are pacified by the sight of his devotee;
and all beings, both stationary and moving, pay him homage. 9.
Therefore, I shall proclaim to you the auspicious single-syllable mantra;
by the mere performance of it, you will attain your desire. 10.
I shall proclaim the performance [of the rite] as it was told to me by Śambhu:
having bathed and put on clean garments, a man, being pure, [should proceed]. (11)
Having prepared his seat with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass, the wise practitioner,
seated upon it, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as well as the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana).
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the internal and external matrices (mātṛkā) without sloth,
and having then performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should mutter the root mantra within the heart.
One should perform the twilight mantra-observance as prescribed in the Āgamas according to the rules, having meditated with an unwavering mind upon the Lord from head to foot. 14.
With a well-composed mind, one should worship him with mental offerings;
thereafter, one should perform recitation according to one's ability, following the path of preliminary purification (puraścaraṇa). || 15 ||
One should remain intent on recitation for as long as Gajānana is favorable and until he reveals his true form to grant the boon. || 16 ||
Bhṛgu said: Having spoken thus to the sage and having observed an auspicious day, Brahmā [bestowed] the single-syllabled king of mantras, the one-syllabled mantra of Gaṇeśa.
Then, being greatly agitated, he taught everything to that best of sages.
Brahmā said:
"He who resembles ten million suns has arrived to grant a boon. (18)
When you behold that God, then steady your mind;
O Gajānana, remain forever established within my very heart. 19.
"Choose a boon from him; he will grant it to you without doubt.
While that god resides within your heart, you shall attain divine knowledge. (20)
"O child, having abandoned deep-seated delusion, you shall know the past, the future, and the present in their entirety; you shall compose various treatises. 21.
Vyāsa said:
"O Father, my delusion has departed because of your instruction;
O Grandfather, by your command I shall perform the observance."
Brahmā said: O Lord,
perform your practice in a solitary and secluded place, free from causes of distraction,
while recollecting the elephant-faced one.
The king of mantras must not be spoken to one who is an atheist, a reviler, cruel, immoral, wicked, or deceitful—even if such a person has come for refuge. 24.
Reveal it to one who is firm in devotion, full of faith, humble, a proponent of the Vedas, possessed of longing, free from cruelty, and learned in the scriptures. || 25 ||
If this king of mantras is revealed to one who should not reveal it, it causes ten preceding and ten succeeding generations to fall into the hells. 26.
Whoever recites this with devotion shall obtain his desired fruit;
he shall be endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain. || 27 ||
By the power of Ekadanta, having attained perfectly pure knowledge and having enjoyed all pleasures here in this world, one shall attain liberation in the end.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narration of Mantras," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 11 ||
