Chapter Twelve, named "The Vision of Gajānana," Sūta said:
Having heard these words issued from the mouth of Brahmā,
the sage, filled with great joy, questioned him again.
Vyāsa said:
"I have attained focused attention by drinking the nectar of your speech;
now, O father, I wish to hear this king of mantras."
Who recited it, and how did he attain perfection from Gajānana?
Cut through this doubt of mine; other than you, there is no guru for me. (3)
Bhṛgu said:
O Vyāsa, best of kings, having been thus questioned by the sage, Brahmā, the most excellent of speakers, spoke with compassion to him who was bowed down in humility. 4.
Brahmā said: Excellent, excellent! You have asked well; you are indeed meritorious now.
For, O Brāhmaṇa, those who lack merit find no delight in hearing this discourse.
I shall now fully explain this path of worship to you;
for there is nothing that should be concealed from a disciple who is affectionate and preeminent in wisdom. (6)
The Blessed One, the Leader of the Gaṇas, has been described as having the form of the syllable Oṃ;
just as this Vināyaka is worshipped in all undertakings.
If he does not create an obstacle for those who possess desire-free intentions, then [the mantras] are joined with the seed-syllable Oṃ and endowed with the sprouts of the syllable Oṃ. 8.
All mantras proclaimed in every scripture, and whatever others are fruitless, as well as the existent and non-existent, the manifest and the unmanifest—all this is indeed Gaṇanāyaka. 9.
Thus all the gods, siddhas, munis, rākṣasas, kinnaras, gandharvas, cāraṇas, nāgas, yakṣas, guhyakas, and mānavas [were present]. 10.
All beings, both moving and unmoving, are the devotees of Gaṇeśa;
therefore, indeed, nothing exists that is superior to Gaṇeśa.
Now I shall relate an ancient story. 11.
Just as this elephant-faced deity was once satisfied by the recitation of the king of mantras, so too, by the turn of fate, when the time of universal dissolution had arrived— (12)
The mountains, shattered by the winds, have fallen in every direction;
the twelve suns scorch the earth, having dried up the great waters.
The great fire, garlanded with flames, burns everything;
the great clouds of the dissolution rain down water on all sides. 14.
O best of the twice-born, with torrents resembling the trunks of elephants,
both the oceans and the rivers transgress their boundaries.
In this way, all things indeed perish, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings;
thus, when this transformation consisting of illusion has perished, that elephant-faced one [remains]. || 16 ||
Having assumed a form subtler than the subtlest atoms, he remained stationed somewhere;
then, after a vast period of time had passed, the world was shrouded in blinding darkness.
Furthermore, the single-syllabled Brahman was born endowed with sound;
moreover, when that form consisting of modification remained permeated by sound. || 18 ||
Having undergone a transformation of Māyā, he himself became the elephant-faced one;
and from that very source, the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas were produced. 19.
From that, the three were born: Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara as well;
by me all this was fashioned—the triple world with its moving and unmoving beings. || 20 ||
Then, deluded by his māyā, those three gods wandered about,
eager to see and question him who was their own progenitor.
O Sage, out of a desire to know what task was to be performed by these [gods],
he first looked upward toward the twenty-one heavens.
By that [power], they went crosswise through the atmosphere and downward into the netherworld;
not having seen the Supreme Self, they then practiced austerities most intensely.
Subsisting on nothing and devoted to silent recitation for a thousand divine years, they became exhausted and fell into despair; thereafter, they returned once more to the earth.
Searching, they went forth to see the forests and groves,
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the peaks, and even the caves.
Then those gods beheld a vast reservoir of water,
filled with various aquatic creatures, trees, and diverse kinds of birds.
The cluster of lotuses was made resonant by cranes, ruddy geese, swans, and also by kāraṇḍava ducks,
all of whom were intent on feeding on pieces of lotus stalks.
Having bathed and rested on its bank, they crossed over and proceeded toward that great reservoir of water, which was filled with various waves. || 28 ||
They gazed upon that most difficult-to-cross [ocean], teeming with large fish and crocodiles,
extremely hard to behold, and resembling the fire of universal destruction.
O Sage, they beheld before them a mass of splendor resembling ten million suns;
yet at the very end, their vision was stolen by that brilliance, and they fell into deep reflection.
Then, emerging from the midst of that splendor by way of the path of the sky,
they were exhausted by hunger and thirst, sighing again and again.
While they were censuring and cursing him, becoming filled with trepidation,
the Lord of the World, the knower of all things, was then overcome with great compassion.
He revealed to them a form that delighted the mind and the eyes,
whose beauty of the toenails surpassed the filaments of a red lotus.
By the radiance of his red garments, he surpassed the orb of the sun at twilight;
by the networks of light from his waist-belt, he outshone the peak of Mount Meru.
His four beautiful arms were adorned with a sword, a shield, a bow, and a spear;
his lotus-face possessed a fine nose, and its splendor surpassed that of the full moon.
Day and night endowed with radiance, with beautiful eyes like lotuses,
and with a head resplendent with a crown that surpassed the splendor of many suns.
His upper garment surpassed the splendor of the sky marked by various stars,
and he was adorned with a single tusk that excelled the beauty of a boar’s tusk.
O Sage, upon seeing the beautiful lotus that struck fear into the guardians of the quarters such as Airāvata,
they suddenly bowed with joy to the Lord;
then, touching his lotus feet, they began to offer praise.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Vision of Gajānana," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 420 + 38 = 458.
Chapter Thirteen, titled "Description of the Praise of Brahmā," Vyāsa said:
How did these—Pañcāsya, Caturāsya, and Sahasramastaka—praise the elephant-faced god who grants boons? || 1 ||
Brahmā said:
Having attained clarity of intellect through the glance of the compassionate side-long look of Vighneśa, who was inclined toward grace,
those Keśas then praised him.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara said:

We worship Gaṇeśa, who is unborn, free from conceptual construction, formless, one, devoid of worldly joy, non-dual, full of bliss, supreme, beyond qualities, without distinction, effortless, and the very embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. 3.

May we worship Gaṇeśa, who transcends all qualities, who is primordial, whose nature is consciousness and bliss, who illumines consciousness, who is omnipresent, accessible through knowledge, the object of meditation for sages, whose form is like space, the Supreme Lord, and the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. 4.

I worship Gaṇeśa, the cause of the universe, whose nature is the knowledge of all causes; the beginning of the gods, the beginning of happiness, and the beginning of the ages; the all-pervading one, adored by the world, the lord of the gods, who is the supreme Brahman. 5.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, who is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman—the form of Brahmā through the yoga of passion (rajas), the knower of the Vedas, whose form is always to be meditated upon with the heart as being intent on his task, the creator of the world, the treasury of all knowledge. 6.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, who is eternally Viṣṇu in form, who always possesses the yoga of existence, who joyfully sports, who destroys the enemies of the gods, who protects the world, who assumes numerous incarnations, and who removes one's own ignorance. 7.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, who is the yogi of darkness, whose form is Rudra, who has three eyes, who sustains the world, who is the deliverer, the cause of knowledge, who always enlightens his own people through numerous scriptures, and whose nature is eternal night. 8.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, the great destroyer of darkness, the remover of people's ignorance, the essence of the three Vedas, the further shore of the Supreme Brahman, the source of the sages' knowledge, free from all transformation, and whose nature is eternally that of Brahman. 9.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, who is the very form of the moon; he satisfies the medicinal herbs with his own rays and the hosts of gods with his digits that flow with nectar; he removes the scorching heat of the sun’s rays, and he is the lord of the twice-born. 10.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, whose nature is light, who takes the form of space and wind, who is the cause of transformations and so forth, who consists of the elements of time and its divisions, whose nature comprises manifold actions and manifold powers, and who is eternally of the nature of power. 11.

We bow to Gaṇeśa, whose nature is primordial matter (pradhāna), whose form is the principle of the Great (mahat-tattva), who takes the form of earth and water, and the form of the lords of the directions; who is both unreal and real by nature, who is the cause of the universe, and who is eternally the form of the entire world. 12.
If a person fixes their mind upon Your pair of feet, they shall not suffer affliction from the multitude of obstacles;
for how could this person, standing within the vast, radiant orb of the sun, ever suffer the pain of darkness? 13.
We have been utterly deluded by the power of ignorance for many series of years, failing to attain Your feet;
now, through Your very grace, we have attained them—O Viśvambhara, protect us who have taken refuge in You forever, O Lord. 14.
Brahmā said:
O great sage, being thus praised, Gaṇeśa became pleased;
filled with supreme compassion, he proceeded to speak to them. 15.
The illustrious Gaṇeśa said: "For whose sake you have been afflicted, and for whose sake you have come here—I am pleased by this hymn of praise; choose from me whatever boon you desire."
And this hymn which has been composed by you of purified souls shall, by my command, be known as the "King of Hymns" (Stotrarāja). 17.

The wise person who, always pure and endowed with devotion, recites this at dawn after rising, or at the three junctions of the day, shall obtain sons, prosperity, and all desires; and at the time of death, he shall become one with the Supreme Brahman. 18.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of his, they—arising from the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas)—were satisfied and spoke to him out of regard for him. 19.
The three said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Cause of creation and destruction, if you are pleased, let there be unswerving devotion to your lotus feet for us. (20)
Furthermore, what should we do? May your lordship command us;
this alone is the boon desired by us, O elephant-faced one. (21)
Having heard their words, Gajānana spoke again:
"O highly fortunate ones, your devotion to me shall indeed become firm."
I shall describe various rites, one by one, so that you may cross over even great difficulties and so that your fame may spread. 23.
O Brahmā, become the creator of the universe, arising from the quality of passion (rajas);
O Viṣṇu, you who are all-pervading and the refuge of goodness (sattva), perform the protection of the world. 24.
"Take away, take away everything; you are born from the quality of darkness (tamas).
Brahmā said: "The Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and even the power of creation [are yours]. 25.
Out of respect for Mṛtyu, the Lord gave the Gaṇa-śoṇī Vidyā to Brahmā;
and to Viṣṇu, he granted through yoga the power to assume forms at will.
The Blessed One gave to Hara the one-syllable mantra, the six-syllable mantra, as well as all the Āgamas, and also the power of destruction.
Then, with a dejected mind, I joined my palms in reverence and spoke to that elephant-faced one, the lord of the three worlds, the teacher of the universe, and the granter of boons.
Brahmā said:
Just as one whose power has been seized does not speak what should or should not be spoken,
so too, having seen this manifold creation, one perceives nothing at all anywhere.
Or how could I venture to violate the command of the Lord?
How has this situation come upon me, such that I must choose between "this well" and "that pond"? 30.
Then the Lord Gajānana, having bestowed divine vision upon him,
spoke to Brahmā, who was an expert in the Vedas and Śāstras and was likewise distressed.
Gajanaṇa said: "O Lotus-born One, behold this very day the countless universes that are revolving within my body, both inside and out. (32)
Brahmā said:
Then, by the elephant-faced one, I was led into his own belly by the wind of his breath;
there the Creator Brahmā beheld numerous cosmic eggs.
They were like the fruits of the udumbara tree on a tree, or like gnats upon them.
There, with his supreme own splendor, he split one [of the eggs];
then, within it, he beheld the entire creation again and again.
And there he saw Brahmā and others— Viṣṇu, Indra, Prajāpati,
Śaṅkara, Bhāskara, Vāyu, the forests, the rivers, and the waters.
The oceans, yakṣas, gandharvas, apsarases, kinnaras, and uragas;
the ṛṣis, puṇyajanas, sādhyas, humans, mountains, and trees.
He created beings born from sprouts, those born from heat, those born from sweat, and those born from eggs;
as well as the earth and the twenty-one imperishable netherworlds.
I indeed beheld the entire universe, consisting of existence and non-existence, and all that is mobile and immobile.
Whatever egg I split apart, in each and every one of them I saw exactly the same thing;
having seen this delusion as before, I fell back into confusion and could not, in any way, find their end. (39)
The lotus-seated Brahmā was unable either to remain still or to move;
then, O Brahmin, having sat down, he praised the elephant-faced god.
Brahmā said:
I bow to the God, the God of gods, Gaṇeśa, for whom there is no numbering of universes within his body—
just as who could count the clouds in the sky, the stars in the ocean, the fish in the sea, or the pebbles on the shore?

O one whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the lords of the gods, I have no shame that I became deluded upon beholding your gracious countenance, a treasury of wisdom; for even liberation seems trivial, so what need is there to mention other matters? 42.
O Lord of the Gods, the entire mass of cosmic eggs, filled with manifold objects, is seen within your belly;
no other god besides you has the power to remain here or even to go forth from it, and thus I seek no other refuge. 43.
Then the blessed Lord Ananta, who has the face of an elephant, being pleased,
caused me, whose mind was distressed, to come out.
Through the passage of the nostrils, the Lord [brought forth] Hari following after me,
as well as Hara, who is characterized by tamas, joined together with Viṣṇu.
The omnipresent elephant-faced one drew them out from the cavity of his ear;
then both Hari and Hara lay comfortably upon his body.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Brahmā," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 13 ||
The total sum of the verses from the beginning is 458 + 46 = 504.
Chapter Fourteen, titled "Description of the Contemplation of Brahman," ends here.
The King said:
Then, having beheld thousands of cosmic eggs, what did Brahmā do?
And how did he carry out the creation after receiving the command from Gajānana? (1)
Bhṛgu said:
He became filled with pride, reflecting thus within himself:
"I know the Śāstras, the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and even the Āgamas. (2)
Endowed with both spiritual knowledge and empirical discernment, and possessing the power to curse or bestow grace,
he has beheld the cosmic eggs as well as the various arrangements of created beings.
"Now, for the act of creation, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for me"—
thus it was when everything had been prepared for the sake of creation by the one born from the lotus.
O King, thousands of various kinds of obstacles appeared;
most terrible, they stood surrounding Brahmā.
Just as bees intoxicated by flower nectar [cling to] a honeycomb,
so too were those with three eyes and five hands, whose mouths were like wells and whose palms were burning hot.
They had three legs and five snouts, or seven snouts and six legs;
they had ten faces and five feet, with palms for teeth and stomachs like those of wolves.
Those great beings were of diverse forms and could not be numbered;
Druhiṇa trembled upon hearing those various roars of theirs.
Some struck him with their fists, while others bowed down and praised him;
grasping him by his four topknots, they swung him about with great devotion.
All four of his faces laughed at him, and likewise others;
some reviled him, some offered praise, and some served him.
Some bound the illusory elephant, others again sought to release it;
while still others dragged it hither and thither in order to free it once more. || 11 ||
Some embraced him, while others kissed him like children;
one with a protruding belly and large hands, seizing him by his eight whiskers, danced about.
Thus, that Brahmā, being dependent on others and filled with anxiety and grief,
abandoned that swelling pride of creation which had taken root in his heart.
He fell into a deep swoon, despairing of his own life;
but when only a moment had passed, he remembered the All-pervading Lord in his mind and, as if weeping, implored the elephant-faced one out of compassion. 14.
Brahmā said:
My lifespan is not at all long, and my mind is attached to various births; I possess no pure knowledge of reality that can carry me across the ocean of existence.
O Teacher of all, having obtained birth upon this earth, when shall I, through devotion to you, attain supreme enjoyment, liberation, or unsurpassed bliss? 15.
"O All-pervading Lord, the devotee anointed with the nectar of your sidelong glance does not suffer;
let this shame belong to you alone, for death does not come to me, who am long-lived. (16)
Bhṛgu said: While he was thus making his request, he heard a voice uttered from the sky saying, "Perform penance. Thereupon, he requested her once again.
And those obstacles, having assumed various forms and possessing great power, vanished from the sky upon hearing that speech, leaving behind only that lotus-seated one.
Once liberated, the highly illustrious one born from the lotus reflected:
"How shall I perform great austerity without a mantra and without a sacred place? (19)
Thus, with his mind agitated, he wandered in the midst of the water,
meditating with undivided attention upon the healthy-faced Gajānana.
He was resplendent with a crown adorned with pearls and gems, auspicious,
his limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste, and his head glowing crimson with vermilion.
His neck shone with a string of pearls, he wore a serpent as a sacred thread,
and he was adorned with arm-ornaments fashioned from priceless gems.
It was adorned with a glittering emerald ring that seemed to throb,
and its great belly was beautiful with a large navel encircled by a massive serpent.
It was resplendent with a waist-band inlaid with various jewels and was draped in red garments shimmering with golden threads.
While he was thus meditating upon that supreme being, whose hand shone with the splendor of a radiant moon and gleaming teeth, there again came a voice from the sky: 25.
"Behold the banyan tree! Behold the beautiful banyan tree!"—hearing these words, Brahmā fell into reflection once again. (26)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Contemplation of Brahman," in the Section on Worship of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 504 + 26 = 530.
Chapter Fifteen, titled "Description of the Worship of Gajānana," ends here.
Bhṛgu said:
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke before Vyāsa:
"O beloved of Soma, I shall narrate that story; listen with respect. (1)
Brahmā said: Then, O best of sages, as I was wandering through the waters of the sky, I beheld a vast dream; there I saw a great banyan tree.
When all things mobile and immobile had perished due to great winds and heat,
only one great banyan tree remained, consisting of mere stalks.
Thus fallen into doubt, he placed the small boy upon its leaf—
the boy who had four arms, a beautiful crown, and was resplendent with two earrings.
Wearing a beautifully adorned necklace made of jewels and pearls around his neck, as well as a crescent moon ornament, red garments, and a waist-belt; || 5 ||
Seeing him thus—with a single tusk, the body of a man, the face of an elephant, and blazing with splendor—he reflected: "How indeed can there be such a child here?"
And with his lotus-like hand, that boy sprinkled water upon my head;
thereupon, filled with both anxiety and joy, I laughed aloud.
While I was laughing, that boy climbed down from the banyan tree;
having come to my lap, he spoke these sweet words. (8)
The boy said: "Though you are old, you are more childish than a child; you are of deluded intellect and are vainly beset by obstacles, preoccupied with thoughts of creation."
O Four-faced One, you who are constantly intent on penance while wandering in the midst of the ocean, I shall provide you with a means that removes all anxiety. 10.
I shall instruct you in this single-syllable mantra of mine;
recite it ten lakh times according to the path of preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
"Then I shall become manifest and grant supreme power.
Brahmā said:
"Having seen this wonderful dream, I indeed awoke."
And he lamented: "When shall I have a vision of the Supreme Lord?
Having seen him in a dream, I am now submerged in an ocean of bliss. (13)
Then, having bathed, he chanted the supreme mantra for many days,
standing on one foot upon a lotus while meditating on the elephant-faced god.
Having conquered his senses and subdued his appetite, remaining as steady as wood or stone,
he performed supreme and great penance for a thousand divine years.
Then, from my mouth, flames difficult to approach appeared;
by them, all living beings suffered most terrible pain.
Then Gajānana, seeing that firm resolve of mine, was pleased by my supreme devotion and appeared before me. 17.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, like the sacrificial fire garlanded with flames,
he seemed to burn the three worlds and to consume heaven and earth.
Holding a parasu and a lotus, adorned with divine illusions, the remover of all evils, the treasury of all beauty;
graced by the face of the lordly elephant, the fulfiller of the desires of devotees, and the sole destroyer of all obstacles for gods, men, and sages. 19.
O Vyāsa, O holy sage, upon seeing that mass of splendor, I trembled; my mind became deeply agitated, and I fell away from my recitation, falling into the utmost anxiety. (20)
Seeing her in such a state—with her eyes covered and her memory having vanished—the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa) then spoke quickly: || 21 ||
Gaṇeśa said: "Do not fear, O Lord of the World! It is I myself who have come, by whom that auspicious single-syllable mantra was instructed to you in a dream. (22)
"Success has been attained by you; I have come to grant a boon. Having assumed a gentle disposition, choose a boon, O observer of noble vows. (23)
Being pleased, I shall grant you whatever resides in your heart;
when I am pleased, all that will come to pass—of this there is no doubt.
The Sage said:
Having heard these pure words of the Lord of the Gaṇas, Brahmā rejoiced greatly as he gazed upon him;
bowing with all his heads to the Teacher of the moving and unmoving worlds, he spoke with a gracious heart: "My birth has become fruitful. (25)
Brahmā said: He who is never within the range of the Vedas, the scriptures, the knowers, the yogis, nor indeed of all the Upaniṣads; || 26 ||
Today, by means of his accumulations of merit, that omnipresent Lord has become manifest—
He who is without beginning or end, infinite, immeasurable, and even devoid of qualities.
O Lord of Gods, O Vighneśa, O Compassionate One, if you are pleased, grant us firm devotion to you, by which no suffering shall touch us. (28)
"Now, O Lord, if you are pleased with me, grant me the power to manifest various emanations, and let all obstacles be pacified. (29)
As soon as you are remembered by me, always accomplish every task;
at the end, grant me firm liberation and stainless knowledge.
Gajānana said:
"So be it; perform you a manifold and abundant creation.
By remembering me, all obstacles shall be destroyed from every side."
"By my grace, firm devotion and auspicious knowledge shall arise;
O Four-faced One, perform all your duties without hesitation."
The sage said:
Having thus obtained the boon, Brahmā worshipped that All-pervading Lord;
whatever he thought of in his mind, that very thing presented itself to him.
For the sake of worshipping Gaṇeśa, the God of gods, by his grace,
two maidens appeared at the time for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
It shines brilliantly with beautiful, clear eyes and faces,
adorned with various ornaments inlaid with many jewels.
To him, who was endowed with divine fragrance and adorned with divine garments and garlands,
the lotus-born Brahmā prepared [offerings] for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having performed the lustration ceremony with the inner core of a plantain tree, he offered a divine handful of flowers;
having praised him with the Thousand Names, he then performed a circumambulation. || 37 ||
Having been saluted, Śaṅkara requested of him, "Become the protector of the distressed.
Thus was he worshipped by that Brahmā, the supreme lord. 38.
Then the blessed Lord Gajānana, the remover of obstacles, being pleased,
took Siddhi and Buddhi with him and the omnipresent one vanished from sight.
With a serene mind, by the command and grace of the Supreme Lord, he caused the creation to proceed as before, extending over time. 40.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Gajānana," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 15 ||
Chapter Sixteen, titled "The Prayer of the Goddess," the King said:
Having heard the story of Gaṇeśa, joy arises in my heart.
Speak further again, O brahmin-sage; I am not satiated by this nectar of your discourse.
When the Blessed One Gaṇeśa, the Supreme Self, had vanished, how did Brahmā fashion the creation? Describe that, O Lord. (2)
O holy sage, I wish to hear in full detail that narrative which Brahmā related in the beginning to Vyāsa.
Bhṛgu said:
The Lord recounted to Vyāsa the majesty of the Siddhakṣetra;
I shall relate that to you in due order, as well as what he created there. 4.
In the beginning, that Brahmā mentally created seven sons and said to them, "Assist me in the work of creation; create [beings] according to your own respective intellects. (5)
Having heard those words, they resolved to perform austerities;
having practiced intense penance, they quickly attained the Supreme Brahman.
Then the Lord of Creatures fashioned seven other sons;
though they were endowed with supreme knowledge, they did not undertake the work of creation.
Then, having beheld Sanaka and the others, the lotus-seated Brahmā himself began [the creation]; from his mouth, he emitted the Brahmins and Agni.
From his arms he created the other three castes; from his heart, the moon;
from his eyes, the sun; and from his ears, the wind and the vital breath.
Likewise, he fashioned the intermediate space from his navel, the heavens from his head, the earth from his feet, and the directions from his ears; thus he created the other worlds.
Whatever else there is in the universe, high and low, both stationary and moving—
the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the grasses, shrubs, and trees— [all these were created by him].
Then, after several days had passed, O best of sages,
two great asuras were born from the ear of the sleeping Mahāviṣṇu.
Known by the names Madhu and Kaiṭabha, they were famous throughout the three worlds;
their faces were terrifying with protruding fangs, and they had tawny eyes and long noses.
Possessing massive bodies and great roars, they were as exceedingly lofty as two mountains; with voices like the thundering of clouds during the rainy season, they bellowed with intense pride.
With many words, the two wicked ones reviled him;
they censured the Brahmins, the gods, the sages, the virtuous, and the scriptures. || 15 ||
At the sound of those two, the earth trembled and Śeṣa as well;
the entire universe became agitated as the sky resounded with that noise.
Then, with eyes red with rage, the two were intent on devouring him;
thereupon he [sought refuge] with the boon-granting goddess who causes the delusion of Viṣṇu.
The lotus-seated Brahmā praised Nidrā, who had entered the eyes of Viṣṇu, for the destruction of Madhu and Kaiṭabha and for the awakening of Hari as well. 18.
Having learned through the grace of Gajānana that the slaughter of those two would come from the hand of Viṣṇu,
and having reflected thoroughly upon it, he was filled with both anxiety and joy.
Brahmā said:
You are Amṛta (Nectar), assuming the forms of Svāhā and Svadhā; you are Māyā, whose nature consists of half a measure;
you are the creator and the destroyer, the mother of all beings, both existent and non-existent; you alone are Śakti. 20.
She is the Veda, the musical note, the Night of Time (Kālarātri), without beginning or end, and imperishable;
she is the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the World, and the cause of the world's creation, preservation, and destruction.
O Pārvatī, you are Sāvitrī, as well as Sandhyā, Mahāmāyā, thirst, and hunger;
you are the power of all categories of existing things.
Your lord, the creator of the three worlds and the slayer of Daityas and Dānavas, Hari—who possesses both knowledge and realized wisdom—has his mind overcome by sleep. (23)
He by whom the world is created, protected, and even withdrawn—
even he is employed by you in the midst of the crises of your incarnations.
"Delude these two evil-minded Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
let knowledge be bestowed upon this [Vishnu], so that he may slay these two who are difficult to overcome. (25)
In a previous birth, I was propitiated by these two without weariness;
I granted them various boons, and they both became invulnerable to me.
I could not endure the many varied sounds they made;
desiring to kill me, they praised me with various kinds of hymns. (27)
Nevertheless, because of my wicked nature, I have not desisted from the intent to kill you;
therefore, O Goddess, I entreat you for the sake of awakening Viṣṇu. 28.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Prayer to the Goddess," in the Section on Worship of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 16 ||
Chapter Seventeen: The Instruction on Mantras.
As long as Viṣṇu remained standing, so long did heaven remain occupied by those two;
the abode of Indra, that of Yama, and likewise that of Kubera were all taken over.
Seeing them from all sides, the gods became intent on flight;
some fell down, some wandered about, others fainted, and still others stumbled.
Then, released from the sleep of the Goddess,
the Lord Hari comforted all those gods and engaged in battle with them.
They acted to prevent the assault upon all the gods,
as well as upon all the nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, the sages, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas.
There Hari shone resplendent, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace;
wearing a crown and earrings, he possessed the luster of a dense, dark-blue cloud.
Then that Blessed One, with great force, blew his conch shell;
by that great sound, he caused heaven and earth to tremble.
Upon hearing the sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, the hearts of those two were rent asunder;
then, agitated by fear, they spoke to one another.
The terrestrial sphere, the netherworld, and the twenty-one heavens were all thoroughly traversed by us;
yet at that time, this sound was not heard.
Since his heart, composed of the essence of adamant, caused the hearts of both to tremble,
he must therefore fight with a man of superior strength.
"Either for the sake of quelling the itch of battle, for victory or its opposite, we shall either slay this enemy or go to rebirth. (10)
Having thus made their resolve, the two said to Hari, who was eager for battle:
"O Supreme Person, you have been seen by us for the sake of quelling our itching for combat. (11)
"How do you attain such supremacy as to come within the range of our vision?
The Sage replied,
"Having heard these words of theirs, Viṣṭaraśravas spoke."
Hari said:
"O great Daityas, you have spoken rightly; fight with me as you desire, for no one indeed desires his own death by his own hand."
The two of them said:
"O Lord of Gods, you possess four arms; grant us a wrestling match.
The sage said:
Thus addressed by them, Hari, filled with joy, said, "So be it."
Having cast aside his weapons, the four-armed one fought with two;
they struck each other's heads with their heads, their shanks with their shanks, their elbows with their own elbows, and their arms with their very arms. || 15 ||
He struck his ankles with his own ankles, his waist with those two [knees], and his nose with his own nose;
he struck the region of the fists with his fists, and his back with his own back.
With slapping, pulling, and even with circular maneuvers of their arms,
the mutual combat then continued for a long time in that manner.
O Great Sage, five thousand years passed;
yet neither Śaśāṅka nor Hari, the Lord, was able to conquer them.
Thereupon, he assumed the form of a Gandharva, skilled in song.
Having gone into the midst of the forest, he performed beautiful lute music;
the deer, beasts of prey, world-protectors, gods, gandharvas, and rākṣasas [all listened]. 19.
Abandoning their respective duties, they all became intent upon him;
Śiva repeatedly heard his conversation on Kailāsa.
The destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes spoke to Nikumbha and Puṣpadanta:
"Bring quickly this man who is singing here in the forest."
Having gone and obtained his audience, the two said to him:
"Upon hearing the sound of your song, Śaṅkara was filled with joy. (22)
"O sinless one, the god summons you to hear your song.
Come quickly with us both; let us go into his presence. (23)
Having heard their words, the Gandharva, who was devoted to Hari,
went together with them to the place where the god Maheśvara was.
She beheld the beloved of Pārvatī, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, who is clothed in an elephant hide, and adorned with a garland of severed heads. 25.
She bowed to the Lord of the Universe on earth, who bears a mass of matted hair tawny like silver and wears a serpent as his sacred thread,
the destroyer of the suffering of those who prostrate before him.
Having raised up that Adhokṣaja with his own hand, Giriśa,
Śaṅkara, offered him a seat and paid him honor.
Then that Hari said: "Today my birth has become fruitful, since today I have obtained your vision, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. (28)
The Gandharva deity, intent on singing, gratified him with the sounds of the lute,
with sweet-toned words, and with various kinds of discourse.
Then Maheśvara affectionately embraced Skanda, Gaṇeśvara, the goddess Pārvatī, the gods, and the sages,
and he openly embraced Hari.
To the auspicious one who bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and was clad in yellow garments, he said: "O Hari! Choose from me all desires without exception."
"Having attained supreme joy through your song, I shall grant it to you.
Bhṛgu said:
Then Svabhū related the supreme account of the two Daityas.
Hari said: While I was sleeping upon the ocean of milk, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the wax of my ears; they went forth to devour Brahmā.
O Bharga, sleep was praised by him, and by her I was awakened;
I then engaged in battle with those two, adopting the playful movements of a wrestler.
"I am not capable of defeating those two; therefore, this was done by me.
Now, O ocean of compassion, tell me the means for their destruction. (35)
Bharga said:
"You went to the field of battle without having worshipped Vināyaka;
therefore, being deprived of power by him, you have come to experience extreme suffering. (36)
"O noble one, go to battle only after having worshipped Gaṇeśa;
he will delude those two by means of his illusory power and bring them under your control. (37)
"By my grace, you will slay those two wicked ones; of this there is no doubt.
Hari said:
"O Bharga, tell me how I may worship the god Vināyaka."
Īśvara said:
Seven crores of mantras belonging to Gaṇeśvara have been declared; among those, the great mantras are preeminent, and among them, the single-syllabled mantra is the greatest. 39.
O Blessed One, I shall tell you one of those two six-syllabled [mantras];
then, having abandoned the single syllable through the application of the *siddha* and *ari* wheels.
Having cleared off his debt and wealth, the Six-Syllabled One spoke to him the auspicious Great Mantra of Gaṇeśa, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
"By the mere performance of this, your purpose shall attain success.
Thereupon, that Hari went away in haste to perform it.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Instruction on Mantras," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 598 + 42 = 640.
Chapter 1.18, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Siddhakṣetra," [begins with] Somakānta saying:
How did Hari recite the supreme mantra, and where?
And how did he attain perfection? Tell me that in detail.
Bhṛgu said:
There is a place renowned on earth as Siddhikṣetra, which is supremely efficacious for attaining perfection.
Having gone there, Mahāviṣṇu performed supreme austerity.
Meditating upon the god Vināyaka according to the ritual of the six-syllabled mantra,
he then propitiated him, having diligently conquered his senses.
Having first performed the binding of the eastern direction with the Bāṇa weapon,
he attentively performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as well as the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana).
Having performed the internal nyāsa of the Mātṛkās in the sequence beginning with the Ādhāra, and the external nyāsa of the Mātṛkās in the sequence beginning from the head; || 5 ||
Having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) and meditated upon the elephant-faced deity by means of the root mantra,
one should worship Him with mental offerings using the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
With various kinds of substances and the sixteen types of ritual offerings,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of the lords of yoga, recited the supreme mantra.
When a hundred years had passed, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the Gaṇas,
who resembles ten million suns and fires, became manifest before him.
With a heart overflowing with joy, he spoke to the one whose banner is Garuḍa:
"O Hari, ask from me whatever boons you desire."
"Being gratified by this austerity, I grant them all;
had you worshipped me even earlier, your victory would have been certain."
Hari said:

"O Gaṇeśa, you who possess both manifest and unmanifest forms, and who appear in manifold forms yet are of a single nature—you whom even Brahmā, Śiva, Indra, and the other principal gods are not able to behold by means of their austerities, it is you that I behold. (11)
You, who are subtler than the subtle and greater than the great such as space, are the very form of pure being (sattva);
by the power of destiny, you repeatedly perform the creation, dissolution, and protection of all living beings. 12.
The Supreme Lord is the Self of all, omnipresent, omnipotent, all-pervading, and the creator of all;
He is the witness of all, the agent of dissolution, the protector, the sustainer, the leader of the universe, and even the father. 13.
O Lord, through the sight of you who are such as this, all perfections shall be mine everywhere; nevertheless, I shall tell you one thing.
At the end of my yogic sleep, two great beings, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the impurity of my ears, are intent on devouring me; who are they? 15.
I then waged war against those two for many years;
subsequently, my strength being exhausted, I came to you for refuge. Therefore, let it be considered how their slaughter may come about at my hands.
O Supreme Lord, grant me supreme fame through victory over other Daityas as well,
and grant me unwavering devotion unto you.
"By this [act], incomparable fame shall purify the three worlds.
Gaṇeśa said:
"O Viṣṇu, whatever you have requested, that shall certainly be yours."
"Renown, strength, supreme fame, and freedom from obstacles shall be yours.
The Sage said:
"Having spoken thus to Mahāviṣṇu, the omnipresent Lord vanished right there. (19)
Then, filled with joy, he considered those two asuras conquered;
he constructed there a palace made of crystal and abounding in many jewels.
He established an image made from the stones of the Gaṇḍakī river within a most beautiful temple that possessed four doors and glittering golden pinnacles.
And the gods and the sages bestowed upon him the renown of "Siddhivināyaka," because it was here that this auspicious success (siddhi) was attained by Hari.
Thereupon, that place became renowned everywhere on earth as Siddhakṣetra;
then Hari went to where Madhu and Kaiṭabha were.
Seeing Hari approaching, the two of them laughed and reviled him, saying:
"Why have you shown us this cloud-dark face today, and where will it be again? (24)
"Let them grant you great liberation; we shall indeed give it to you from this point on.
For what reason have you come to the battlefield, having already fallen into such insignificance?"
Hari said:
A fire that is small indeed consumes everything suddenly;
just as a small lamp dispels great darkness during the night. || 26 ||
"Or rather, I am capable of destroying these two intoxicated ones this very day.
The sage said:
Having heard these words of his, Madhu and Kaiṭabha became exceedingly enraged.
Suddenly they struck Viṣṇu violently in the chest with their fists;
thereafter, their wrestling match with him continued to intensify. 28.
Having fought with them for many days and being very eager to grant them a boon,
Hari spoke to Madhu and Kaiṭabha in gentle words.
"O foremost of Daityas, for many years you have endured my blows;
I am pleased with your manly exertion. (30)
"Equal to you two have never existed before, nor will they ever exist.
They both said:
"O Hari, choose boons from us; we shall grant them to you in abundance. (31)
"For we two are indeed greatly satisfied with you by means of this battle.
The sage said:
Having heard the words of those two who were deluded by illusion, Hari—
Hearing this, he said: "The two Daityas are prepared to grant me boons;
therefore, let them meet their destruction at my hands—this is the boon chosen by me."
Then, seeing everything to be composed of water, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, being exceedingly pleased, said: "Death at your hands is auspicious for us. (34)
Before their thoughts turn to You, they immediately attain eternal liberation.
O Mādhava, cast us into that place where there is neither earth nor water.
"Let us abandon everything; truth alone is real, for everything is established upon truth.
The sage said:
"Having heard their words in this manner, he indeed held them both by the waist. (36)
With his razor-edged discus, he severed their two heads;
then the gods rejoiced and rained down flowers.
All the Gandharvas danced and the hosts of Apsarases sang;
then Viṣṇu, having approached, [spoke] to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Filled with joy, he related the entire account of what had occurred.
Hari said:
"When I was unable to conquer those two, I then went to Giriśa. (39)
Instructed by Śaṅkara, I worshipped the omnipresent Lord Vighneśvara with that supreme six-syllabled mantra. 40.
By him were granted excellent boons that bestow the fruits of various desires;
through their power, the two wicked ones, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were slain by me.
Then, having been praised and fully worshipped, that omnipresent Lord vanished right then;
thus was the majesty of the high-souled Gaṇeśa made known. 42.
"By the grace of Śaṅkara, I shall slay the Daityas and Dānavas.
Then all the gods and sages, having praised the elephant-faced god, [spoke]. 43.
Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and I each went to our respective abodes.
Whoever should constantly hear this greatness which destroys sin— || 44 ||
One shall have no fear from anything whatsoever and shall obtain all that one desires. || 45 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Siddhakṣetra," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 18 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 640 + 45 = 685.
Chapter Nineteen, titled "Description of Kamalāputra," ends here.
Bhṛgu said:
Having heard this narrative and the ritual procedure for the six-syllabled mantra, Vyāsa, whose heart was not yet fully satisfied, spoke again to the Creator.
Vyāsa said:
You have heard the entire majesty of the Siddhakṣetra and indeed of Gaṇanātha; it removes all sins and increases both desires and merit.
Speak again to me, O Brahmin, the narrative of Vināyaka;
for I do not reach supreme satisfaction even while drinking the nectar of your story.
Brahmā said:
O son of Parāśara, I shall relate before you the auspicious and great narrative of the all-pervading Gaṇeśa, the supreme deity of all gods. 4.
In the land of Vidarbha there was a king, a hero in generosity and possessed of great strength;
known by the name Bhīma, he was a donor of formidable prowess.
O Mahāmati, his residence was in the city of Kauṇḍinya;
he was a sovereign to whom neighboring kings paid tribute, as did all other kings.
He possessed ten crores of horses, elephants, and foot soldiers. (6)
Thousands of Brahmins followed him, going both before his chariots and behind them, and they found great joy by taking refuge in him. His wife was highly fortunate, and she was named Cāruhāsinī.
With a face like a blooming lotus and eyes like those of a young fawn,
she was devoted to the Brahmins, dedicated to the gods, and always intent on righteousness;
she was a faithful wife who held her husband as her very life and was ever devoted to his word.
By the turn of fate, that woman of excellent complexion was born sonless;
then Bhīma beheld her, who was beautiful in all her limbs.
Deprived of his son, the best of kings, filled with grief, spoke these words:
"Abandoning the entire kingdom, I must go to the supreme forest."
For one who has no son, there is no destination, nor heaven, nor even happiness;
the gods do not accept his sacrificial offerings (havya), nor do the ancestors his ancestral offerings (kavya). 11.
In vain are my mother, my birth, my father, my home, my wealth, and my lineage;
all my actions are certainly fruitless without a son. 12.
Having made that very resolution, he summoned two ministers:
one named Manorañjana and the other named Sumantra. || 13 ||
O Sage, having mastered the sciences of logic, the three Vedas, and economics— the sixteen branches of knowledge—
they arrived at that very moment and bowed down to the king.
Then Bhīma said to them: "Let my kingdom be protected for me, or for my wife, from the evil born of a previous birth."
Therefore, there is no continuity for us that brings happiness in both worlds.
If I am to return again, then let my mind be given to me. 16.
"If you two do not accept it, let my kingdom be divided between you.
Having thus resolved, that king, preceded by the recitation of benedictions, [proceeded].
Having bestowed many gifts upon the Brahmins,
that best of kings departed from the city together with his wife, his two ministers, and the citizens.
Having gone only a distance of one gavyūti, he then dismissed all his attendants.
The two ministers said, "O King, let us two go along with you. (19)
His friends and the citizens, being deeply distressed, wept;
he spoke to them, saying, "No fear should be felt, for two ministers have been appointed as your rulers."
"Just as I am, so shall these two provide for you. Having thus reassured them, the king spoke again to those two.
"The kingdom has been given to you; protect the city in every way. Having thus dismissed them all, he departed from the city together with his wife.
Wandering about, he beheld a certain lake filled with lotuses,
beautified by blossoming trees, and inhabited by various water-dwelling creatures.
Then, as he beheld nearby that beautiful and auspicious hermitage which increased the joy of all, the king and the queen [were filled with delight].
There, those who were natural enemies— elephants and the like, lions and mongooses, serpents and cats, mice and so forth— ceased to harbor enmity toward one another.
There they both beheld the sage Viśvāmitra upon a seat of kusha grass,
surrounded by his disciples who were peaceful and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Having prostrated before the Great-Souled One with palms joined in reverence,
they both placed their hands upon his feet and offered salutations again and again.
Then Viśvāmitra, that tiger among sages and treasure-house of asceticism,
having raised him up and understood the matter, spoke to the king in gentle words.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, a son endowed with virtues and great fame shall be born to you.
From where have you come? What is the name of your city? Tell me that. (29)
"Therefore, O best of kings, I shall strive for the destruction of their sins.
Bhīma said: "O Lord, my city is Kauḍinya in the territory of Vidarbha. (30)
Her name is indeed Bhīma, and she is a wife of lovely smiles;
for the sake of a son, I have exerted effort through asceticism, charity, vows, and other such means. (31)
O Sage, compassion has not come to the gods because of the sin committed in a previous birth;
for, having seen your feet, they abandoned their kingdom and went to the forest.
Wandering through many forests, I have been brought here by fate;
the company of the virtuous instantly yields the highest fruit. (33)
Therefore, by your blessings, a son has been born to me; of this there is no doubt—a son who will practice learning, vows, austerity, charity, sacrifice, and the private recitation of the Vedas.
O Sage, for you who possess compassion and self-restraint, may this blessing not be in vain today;
yet, O Sage, what defilement have I committed in a previous birth? (35)
"Tell me the remedy for that, for you are considered by me to be omniscient.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his, the great sage Viśvāmitra respectfully related an ancient tale to that king.
Viśvāmitra said:
O evil-minded Mandādha, you have utterly abandoned the family duties established in the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and in worldly tradition. 37.
All those ancestors constantly worshipped Gaṇanāyaka;
because of his wrath, no offspring was born to you. || 38 ||
O Great Hero, tell him this: listen with respect from the very beginning as to how that elephant-faced one attained the status of your family deity. 39.
Seven generations prior to you, there was a king named Bhīma, who was handsome, endowed with wealth, and a most excellent beloved; O best of men,
after a long time, he too had an only infant son.
Then his body became mute and deaf,
emitting an extremely foul stench, oozing pus, and he became hunchbacked.
Seeing him, his mother Kamalā was deeply distressed;
she reflected within her heart that in this world, being truly childless is the worst state.
Such a state of having a son is not praiseworthy, for it causes intense suffering;
why has death not been ordained by the Creator for him now? 43.
"How indeed shall I show my face to my friends?
Lamenting thus in her grief, she wept most piteously.
Hearing that crying, the husband came to the lying-in chamber;
seeing the infant in such a state and his wife deeply distressed, [he was overcome with grief]. (45)
Knowing the path of action, he spoke with gentle words to comfort her:
"Do not grieve, O auspicious lady; such is the course of actions."
A man born from the evil committed in a previous life becomes a partaker of suffering;
one who possesses suffering attains happiness, and likewise, one who possesses happiness attains that [suffering] again.
For this child is not to be pitied, as he will become right;
as was his former conduct, so shall it be for him.
And we shall strive by means of gems, mantras, and great medicinal herbs,
as well as through austerities, recitations, and the performance of worship and processions for the gods.
"O lady of beautiful brows, perform that which you have undertaken so as to properly care for the child.
Thus exhorted, the virtuous woman then cast aside her grief for the child.
Having washed him with water, he rejoiced together with his friends;
he performed every auspicious rite appropriate for the birth of a son.
He honored those brahmins and their wives many times over.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kamalā’s Son," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 685 + 52 = 737.
Chapter Twenty, titled "The Praise of Dakṣa.
Brahmā said:
Then, having summoned virtuous brahmins who were experts in astrology and devoted to the Vedas, he first honored them with jewels, garments, wealth, and other gifts.
Having questioned them thus, Dakṣa gave his son the name "Dakṣa," and he performed the application of mantras for silent recitation and gathered collections of medicinal herbs.
And she herself performed supreme penance for twelve years,
for the sake of liberation from the disease of her son and for the increase of her own progeny.
That king never saw his son free from disease;
then, overcome by despondency and frantic with anger, he spoke.
"Go from my palace, O Queen Kamalā, together with your son;
henceforth, I shall not be able to look upon this son nor upon you."
Thus rebuked by her beloved at that time,
Kamalā took her son and departed from that city for the forest.
Weeping, agitated by grief, and distressed, she wiped away her tears;
emaciated by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, she carried him upon her back.
Wandering from village to village for alms, she became severely distressed;
her clothing, ornaments, and other possessions were plundered by thieves.
Then, having gone to another village and entrusted her son to a temple of Śiva,
that beloved of the king wandered through the city for alms.
Once, she went to the city with her son to beg for alms;
there, that boy was touched by the wind from the breath of a certain eminent brahmin.
Through the intensity of his devotion, he was directly perceived by Lambodara;
at that moment, he became possessed of sight, endowed with the power of hearing, and possessed of a divine body.
Beholding him as he repeatedly uttered sweet and comforting words, Kamalā cast off all her sorrow and rejoiced. 12.
Kamalā reflected: "He who was not properly restored by means of jewels, mantras, great medicines, ritual practices, and grand fire-offerings—" || 13 ||
"How did that son become well-formed through the touch of the wind?
And where shall I see that man who destroyed my evil deeds? (14)
Having spoken thus and embraced her son, she stood there, her fever of grief departed;
then, taking him with her, she went again into that city to beg for alms.
The citizens, having respectfully invited both of them, fed them with various kinds of cooked foods, vegetables, and the like, as well as sugar, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 16 ||
Thus, eating every day with joy, the two of them obtained new and excellent wealth and garments day after day.
The city-dweller asked him: "Tell me your father's name;
what is your country, what is your city, who are your kinsmen, and what indeed is your occupation? (18)
Having heard these words from Tagdi, Dakṣa by name spoke to him:
"Then, having approached your mother, your father, your city, and your family... (19)
He then inquired about his conduct and spoke to him again:
"In the city of Bhānu in Karṇāṭa, my father was a great favorite. (20)
He was a Kṣatriya endowed with great strength, renowned as the destroyer of enemy forces;
this Kamalā is his wife, and I am their son, named Dakṣa.
O Brahmin, when I was born blind and deaf,
and covered with many wounds, my mother was then intent on abandoning me.
Though forbidden by her father, she exerted herself greatly;
having performed penance for twelve years, she offered the merit to her father. || 23 ||
When my father saw that there was no longer any vigor in my body,
he then dismissed my mother and me, O Nāgara.
Thus Dakṣa recounted to him everything that had issued from the mouth of his mother:
"In this matter, I have become fortunate through the touch of someone's wind. (25)
Having heard this as that man had departed, Dakṣa, a resident of the city,
went quickly to greet his mother.
Then, in that city, those two were instructed by the twice-born one,
whose heart was filled with compassion, in the ritual for the worship of Gaṇeśa.
Then that Kamalā and Dakṣa,
intent on the worship of Gaṇeśa through austerity, attained supreme liberation by means of a single big toe.
Devotedly intent on their worship, they were muttering the supreme eight-syllable mantra, which consists of the names of the gods in the dative case followed by the sprout of the syllable *oṃ*.
Then, seeing them with their bodies withered from subsisting on air alone, the Blessed Lord Vināyaka,
an ocean of compassion, appeared before them.
Four-armed and of massive body, with the face of an elephant and exceedingly beautiful, he resembled many suns, like the sun risen in the night. || 31 ||
His head shone with a crown set with jewels, gold, and pearls;
he was clothed in yellow silk garments and adorned with golden armlets.
Seated upon the great throne with one knee bent,
he wore a golden girdle and a ring set with jewels.
They saw him bearing a great serpent in his belly and a single tusked half-elephant;
thus they beheld him in that form, and again in the form of a twice-born brahmin.
Satisfied by your attainment of liberation, that twice-born one said to them both:
"I have come to grant a boon; choose whatever you desire in your hearts. (35)
Viśvāmitra said:
When the Lord of Obstacles had thus become gracious and was manifest before him in the form of a brahmin,
he bowed with supreme devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, addressed him.
Dakṣa said:
O best of the twice-born, the merit accumulated in my previous birth has borne fruit for me, since you have shown me this twofold, supreme, and great form. (37)
My birth as a son of Vināyaka and as a son of a Brahmin has become meaningful;
for you are the cause of all causes, and even the source of the Vedic meters.
The supreme object of knowledge, the supreme Brahman, eternal and sought through the Vedas—you alone are the witness of all, both within and without everything. 39.
You alone are the creator of all effects, whether possessing subtle or gross bodies;
you are of manifold forms yet of one single form, and you are both formless and without material shape.
You alone are Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu; you alone are Indra, Anala, and Aryaman;
you are the very nature of earth, wind, and ether, and you possess the forms of water, the moon, and the stars.
He is the creator of the universe, the protector of the universe, and the cause of its dissolution;
he is the teacher and guardian of all that is moving and unmoving, and he possesses both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom.

You alone are the past, the future, and the present; you are the deities of the senses, as well as the divisions of time—kalās, kāṣṭhās, and muhūrtas—and you are indeed prosperity, fortitude, and loveliness.
You alone are Sāṅkhya and Yoga, the scriptures and the Vedas themselves;
likewise, you are the Purāṇas, the sixty-four arts, and the Upaniṣads. 44.
You alone are the Brāhmaṇa, the Vaiśya, the Kṣatriya, and indeed the Śūdra; you are the home country and the foreign land, as well as the sacred field and all other holy places of pilgrimage. 45.
You are the measurable and the immeasurable, the object of knowledge for yogis;
you alone are heaven, the netherworld, the forests, and the groves. 46.
Herbs, creepers, trees, bulbs, roots, and fruits;
living beings born from eggs, born from wombs, born from sweat, and even those born from sprouts. 47.
Desire, anger, hunger, greed, hypocrisy, pride, compassion, forgiveness, sleep, lassitude, sportiveness, joy, and even sorrow—you alone are all these. 48.
Viśvāmitra said:
Having heard these words of Dakṣa, Vināyaka, being well-pleased, spoke to him as if smiling, in a voice as deep as a thundercloud. (49)
Gajanana said:
"O illustrious one, I am pleased with this profound hymn of praise;
yet, though I am eager to grant you a boon, I do not bestow one upon you. (50)
"If I am the granter of boons to you, yet my devotee should be angry with me,
he alone shall grant the boon that [comes] from the shattering of Aṅga by the Wind-god."
Having attained a divine body and being endowed with sight and hearing, you have been born; I shall even tell you his name, which is Mudgala.
O lord of brahmins, as soon as he is meditated upon, he will reveal his own form;
whatever desires you may wish for, he will grant them all to you.
Having spoken thus, that Supreme Self vanished right there;
when he had disappeared, Dakṣa wept, overwhelmed with intense grief.
Just as a poor man, having found a treasure, laments intensely when it has vanished, or like a calf that cries out piteously when its mother cow has gone away. || 55 ||
Shedding tears from his eyes, Vināyaka fell upon the surface of the earth, crying out again and again, "Where has he gone? Where has he gone? (56)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Praise of Dakṣa," in the Section on Devotion of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 20 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 737 + 56 = 793.
Chapter Twenty-one, titled "Description of the Instruction on Mantras," ends here.
Viśvāmitra said:
Then, wandering and running here and there, the son of his beloved,
being utterly distraught, did not notice that his garment and ornaments had vanished.
He questioned the brahmins along the way, as well as the trees and Vināyaka:
"Where has Vināyaka gone? Has he been seen anywhere? Let them tell me. || 2 ||
With his heart thus bewildered and his vision clouded, O best of kings,
he wandered about and fell to the surface of the earth for a moment, deprived of consciousness.
In the meantime, he saw in a dream a Brahmana before him, who said:
"O child, that which you desired has indeed been granted to you by Mudgala and by me."
"O best of kings, when that Brahmin had departed after saying, 'That which was previously requested by you from Vighneśa [Ganeśa] has come within the range of my vision,'" 5.
Like one who has just awakened from sleep, Dakṣa became joyful in mind;
he questioned a certain hurried twice-born man.

He showed him the nearby, supreme, and divine hermitage of the exceedingly devoted Mudgala, who was fond of Gajānana (Ganesha) and adorned by many disciples; it grants fearlessness to all living beings.
Meditating on Mudgala in his mind, he wandered and arrived at that hermitage,
which was filled with various wonders, delightful, and surpassing even the pleasure grove of Alakā.
There he beheld the twice-born Mudgala seated upon a most excellent throne,
