"Where has my divine-bodied husband gone today? What indeed shall I say to my own wife?
Shame on me and shame on Smara, by whom I have been brought to this contemptible state! (26)
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, karma is experienced by living beings;
having entered the womb of an animal, I shall exhaust my own evil.
I shall remain within the bud of a lotus, assuming the form of an Indragopa insect.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Indra’s Curse," in the *Upāsanākhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1144 + 28 = 1172.
Chapter Thirty-two, titled "The Narration of Mantras," ends here.
Nārada said:
When Śakra had gone to Nalinī, I arrived at that city;
there I saw those gods standing with Bṛhaspati at their head.
To them, I related everything regarding the cause of the curses for both parties—
the union of Ahalyā with Mahendra and the resulting deformity.
Due to the curse of Gautama, Śakra was reduced to a thousandth part [of his power];
because of his violation of Ahalyā, O gods, she became a stone through contact with him.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words spoken by Nārada, all the gods were overcome with grief;
out of extreme sorrow, they wept, their breaths faltering with sighs and gasps.

The gods said: "By whom a hundred sacrifices were performed, by whom the Dānavas were utterly defeated, by whom the three worlds were protected, and by whom the auspicious station of Indra was enjoyed. (5)
Many gods have been worshipped, and Brahmins most proficient in the knowledge of Brahman have been honored;
various enjoyments, exceedingly difficult for others to obtain, have been experienced.
Where will this god stay? How will he eat? How will he sleep? Whom shall we seek for refuge today—for our own sake, or for his sake? (7)
Whom indeed will he protect—the position of Indra, or likewise Śacī? How might Gautama, the best of sages, attain a state of favor toward us? (8)
Separated from his own wife and remembering the offense she had committed against him, he was filled with rage;
yet, through the grace of Gautama, we see no other remedy. 9.
"Therefore, O Nārada, we shall go to pacify the sage Gautama.
Thus those gods set out, accompanied by Nārada.
Having approached the sage Gautama with their palms joined in reverence,
they sought refuge in him alone and praised him with various words.
The gods said:
"O sage, we do not possess the power to describe your majesty.
For who indeed could speak of the greatness of Mount Meru or even of the Himalayas?"
The streams of rain, the dust of the earth, and even the sands of the Ganges—[are all equal in number]. 12.
What deluded person could possibly enumerate the virtues of Viṣṇu, who is like an ocean of nectar? It is as if one were to expect a harvest of grain at midday from seeds sown only this morning.
In the past, you protected the most excellent sages;
by performing a sacrifice with the Vālakhilyas, another Indra was created.
Entreated by Brahmā and the other gods, they ordained the end of the birds,
since the ocean had been swallowed by him with a single handful of water.
Another creation was undertaken by the wise son of Gādhi;
the arm of Indra was paralyzed by the high-souled Cyavana. || 16 ||
Therefore, for you men, service with one's whole being, bowing down, beholding, speaking, worshipping, and touching [him] destroys all sin. (17)
"You ought to show compassion toward those who delight in doing good, who bestow favor upon the wretched, and who have sought refuge for the sake of Indra. (18)
Gautama said:
"The vision of you all does not arise for those with physical eyes;
it has been produced by my merit, serving as the fulfillment of the desires of men. (19)
Indeed, by this very glance of yours, your birth, your stages of life, your austerities, your gifts, your body, your self, and your vows have truly become meaningful. (20)
Now, what is it that you have requested? Let that be examined before me; if it is possible, I shall perform it through the power of your remembrance.
The sage said:
Having heard those words, those dwellers of heaven rejoiced,
just as the ocean clearly attains joy at the rising of the moon.
Just as parents find joy through the speech of their children,
so did they all offer prayers to that great sage, Gautama.
The gods said:
"Through the offense against the Lord, Kama has been reduced to ashes;
yet the offender, O Śakra, has not been deprived of his life by you. (24)
Now, O Sage, having forgiven his offenses at our request, let him regain his own rightful place. 25.
"When that favor has been granted, the desire of all shall be fulfilled.
Nārada said:
Having heard the words of the assembly of gods, that Gautama—
Laughing, Gautama replied thus to all the hosts of gods:
"I shall not even utter the name of that fallen man who has committed a transgression. (27)
For one who is deceitful, treacherous, wicked, lacking in discernment, and devoid of remorse, no atonement whatsoever exists. 28.
Nevertheless, O gods, I shall do that which is pleasing to you because of your words;
yet when you are angry, then a curse may fall upon me.
For a person who is favored by many becomes purified;
therefore, I shall speak a single mantra for him, and let them bestow it upon him. 30.
The creator of all, the destroyer of all, the protector of all, a treasure-house of compassion, the leader, the god of gods, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (31)
His mantra consists of six syllables and bestows great siddhi;
once it has been imparted as instruction, he shall attain a divine body.
"As many marks as he possesses, so many eyes shall he have;
Śakra will regain his own kingdom—this I tell you as the truth. (33)
Having spoken thus to the gods, that Gautama became silent;
and they, having honored him, bowed down to him filled with joy.
Having circumambulated him and received his permission once more, the gods departed,
praising the sage as they went to where the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra was staying.
Among those endowed with knowledge, there exists no other who is more sattvic than Gautama.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of Mantras," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total sum of verses from the beginning is 1172 + 36 = 1208.
Chapter Thirty-Three.
Nārada said:
The gods said to the slayer of Vṛtra: "O Śatakratu, go outside;
for we shall remain there together with the celestial sage Nārada."
Having gone to that sage Gautama and propitiated him, we have returned here;
he explained the means to us and granted this boon to you as well.
When a fault has arisen, the virtuous themselves proclaim it among the people;
they then properly apply a remedy, thereby rendering that fault useless.
If he is concealed, his faults will increase; but if he is made known, his destruction will follow.
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, you too should come outside and speak with him.
Speak this to the celestial sage:
"Accept from me, O sage, the six-syllabled great mantra dedicated to Vaināyaka, which is the means for the accomplishment of all goals."
At the wedding of the Lord of Girijā and [Śiva], Brahmā beheld [the god's] thumb;
then, overcome with shame and with his face cast downward, he discharged his semen. (6)
"Having understood this, Maheśa rendered him faultless through a skillful means.
As soon as he heard these words uttered by the assembly of celestial sages, [he was reassured].
O King, having heard the respectful words of all those gods there, Śakra emerged from the interior of the lotus stalk.
Seeing the Lord of the Gods in such a state— his limbs smeared with pus and blood, soiled, and emitting a foul odor— all the gods bowed down to him.
Having covered the openings of his nostrils with the ends of his garment, O best of kings,
Vākpati then addressed that Indra, who was well-bathed and had sipped water for purification.
He imparted the great six-syllabled mantra of Gaṇeśa;
once it was taught by him, he attained a divine body.
The glorious thousand-eyed one shone like another sun;
then, amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the cries of "Victory! from the dwellers of heaven, [he appeared].
The intermediate and main directions resounded with the songs of the Gandharvas;
all the gods, filled with joy, released showers of flowers in various colors.
Then all the sages, Nārada and the others, gave their blessings;
the gods embraced him with joy, while others offered hymns of praise.
Some of those well-disposed ones said to him: "Indeed, we have found our protector in you;
without you we do not shine at all, just as the sky does not shine without the moon. (15)
Just as children never find happiness without their parents, so too we find no peace anywhere without you. 16.
The sage said:
Having heard these words of the god, Śatakratu rejoiced;
and with a tranquil soul, he spoke these truthful words to the deities. 18.

Indra said: "A most difficult deed was performed by me when, deluded by the words of the celestial sage, I obtained today a fruit that is unbearable for all; I have been rescued from the fury of calamity. (18)
I bow to all the foremost of the immortals and to all the sages of great spiritual power;
therefore, may you all deign to uplift me and protect me, who have come to you for refuge. 19.
"How was this effort undertaken by you to win over this Gautama?
How indeed did he speak that supreme counsel for my sake? Let everyone tell me that. (20)
The gods said:

"O Sage, having placed our preceptor at our head, we went to that sage and prostrated ourselves before him properly. Being propitiated by us with various nectars of speech and earnestly entreated, he spoke his own mantra. (21)
O Lord, by whose instruction you have become thousand-eyed for the sake of the happiness of all,
proceed now to your own divinity in Amarāvatī and govern all the gods and the worlds.
Indra said:
"O best of celestial sages, I shall not go to my own city without the grace of Gaṇeśa. You, having accomplished your purpose, may depart and rejoice with joy in your divine abodes. 23.
Enough of this; I have been revealed as one who is dissolved in shame and fallen into many miserable states.
Since the sage of fierce splendor has been propitiated, it is by your grace that I have attained the state of having many eyes.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the Section on Worship of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 33 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1208 + 24 = 1232.
Chapter Thirty-four, titled "Description of the Cintāmaṇi Tīrtha.
Nārada said:
O King, having placed his gaze upon the tip of his nose at the foot of a kadamba tree and having fixed his mind upon the supreme seat, that enemy of Jambha then chanted the six-syllabled mantra.
A thousand years passed for that lord of Maruts, who subsisted on air alone;
indeed, anthills and shrubs grew upon the parts of his body, which remained as firm as a mountain.
Then the blessed Lord Gaṇeśa, who is all-pervading, all-knowing, and of fierce splendor, being pleased,
eclipsed with his own radiance the lights of fire, moon, and sun, as well as all eyes.
Four-armed, wearing a crown and garland of jewels, with beautiful armlets and cheeks adorned by earrings, he bore a pearl necklace and high, precious anklets and a waistband.
He whose eyes were like lotuses, who possessed broad lotus-palms and large hands, and who wore a garland of lotuses—
manifesting as the embodiment of all the gods, he appeared before Indra, radiant with vermilion.
Seeing him, he became terrified with fear: "What is this? What has come here?
And how might I, whose life consists of mere bones and breath, continue to live?"
"O Great River, what is this obstacle? I do not know by whom it was created.
My body is dripping with sweat and trembles like the leaves of a Bodhi tree. (7)

The all-seeing Vināyaka perceived his entire distress and spoke these charming words to Mahendra: Thus did the all-seeing Vināyaka perceive his entire distress and speak these charming words to Mahendra. (8)
Vināyaka said: "Do not fear, O Lord of Gods; how is it, O Surasura, that you do not know me?
I am that which is devoid of qualities, changeless, eternal consciousness-bliss."
O Lord, you meditate with unwavering mind upon this deity through this mantra—the unmanifest, which transcends all causes, and which is the cause of the cause of the universe. 10.
"You have been weary for a long time," he said, appearing before him in person;
"I am pleased by this austerity and have come here to grant you a boon. (11)
Know, O sinless one, that the origin and dissolution of infinite universes proceed from me alone; choose whatever you desire.
Nārada said: Having heard his delightful speech, the destroyer of Bala recognized the Lord Vināyaka, the god of gods, who possessed a massive body. 13.
Having bowed with supreme devotion, he then rose quickly; desiring to see the beloved of Śacī, he beheld him visibly present in the form of Brahmā.
Indra said:
"Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, along with the world-regents, do not know you, O mighty-armed one, nor your qualities that bring about creation, preservation, and destruction. (15)
But this station of mine is artificial, arising from a hundred sacrifices;
even there, many obstacles arise for me in various ways.
O Gajānana, how indeed am I to understand your greatness, O Maheśvara, for which your full favor shall be bestowed upon me? 17.
Only he, O cause of obstacles, would know your greatness;
he alone will have the power to describe your qualities and forms.
He is without support yet the support of all; he possesses eternal knowledge, is undecaying and immortal;
he is filled with eternal bliss, the master of māyā, and indeed the perishable as well. 19.
The Imperishable One, the Supreme Self, whose form is the universe and who is the Lord of all—
having known You through fierce austerities, Sanaka and the others attained liberation.
O Supreme Lord, you have been seen through the power of the six-syllabled mantra;
indeed, this mantra was formerly enjoined upon me by Brahmā out of his grace. 21.
And Brahmā said to me: "When you forget this, at that very moment you shall fall from your station and undergo a state of misfortune."
Then, being excessively greedy and overcome by misfortune, I violated that sage’s wife; consequently, I fell into a state of wretchedness.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, by means of that mantra spoken by Bṛhaspati, you have now beheld your own true form with a thousand eyes.
"I ask for one other boon, since you are the granter of desired objects:
let this city of Kadamba be known as Cintāmaṇipuram. (25)
O Lord of Obstacles, you have granted me the fruit of my practice: your firm lotus feet. Now, however, I beg for a boon; grant that to me. 26.
O Lord, act in such a way that there may be no forgetfulness of you in me;
O All-pervading One, let my mind delight in the lotus of your feet. 27.
From this day forward, O Gajānana, let this sacred site attain renown in this world as "Cintāmaṇi," and let this lake also become famous by that name. 28.
By bathing and giving gifts here, may dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation be accomplished for people through your grace, O Teacher of the World. (29)
The sage said:
Having heard the words of Śakra, Vighneśa, the lord of the worlds, whose voice was as deep as a thundercloud, spoke with gentle speech.
Vināyaka said:
"O Lord, all this that has been requested by you shall be accomplished.
Let there be one other boon for you: may you remain firm in your own position."
"And may there be constant non-forgetfulness of you on my part, O Lord of the Gods;
and whenever you should encounter distress, then remember me, O Vāsava. (32)
Through my manifestation, I shall constantly accomplish all your tasks;
this city shall become renowned on earth as Cintāmaṇipura.
This sacred site is known as Kadambapura and Cintāmaṇi;
by bathing here, all spiritual perfections (siddhis) are held within the grasp of everyone.
"And I, Vināyaka, shall grant whatever is thought of, like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Nārada said:
"Having thus obtained that boon, Hari then went from there to the celestial river (Sindhu)."
Having performed the consecration through him, he worshipped that omnipresent Lord, the illustrious elephant-faced one, together with his retinue. || 36 ||
Honored by the Lord of the Gods, the omnipresent one vanished right there;
Śakra, for his part, reverently installed a crystal image.
He caused a magnificent temple to be built for the auspicious and divine image of Vaināyakī, beautiful in all its limbs and adorned with jewels and gold.
Having bowed and circumambulated it, Śakra departed for his own abode.
Thus, this great lake known as Cintāmaṇisaras became famous on earth. 39.
Even today, by the command of Śakra, that Gaṅgā of auspicious waters,
having performed her ablution upon his form, always returns to her own abode.
Thus has the greatness of that field been described to you—wondrous to behold, glorious, auspicious, the remover of all defects, and the bestower of all desires. 41.
Having gone there, O protector of the earth, perform your ablutions according to the prescribed rite;
you will be liberated from all defects, of this there is no doubt. || 42 ||
Brahmā said: Then the sage, having respectfully honored Rukmāṅgada with blessings and having taken leave of that king, departed quickly.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Cintāmaṇi Tīrtha," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1232 + 43 = 1275.
Chapter Thirty-Five, titled "Description of Reaching Kādambapura," Vyāsa said:
When that celestial sage had departed, what did the king do then?
O Rukmāṅgada, tell me this delightful story. || 1 ||
Brahmā said:
O son Nārada, after the great sage had thus given this extensive instruction and departed,
Rukmāṅgada, filled with joy, beheld his own fourfold army.
She too beheld the king, who was deformed, though he possessed the golden luster and the form of the husband of Rati;
wondering how he could have become thus in the city, she questioned the king regarding the cause.
The generals said:
"O Indra among kings, having wandered through mountains, forests, and rivers, we have returned; overcome by hunger and thirst, we are eager for the sight of you."
Beholding [the Lord] at every step, they have reached His lotus feet;
yet, seeing Him in this state, they have gone from sorrow to even greater sorrow. || 5 ||
"O best of kings, tell us what was the cause of that.
The king said:
"I had arrived ahead of you, and indeed I was both thirsty and hungry. (6)
I quickly beheld before me the householder's hermitage of Vācaka;
having gone there, I saw his wife of beautiful countenance.
I requested water from that auspicious woman named Mukundā;
however, she was wicked and wanton, and she spoke these evil words to me.
"Take pleasure with me; otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you.
But she was rejected by me, for my mind was pure and firm. || 9 ||
When her husband had gone to bathe, that wicked woman cursed me in anger;
thereafter, I sat down at the foot of a tree, indeed distressed.
By the power of my former merit, I beheld the sage Nārada;
he explained to me this supreme rite which destroys all misfortune. || 11 ||
Having gone to the Cintāmaṇi field and resorted to the Gaṇeśa-tīrtha,
he described the greatness of that sacred site in detail.
In this regard, bathing has been proclaimed by the sage who possesses divine vision;
therefore, I shall go to bathe for the removal of my own fault.
If you so desire, let all of you go with me there to bathe;
having bathed, and having given according to your ability, and having fully worshipped Vināyaka. || 14 ||
"Purified by their power, we shall then go to our own city.
Ka said:
"Having understood their resolve, they departed with the king at their head."
Having seen the sacred ford named Gaṇeśa, the king shone with a divine body.
O Lord of Sages, he shone with the color of molten gold as before;
then Rukmāṅgada considered the words spoken by Nārada to be the truth.
Having bathed there,
King Rukmāṅgada, filled with supreme joy, then gave many gifts to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped Vināyaka, he beheld a mass of splendor—a celestial chariot resembling the sun—along with those Brāhmaṇas and servants. 18.
Having bowed to those who were frequented by hosts of Vināyakas and accompanied by Apsarases and Kinnaras, the king asked them: "Who are you, and from where have you come? (19)
"O messengers, for whom are you? What business is there here? Tell me that respectfully.
Brahmā said:
"Having heard the king's charming words, those traveling in their celestial chariots [replied]. (20)
The messengers of Vināyaka said: "O best of kings, you are blessed, for by you the Lord Cintāmaṇi has been meditated upon with your whole being."
You have properly performed a pilgrimage to sacred sites after giving gifts according to the prescribed rites;
you have also worshipped the Cintāmaṇi jewel, and thus you have now accomplished all that was to be done.
For it is because of granting what is thought of that this is known as the *cintāmaṇi*;
and we, O observer of noble vows, have accomplished our purpose by the very sight of you.
O best of kings, we do not know the full extent of the greatness of devotion to you, even through the offering of one's body, speech, intellect, and very life. (24)
O King, you have propitiated the Lord who is the leader of the entire universe;
Vināyaka and his messengers were sent by him.
Eager, he said to us, "O swift-moving ones,
bring my devotee Rukmāṅgada to my presence by means of the celestial chariot."
Having heard this, we have come; ascend the sky-faring vehicle.
O Lord, proceed more swiftly with us and Vināyaka.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of theirs, King Rūkmāṅgada said:
"O messengers, where am I, dull-witted as I am, and where is he whose body is unimpaired? (28)
He is immeasurable and inconceivable, pure consciousness alone, all-pervading and imperishable; he who is the cause of creation, sustenance, and dissolution, yet transcends all causes.
I do not know how his regard for me arose from the fruit of visiting sacred fords;
has some supreme merit from a previous birth borne fruit for me? (30)
Therefore, this first vision granted to you is exceedingly fruitful and auspicious;
you are most blessed, for the All-pervading Lord is manifest before your eyes day and night.
Having spoken thus, my father, that best of kings— devoted to Brahmanas, truthful, and possessed of terrible prowess— bowed at his lotus-feet, worshipped him, and made a request to all of them. (32)
Without her, how can I approach the sweetly smiling Mānara?
By her also was the god Vināyaka, the god of gods, propitiated. || 33 ||
Until the end of her life, she did not perceive any other deity whatsoever.
The messenger said:
"If it is so, then perform a bath in this sacred ford for the sake of those two as well."
And let that which is most beneficial be bestowed upon him, upon her, and upon his father and mother. || 35 ||
Then we two shall also lead them away, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, he fashioned an effigy out of kuśa grass:
"You are Kuśa; you are the son of Kuśa, created by Brahmā in ancient times. (37)
"Once you have bathed, he for whom this book-binding exists has also bathed.
Having thus recited the mantra, [he did so] for all of them in due order. (38)
The king established the ritual for bathing for all the people of the villages at the sacred ford named Gaṇeśa, located within the Cintāmaṇi field.
Then King Rukmāṅgada, together with his army, having mounted an excellent celestial chariot at the word of the messenger, went to the city of Kauṇḍinya.
The sky and the ten directions were made to resound by that celestial chariot with the sounds of musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and the voices of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
King Rukmāṅgada bestowed this blessing upon his parents:
"May there be the merit of bathing for all people in the presence of Vināyaka. 42.
As soon as that auspicious merit born of bathing in the Kauśeya was bestowed,
other celestial chariots arrived by the command of Vināyaka.
Each of them mounted a single sky-ranger;
likewise Rukmāṅgada, Bhīma, and his mother Cāruhāsinī.
All the people went there where the god Vināyaka was;
thus, that entire city, from the children down to the dog-cookers (outcastes), [followed him]. 45.
"Through the merit arising from bathing at Gaṇeśatīrtha, he attained the path to heaven.
Ka said:
"O sage, thus everything that was asked by you has been told to you."
The man who listens with devotion to this greatness arising from the sacred ford, situated in the Cintāmaṇi field, shall attain that same destination.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Kādamba-pura," in the Upāsanā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa.

Chapter Thirty-Six, titled "The Narrative of Gṛtsamada," ends here.
Vyāsa said:
O Lotus-seated One, I have heard the majesty of Gaṇeśatīrtha, the life of Rukmāṅgada, and [the account] of the inhabitants of Kauṇḍinyapura. || 1 ||
"Nevertheless, O Brahman, tell me the auspicious life-story of Mukunda.
Brahmā said: "When Rukmāṅgada had departed, she burned with the fire of passion."
Just as a great forest region scorched by a wildfire in summer finds no relief even when a cool breeze blows through the woods, so too did Mukunda find no peace in the forest.
Even in a place filled with the flowers of creepers, and even more so than sandalwood cooled by the moon,
laughter, song, dance, and other conversation did not please her.
O Lord of Sages, for her whose mind was fixed on him, food, water, and even her feeble speech were of no avail;
yet, due to the exhaustion of hunger and thirst, sleep came upon her for a moment.
O son, Indra perceived that lovely woman sleeping in the lonely forest—
distraught and afflicted by passion on account of Rukmāṅgada.
Assuming the form of a golden-armored youth, Śakra enjoyed that lustful woman;
he embraced her with joy, while Mukunda rejoiced exceedingly.
She, too, kissed that son Rukmāṅgada very deeply;
he, for his part, firmly massaged her full breasts with his fist.
The naked one, being himself naked, dallied with her without hesitation;
then she, as if feeling ashamed, returned to her own home.
Indra, having become Rukmāṅgada, vanished right there before her eyes.
Thinking that Rukmāṅgada had been enjoyed, she then conceived a child.
In the ninth month, at an auspicious hour, she gave birth to a beautiful son,
whose every limb was lovely and faultless, and who in beauty surpassed even the god of love.
At the great sound of him as he fell upon the earth,
the ten directions, the sky, the earth, and the subterranean realm all became filled with noise.
All the birds flew away here and there;
Vācaknavī arrived, having abandoned her own daily ritual duties.
He never understood the true nature of Mukunda's deeds;
nevertheless, filled with great joy, he performed all the rites beginning with the birth ceremony.
He gave gifts to the Brahmins according to his ability and as was appropriate;
then, when ten days had passed, that sage performed the naming ceremony.
Permitted by the twice-born experts in the science of astrology with the words "O Gṛtsamada," he then performed the investiture of the sacred thread for him in his fifth year.
He performed the four Vedic vows for the young student;
by the power of his Brahmanic luster, the boy mastered them with a single recitation.
Born as a treasury of the Vedas and scriptures, and skilled in his own duties,
the father Vācaknavī once, at an auspicious moment, [addressed] his son.
He taught the great Ṛgvedic mantra, "gaṇānāṃ tvā," and spoke two other great Vedic mantras that grant all perfections.
Among all the mantras taught in the scriptures, this one is indeed the most excellent;
having meditated upon the elephant-faced deity, one should recite it with a steady mind. (20)
"Having attained supreme perfection, you shall indeed attain renown in the world;
then, O Brahmins, Gṛtsamada, having received the mantra from the mouth of his father," (21)

Devoted to the performance of rites, he became intent on recitation and meditation. Thus, after a long time had passed for that sage engaged in great austerity, there was a king in that Magadha country known as Magadha. (22)
Of beautiful form and great pride, an arrow in the form of a donor, he was the crusher of enemies;
enriched by the splendor of various ornaments, he sat upon a costly throne. || 23 ||
Seated upon the Sudharma throne, the steadfast one was like another Indra; endowed with a fourfold army, he was a knower of wisdom who bestowed honor upon the learned.
He had two ministers who were treasuries of knowledge, possessing qualities superior even to Vācaspati;
his wife was named Ambikā, beautiful in form and preeminent in virtues.
The illustrious and devoted wife, capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, arrived at the ancestral Śrāddha ceremony for her father, that king, along with the great ṛṣis. || 26 ||
Summoned by the king were Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others who had reached the further shore of the Vedas;
Gṛtsamada, the ascetic of pure mind, was also invited.
Then, in the course of a discussion on the scriptures, Gṛtsamada spoke with arrogance;
at that, Atri, in the presence of the sages, said to him, "Fie, fie! (28)
"You are to be honored as an ascetic, yet you are not a sage;
consider that your birth arose from Prince Rukmāṅgada. (29)
"He is not worthy of worship in our presence; go from here to your own hermitage.
Hearing these words of Atri, he blazed up as if inflamed with anger.
As if burning the three worlds and as if devouring those sages,
they fled away like deer upon seeing a lion.
There, in that assembly, he spoke to the sages headed by Vasiṣṭha.
Gṛtsamada said:
"O lords of sages, when I shall no longer be the one with golden armlets..."
Then, with the fire of my curse, I shall reduce you to nothing but ashes.
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus to all those sages, he went toward his mother.
Gṛtsamada questioned her, saying: "Speak, O wicked woman, you who are so excessively lustful! (33)
"O dear one, speak to me regarding Mukunda, or else you shall become ashes!
Upon hearing these words of his, she trembled, utterly overwhelmed.
Like a plantain tree with its buds shaken by a gale, Mukundā, being virtuous,
spoke with a piteous voice, her hands joined in reverence.
Mukunda said:
"O best of kings, with my mind intent on hunting, I became separated from my caravan;
then I beheld that auspicious Rūkmāṅgada, who is the delight of the three worlds. (36)
"Since my beloved husband Vācaknavī is devoted to the performance of his duties, I have uttered this speech, mindful of the traditional saying that 'women are not to be restrained. (37)
"O father of yours, my mind became attached to that king.
Having heard these words of hers, the sage departed in silence. (38)
With his face cast down in shame, he pronounced a curse upon his mother.
The son said:
"O wicked, foolish, and sinful woman, become a thorny plant in the forest! (39)
Though she possessed immeasurable fruits, she was nevertheless shunned by all living beings;
yet, overcome with anger, she indeed uttered a curse upon her son.
"Since you have indeed cursed me by disregarding my status as your mother, therefore, O son, I curse you: from you shall come a son who is exceedingly cruel. (41)
"A Daitya of great strength shall become the bringer of fear to the three worlds.
Thus did the mother and son curse each other. 42.
Ka said:
At that very moment, having abandoned that body, she became a tree in the Badarī forest, shunned even by flocks of birds, including those born from eggs and those born from moisture. 43.
Then a voice arose in the sky: "From Indra, Gṛtsamada was indeed born.
O Brahmin, that Gṛtsamada has gone forth to perform spiritual practice. 44.
That best of men who hears this narrative of Gṛtsamada encounters no distress and obtains everything he desires. 45.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Gṛtsamada," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1322 + 45 = 1367.
Chapter Thirty-Seven, titled "The Narration of the Boon," Brahmā said:
Wandering along, the sage beheld before him a forest named Puṣpaka,
filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with diverse kinds of flowers.
Adorned by mountain streams and by the foremost of sages who were like the immortals,
Gṛtsamada bowed to them and dwelt there by their command.
Having bathed there, he performed his recitation (japa), standing firmly balanced on the tips of his big toes,
meditating with a steady mind upon the omnipresent Lord Vighneśvara.
With his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, looking in every direction,
he had conquered his senses, mastered his breath, and subdued his self, subsisting only on air.
For a thousand divine years he performed most rigorous penance;
when the sage Gṛtsamada opened his eyes, he beheld [the Lord].
Then the fire arising from his eye tormented the gods;
at that time, the deities wondered, "Whose portion of the sacrificial offering could this be? || 6 ||
Furthermore, eating only a single fallen leaf that had dropped,
he applied supreme effort and remained utterly motionless like a pillar.
With a steady mind, he performed austerities for fifteen thousand years;
then Vināyaka, seeing that his penance was difficult to accomplish, [approached him].
Then, for his benefit, a brilliantly radiant [light] appeared, just as a cow runs swiftly upon hearing the lowing of her calf. 9.
Likewise, the god Vināyaka, resembling a thousand suns in brilliance, went swiftly to Gṛtsamada, illuminating the entire universe with his splendor.

With flapping ears like palm-leaf fans, sporting with great tusks, joyfully engaged in beautiful play, with a shining moon upon his forehead, wearing a garland of large lotuses, the root of the world’s purpose, with rays of light from his lotus-like trunk, he is the assembly of those who bow and serve him. 11.
Mounted upon a lion, with ten arms, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
he was anointed with saffron, agallochum, musk, and beautiful sandalwood paste.
Endowed with perfection and wisdom, glorious, and possessing a radiance exceeding ten million suns, he whose nature is ineffable appeared before the sage as if in sport. 13.
The splendor of that high-souled sage was eclipsed by his brilliance,
just as the light of the stars and the moon is overwhelmed by the radiance of the sun.
Then, closing his eyes, he trembled, utterly overwhelmed;
forgetting his meditation and auspicious rites, he fell to the ground in a swoon. 15.
Furthermore, meditating in his mind upon the unblemished elephant-faced god and reflecting mentally on the cause of the obstacle, the sage became distraught.
"What is this that has suddenly arisen, causing such agitation?
How can all that I have practiced as penance from this day forward have gone in vain? (17)
Protect me, O Lord of gods, O Soul of all, from this terrifying obstacle! To whom else but you, the Lord of the universe, shall I go for refuge? 18.
"O Lord, by what cause have I encountered such great suffering, that my mind is consumed by the thought: 'I am not worthy of worship in this assembly'? (19)
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, that Vināyaka spoke.
Gaṇeśa said:
"Know me to be the leader of the Gaṇas, arrived here for the sake of bestowing grace. || 20 ||
"O best of sages, casting aside all fear, tell me what you desire—that which was unattainable even by Sanaka and others who remained long established in their observances. (21)
"I have been constantly gratified by you through the austerity of [holding] a single big toe.
Brahmā said: "Having heard these auspicious words of the God of gods," || 22 ||
Overwhelmed with his own bliss, he prostrated before him like a staff;
supremely delighted, he spoke to that Vināyaka, the bestower of boons.
Gṛtsamada said:
Today my birth has become fruitful, as well as my austerity and my observance, since You,
who are formless and of the nature of unbroken bliss, have become manifest as Brahman.
Shedding tears from his eyes out of joy, he danced;
he was a mass of consciousness and bliss, beyond even the reach of the Vedas and the scriptures. || 25 ||
O Lord, having been seen by me directly this very moment, what more could I possibly ask for?
Nevertheless, O elephant-faced one, I shall ask for one thing by your command. (26)
O highly fortunate one, among the eighty-four hundred thousand types of births and the most excellent ones,
the castes (varṇas) of human beings are the greatest therein.
Even among those, the Brahmins are the best; even among them, the men of knowledge are supreme;
among the men of knowledge, those devoted to spiritual practice are superior; and among them, the knowers of Brahman are the highest.
O Lord of the Universe, grant me that knowledge which is the knowledge of Brahman, as well as very firm devotion toward You and the state of never forgetting You. 29.
O Gajānana, among all your devotees, you are the most excellent;
O Śaṅkara, I ask for one other boon as well—grant that to me.
It is the sole abode of devotion to you, capable of attracting the three worlds,
renowned throughout the three realms, and worthy of salutation by gods and humans alike.
"O Vighneśa, O granter of all desires, if you are pleased with me,
O Lord of the gods, let this grove become famous by the name 'Puṣpaka'."
And remaining here, forever fulfill the desires of your devotees;
and this city of Puṣpaka, especially in its four directions.
"O Gajānana, let it thus attain fame as Gaṇeśapura.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the elephant-faced one replied. (34)
Ganeśa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! Since I am pleased with you, O bull among sages, there is nothing difficult to obtain for devotees in the three worlds. (36)
O Brahmin, everything that you have requested shall come to pass;
this state of being a Brahmin, which is exceedingly difficult to attain, has been granted by me out of my favor.
"O sage, because you have performed the recitation of this Vedic mantra beginning with 'gaṇānām tvā', you shall therefore become the seer (ṛṣi) of this hymn. (37)
Among the gods beginning with Brahmā and among the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha,
you shall attain renown everywhere, having reached the highest preeminence.
"Among all those who have undertaken their tasks, those who shall remember both you and me first, for them there will be success. (39)
Without knowledge of the deities, the seers, and the meters, ritual action is fruitless;
and a powerful son is a source of great terror to all the gods. (40)
He will attain great renown throughout the three worlds and shall become invincible to all the gods, with the exception of Rudra.
My devotee, whose life-breath is dedicated to me, who is intent on me, and for whom I am the supreme goal;
and this city, O Lord, known by the name Puṣpaka, [shall be his]. 42.
In the Tretā age it shall be Maṇipūra, and in the Dvāpara age it shall be Bhānaka; but in the Kali age, it will become famous in the world by the name Bhadraka.
"By bathing and giving gifts here, one shall obtain all desires.
Brahmā said:
"Having thus granted these boons to him, the Lord vanished on that very spot. (44)
When he had vanished, the sage established the image of Gaṇeśa there and caused a beautiful temple to be constructed.
And he established that name "Varada" as eternal;
and by the grace of Gaṇeśa, that place became a site of spiritual accomplishment (siddhisthāna). 46.
Nourishing the desires of all, he also regarded that field as Puṣpaka;
filled with a spirit of devotion, he worshipped that image.

O Lord of Sages, whoever hears this discourse revealing the boon of the illustrious Vighnarāja shall obtain all desires, firm devotion to Gaṇeśa, and liberation from the cycle of worldly existence. 48.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Varadā," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1367 + 48 = 1415.
Chapter Thirty-Eight, titled "The Bestowing of Boons," Vyāsa said:
O Lord of the Gods, O Lotus-born One, tell me with care how Gṛtsamada sustained his livelihood, for I am full of faith. 1.
Brahmā said:
Then all the hosts of sages honored him with respect;
they bowed to Brahmā, the best among the foremost of sages, and to Gṛtsamada as well.
By virtue of Gaṇeśa’s boon, they performed that sacrificial rite;
and at the commencement of every undertaking, they remembered Gaṇeśa first, beginning with his worship. || 3 ||
Thus that sage became renowned among the leader of the Gaṇas;
remaining perfectly steadfast, he offered supreme devotion while muttering the mantra.
Once, that sage Vyāsa let forth a supreme roar,
making the quarters, the sky, and the earth resound, as well as the mountain caves.
As he was going forward, he saw before him a terrifying child,
red in color, with a great roar, resembling a hibiscus flower.
Seeing such a boy— a mass of splendor that repeatedly stole away the path of his vision— he trembled, overwhelmed by fear.
He reflected in his mind: "What obstacle has come here?
I do not know; has this wonderful son been given to me by the Lord of the Gaṇas?"
He beheld again that one with a beautiful face and lovely eyes,
adorned with beautiful golden armlets, a beautiful crown, and beautiful anklets.
The sage questioned his son, whose hips shone with a beautiful waist-belt: "Who are you? To whom do you belong? And what do you wish to do? (10)
"And where are your parents? Give me a place, O child, you who are a treasury of splendor!
Ka said: Having heard these words of his, the boy spoke to the sage. (11)
The boy said:
"O knower of the past, future, and present, why do you question me?
Nevertheless, under the power of your command, I shall speak: my birth was from your hunger. (12)
"You alone are my father and mother; show me compassion!
O Sage, protect me for a few days, O Father. (13)
"O Lord of the Gods, once I am capable of subduing the three worlds, I shall bring Vaśavartin under my control; of this there is no doubt—you shall witness my prowess."
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words of his, filled with both fear and joy, the sage Gṛtsamada spoke these words in a gentle voice. (15)
"If even as soon as he was born, he is capable of attracting the three worlds, then I shall indeed bestow my own mantra upon him, my own son. (16)
"By this, the god Vināyaka, the Lord of the World, being well-pleased, will grant my desire; my fame shall endure. (17)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he imparted his own mantra to him;
and saying "gaṇānāṃ tvā," he made him perform the ritual with devotion.
"O son, fix your mind on Gajānana and recite Vedic mantras;
when he is satisfied, he will grant you all your desires. (19)
Having thus obtained the great mantra, he went to the forest for asceticism;
standing on his big toe, abstaining from food, he subdued his senses. || 20 ||
Meditating on the elephant-faced god with a steady mind,
he remained motionless while reciting prayers for ten thousand and five hundred years.
From his mouth issued forth fire that blazed toward the quarters;
fear arose among the gods and the Daityas who dwelt upon their surface.
Then, gratified by that asceticism, the elephant-faced god appeared,
dispelling the darkness from the quarters and obscuring the orb of the sun.
Wandering joyfully with his beautiful and excellent tusks, he trumpeted loudly;
hearing that roar, the young elephant became as if overwhelmed with distress.
Opening his eyes, he beheld the Lord standing before him—four-armed, of massive form, and adorned with various ornaments. (25)
Bearing an axe, a lotus garland, and sweetmeats in his hands, he was overcome by the other's splendor;
summoning his fortitude, he bowed down before him.
With palms joined in reverence, the boy addressed that Lord:
"O God, why do you oppress me, your devotee who has come to you for refuge? (27)
"O Lord, become even more gracious; grant me all that I desire.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of his, he withdrew his own splendor. 28.
Extremely pleased, he said: "O child, be attentive;
I am he whom you meditate upon day and night, and I now grant you a boon."
"This is my supreme form, self-luminous and consisting of the universe;
Brahmā, Rudra, and the others do not know it, so how could human beings know it? (30)
Neither all the gods nor the sages, nor other royal seers;
neither the asuras, siddhas, and gandharvas, nor the nāgas, nor the dānavas [possess such power]. || 31 ||
Thus, bound by your asceticism, I have come here to grant you a boon;
choose from me whatever boons you desire in your heart.
Then the boy said: "I am blessed by the sight of you;
my father is even more blessed today, and my birth and my ascetic penance have become fruitful."
O Lord of the Gods, I do not know how to offer praise due to my childish nature,
since you are the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of all the worlds.
By your radiance, this sun, fire, and moon shine;
and by your own majesty, O Great-minded One, you cause the moving and the unmoving to perceive.
Even your great hair does not truly know your immense majesty;
if you are the granter of boons to me, O elephant-faced one, then grant that to me. 36.
O Lord, grant me a distinguished power for the attraction of the three worlds—
the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, humans, uragas, and rākṣasas.
May the sages, kinnaras, and cāraṇas always be under my control;
may whatever I have conceived in my mind be accomplished at all times. 38.
May Indra and the other guardians of the world always perform service for me;
grant me manifold enjoyments here and liberation at the end. 39.
And I ask for another boon from you: by your command, let this city become renowned because of the fierce austerity that was practiced here by me. 40.
"May it attain fame among people as Gaṇeśapura, which bestows what is desired by the world.
Gaṇeśa said:
"You shall achieve the conquest of all three worlds. 41.
"You shall have no fear from anyone, and all shall always be under your control;
I have granted you these three cities made of iron, gold, and silver."
Impenetrable by all the gods, moving at will except for Śaṅkara,
it shall attain fame in the world by the name "Tripura."
"When Śiva pierces your city with a single arrow, at that very moment you shall attain liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (44)
"Whatever else you desire shall all come to pass through my grace.
Brahmā said:
Having thus granted these boons, the omnipresent Lord vanished on that very spot.
O Lord, the Asura Tripura fell into despair due to that separation. 45.
He experienced immense joy upon obtaining the boons as he desired,
and thereafter strove by force to achieve victory over the three worlds.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons to the Asura Tripura," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1415 + 46 = 1461.
Chapter thirty-nine, titled "The Defeat of Indra," ends here.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahman, what did Tripura do thereafter, being arrogant due to the boon?
You ought to tell me all of that in its entirety, for it is a source of great curiosity to me. || 1 ||
Brahmā said: Then, he installed an image of Gajānanī made from Kashmir stone, according to the prescribed rites, by means of Brahmins skilled in mantras.
In the midst of Gaṇeśapura, he constructed a great, divine, and auspicious palace made of gold and adorned with jewels and pearls.
He worshipped that Lord with the sixteen types of offerings,
as well as with innumerable prostrations, hymns of praise, and prayers.
Having asked forgiveness from the Lord of the gods and having received his permission, he went outside;
he bestowed many gifts upon the Brahmins according to their merit.
Thereupon, that place in Bangala became known as Tripura;
it is called Gaṇeśapura, bestowing all perfections upon everyone.
Then that Daitya Tripura, emboldened by the obstruction of Gajānana,
protected the worlds of men while remaining intent on attacking the gods.
Foot soldiers, cavalry, elephants, and chariot-warriors likewise went from the ten directions to serve him, being exceedingly powerful.
The kings became his servants through their compliance;
those who were hostile perished, being unable to wage war against him. || 9 ||
Having thus seized that portion of the earth, he then went to Amarāvatī;
there, Indra was surrounded by hosts of gods engaged in various forms of combat.
Mounted upon Airāvata and clad in armor, he advanced for battle;
that one of great strength also divided his fourfold army into three parts.
The great Daitya Bhīmakāya and the Dānava Vajradaṃṣṭra were both experts in bow-fighting,
mace-fighting, and combat with handheld weapons.
He spoke to that bull among the Daityas, who was skilled in combat with missiles and in wrestling and possessed a fearsome body: "Become the sovereign of the world of men."
The powerful Tripura spoke to Kālakūṭa and Vajradaṃṣṭra:
"Go to the netherworld (rasātala) with this third portion of the army."
O sacrificer, bring all the principal and remaining nāgas under my control;
with one-third of myself, I shall overpower Śakra and all the gods.
With his formidable body and adamantine fangs, he set forth as commanded;
accompanied by the fourfold army, he himself came to the Nandana grove.
Though being restrained by the soldiers, they broke down the celestial trees;
standing there, the king of the Daityas dispatched messengers to Śakra.
"Let them bring Śakra here with haste to see him;
let them either speak my words to him or depart for the world of death this very moment. (18)
There I shall protect you; give Amarāvatī back peacefully. If, however, your mind is set on battle, then come against me quickly.
Having gone, they reported to Śakra the deeds of the Tripura Asuras;
upon hearing these words of theirs, he was like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
He trembled like a tree shaken by the wind—the enemy of the mountains—becoming agitated with anxiety and wondering, "What is this? (21)
With all his eyes bloodshot, he blazed with the fire of anger,
as if turning the worlds to ashes and drying up the oceans.
He said to his messengers, "Go! Let them go quickly to battle!
Then the slayer of the enemies of the gods himself mounted Airāvata and roared.
Agitating the three worlds with that great roar,
those messengers, having heard his words, departed as they had come.
The gods also stood ready for battle, with various weapons and swords in their hands;
some held slings, while others carried spears and double-edged swords.
Some held mallets and sword-blades, others held bows and arrows;
some held clubs and shields, while others held staffs in their hands.
Thus accompanied by hosts of gods, the wielder of the thunderbolt went forth,
having had the rites for his well-being performed by the brahmins amidst the sounds of various musical instruments.
Having learned of that military exertion through the words of the messenger from Tripura, he made his fourfold army ready and joyful. || 28 ||
Having taken up countless [troops], he set forth mounted upon his horse;
those two armies, adorned with heroes, beheld one another. (29)
A great tumult arose from trumpeting and neighing,
from war-cries and the rattling of chariots, and from the sounds of various musical instruments.
Then, urged by Tripura with a mere "huṃ" sound, those heroes fought with the gods; that encounter was a great one.
Even those who did not distinguish between themselves and others struck one another;
thus, in that tumultuous battle, many of those Dānavas were slain. 32.
Though their minds were dejected, the soldiers there, fallen and tormented by the weapons of the Daityas, appeared like Kimshuka trees in full bloom.
Some who had not slept lay down, while others were deprived of their feet; camel-drivers became elephant-keepers, and chariot-warriors and horsemen became foot-soldiers.
Then, upon seeing the lion, the Daityas, desiring to live like deer, suddenly fled in the ten directions. || 35 ||
Then, having restrained that army himself,
the enemy of the gods— blazing with the great flames of the fire of his wrath like another roaring cloud— [advanced].
Approaching the presence of Śakra as if devouring heaven and earth, he struck the hand of Indra,
the wielder of the thunderbolt, violently with his own sword.
The vajra fell from his hand, and that was like a marvel;
seizing it, the Daitya struck the elephant Airāvata with that very same weapon.
Airāvata fled, intent on escape due to the blow;
then that Hari struck the bull among the Daityas with his fist. 39.
Having fallen to the ground for a moment, he rose up with great speed and struck Śakra with his fist, knocking him down to the earth.
Then, rising up, Maghavan, filled with wrath, said to the Daitya:
"O Lord of Asuras, prepare now for a wrestling match! (41)
Then, overcome with amazement yet proud of his own strength, he said:
"O Lord of the Gods, for what reason are you so merciless toward your own life?"
"Life is considered exceedingly dear even to worms, insects, and moths.
Go, O God, to the earth; a beautiful place has been granted to you by me. (43)
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra spoke:
"O enemy, if I do not indeed deliver you from death, [then let it be so]. 44.
"Then, O base one, I shall go to the earth, subject to your command;
you alone, O wicked one, shall go to the earth today with your head severed! 45.
While the lord of gods was speaking thus, the wicked lord of the Daityas struck him in the heart with his fist; thereafter, a battle ensued between the two.
Just as Cāṇūra and Kṛṣṇa, each desiring victory over the other,
struck heart against heart and hand against hand.
Kneeling on their knees, they struck knee against knee and thigh against thigh;
likewise, they struck head against head and elbow against elbow.
They struck each other back with their backs and feet;
then the Daitya, seizing his feet, whirled him around again and again.
He left Śakra far behind so that he might not be recognized anywhere;
then he himself mounted that lordly elephant with four tusks. 50.
Then all the hosts of gods, tormented by the fear of the Daityas, went to the caves of the Himavat mountain searching for Śakra.
"Where has the god fallen, or how shall we behold the Lord?"—
thinking thus and wandering about, they saw him.
As the lord of the gods was thus approaching with his face turned downward,
the hosts of deities prostrated before him, while others embraced him.
Others worshipped him, while another fanned him;
and some, out of devotion, performed the massaging of his feet. || 54 ||
Then all the gods dwelt in that very place in concealed forms,
while the Daitya, mounted upon Airāvata, went toward Amarāvatī.
Seated himself upon Indra’s throne, he divided the abodes of the gods among the Daityas, the enemies of the deities, bestowing them one by one with due honor.
Hearing the sounds of celestial musical instruments and the melodies of the Gandharvas,
he took delight while being attended by Kinnaras and throngs of Apsarases.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Defeat of Indra," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1461 + 57 = 1518.
Chapter Forty, titled "Description of the Hymn," ends here.
Brahmā said:
Having assailed the abodes of the gods, the Daitya went to the realm of Brahmā,
having previously heard from the mouths of the gods about the prowess displayed by the Daitya.
Brahmā went to the navel-lotus, and Viṣṇu went to the ocean of milk.
The two mind-born sons of the Daitya were Pracaṇḍa and Caṇḍa.
He established Pracaṇḍa as the presiding lord in the world of Brahmā;
then he himself made Caṇḍa the master in Vaikuṇṭha.
Then he went to Kailāsa and shook it with his arms;
terrified by fear, Girijā embraced Śaṅkara tightly. || 4 ||
Then the great asura went to Kailāsa, desiring battle;
Mahādeva was pleased by that daitya’s prowess.
He went outside to grant a boon, bestowing happiness upon his devotee;
he beheld the Daitya Tripura and then said, "Choose a boon."
He chose [this boon]: "If you are pleased, grant me Kailāsa today;
go to the peak of Mandāra as long as my heart's desire lasts. (7)
Śaṅkara also gave Kailāsa to him after a short time;
Giriśa himself, surrounded by his attendants, went to Mount Mandāra.
Having ascended the peak of Kailāsa, the Asura Tripura rejoiced;
thus having brought the gods under his control, he returned once more to the netherworld (rasātala).
Though possessed of a formidable body and great strength, he traversed the circle of the earth by force;
he brought kings under his control and bound all the sages.
He quickly destroyed all the sacrificial fire-pits that gratify the gods, as well as the hermitages and especially the sacred fords (tīrthas). || 11 ||
He terrified the ascetics from their refuge in the prison,
as well as the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ, and the recitations of the Vedas.
Always full of pride, Vajradaṃṣṭra constantly hated those of virtuous conduct; he then brought even the seven netherworlds (pātālas) under his control.

He made Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and all the serpents— both those that were venomous and those that were non-venomous— subject to his will. Vajradaṃṣṭra enjoyed the collection of jewels and sent them [to him].
Always sporting with curiosity and excessive joy alongside the Naga women, that self-controlled lord, enjoying various pleasures and taking diverse jewels, went to the vicinity of Tripura. || 15 ||
By proclaiming his mastery over the netherworld (Pātāla), he received even greater honor than that. || 16 ||
And having brought costly garments, villages, and numerous servants under his control—thus having brought the three worlds into subjection—the Daitya rejoiced. 17.
All the gods who dwell in the caves reflected daily:
"How will his slaughter come about, and at what time will it occur? (18)
"O best of sages, while the gods were thus perplexed in mind, they did not know for what reason he had obtained this boon, nor from whom."
Nārada, who wanders at will through the three worlds, arrived there;
seeing those gods in distress, he descended from the path of the sky.
Upon seeing Nārada, they all rose up suddenly with reverence; they embraced him, bowed to him, and honored him in due order.
When he had rested, they questioned him concerning Tripura and its excellence.
The gods said:
"The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, have been overrun by Tripura."
Our fortresses have been seized and even our hair has been conquered by him.
To whom shall we go for refuge today, and how can his death be brought about? 23.
"O sir, tell us by whom these boons were granted to this Tripura.
Nārada said:
"I shall relate in brief the great deeds of that Daitya."
For a thousand divine years, he performed supreme austerity and propitiated the Lord, Gaṇeśa, the leader of the gods.
Therefore, Durdharā granted him boons that cause terror to all—against gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas. || 26 ||
No fear has been granted by the Nāgas, except for the one Lord Śaṅkara;
let them propitiate with reverence the God of gods, whose face is that of an elephant. 27.
"May all of you propitiate Vighneśa, the bestower of all perfections.
The gods said: "How is the propitiation of that wise god of gods to be performed? (28)
"O tiger among sages, please tell us out of compassion what must be done.
Nārada said:
"I shall declare the single-syllable mantra to all of you."
"By means of that mantra which has been given by me with devotion, let all of them perform the ritual practice with steady minds. (30)
As soon as that Lord Gaṇanāyaka comes within the range of their direct perception,
he himself will tell everyone the means for his destruction.
"I see no other means; therefore, do as I say. Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus and having instructed all of them and Manu, Nārada [departed]. 32.
At that very moment, the sage departed, intent on singing with his lute;
thereafter, all the foremost of the gods became absorbed in meditation upon Gaṇeśa.
Some stood on one foot, some were seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana),
some were in the hero posture (vīrāsana), and some had their eyes closed;
abstaining from food and having conquered their breath, they muttered the mantra uttered by the sages.
Then, after a long time had passed, Gajānana, the ocean of compassion,
observed this long-standing performance of these gods.
Gaṇapa appeared before them as the bestower of boons,
adorned with a shimmering golden crown and beautiful earrings.
With his hands resting upon his teeth, adorned with a shining waist-string and excellent armlets,
he held a noose, a goad, an axe, and a lotus in his arms.
Adorned with red sandalwood, musk, vermilion, and the moon,
his splendor blazes with the brilliance of lightning, and his radiance is equal to ten million suns.
Upon suddenly seeing the Lord Vināyaka, who is free from ailment, they were all overwhelmed by his splendor, and some fell into fear. || 39 ||
Some gods suddenly bowed down to that elephant-faced one,
while others worshipped him, their voices faltering with joy.
To destroy their own distress, they praised that all-pervading Lord—the gracious-faced deity, the benevolent one who removes all misfortune. 41.
The gods said:
Salutations, salutations to you whose form is the supreme reality; salutations, salutations to you, the cause of all.
Salutations, salutations to you, the cause of all, who likewise dwell within all the senses. 42.
Salutations, salutations; let there be salutations to you who consist of all beings, O Lord of Gods! Salutations, salutations to the creator of beings!
Salutations, salutations to the awakening of all intellects! Salutations, salutations to the source of the dissolution and birth of the universe! 43.
Salutations, salutations to the sustainer of the universe, O Lord of all; salutations, salutations to the cause of causes.
Salutations, salutations to the one invisible even to the knowers of the Vedas; salutations, salutations to the bestower of all boons. 44.
Homage, homage to you who have become the very movement of speech; homage, homage to the dispeller of obstacles!
Homage, homage to the destroyer of the desires of the faithless; homage, homage to the knower of the desires of the faithful! 45.
Salutations, salutations to the Lord who fulfills the desires of the devoteless; salutations, salutations to the one skilled in the creation of the universe.
Salutations, salutations to the cause of the destruction of the Daityas; salutations, salutations to the destroyer of distress. 46.
Homage, homage to the supreme compassionate one; homage, homage, let there be homage to you who consist of wisdom.
Homage, homage to the destroyer of ignorance; homage, homage to the bestower of prosperity upon devotees. 47.
Salutations, salutations to the destroyer of the prosperity of the non-devotees; salutations, salutations to the liberator of the devotees.
Salutations, salutations to the binder of the non-devotees; salutations, salutations to you of manifold forms. 48.
Salutations, salutations to the awakener of reality; salutations, salutations to the supreme knower of reality.
Salutations, salutations to you, the witness of all actions; salutations, salutations to you, the leader of the qualities. 49.
Brahmā said: Thus praised by the gods, the Lord, the elephant-faced one,
being supremely pleased, spoke, gladdening the best of the deities.
Gaṇeśa said:
"O lords of the gods, I have attained satisfaction through this hymn and penance; I shall grant all your desired objects, so choose them, O sovereigns of the immortals. (51)
The gods said: "O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, slay Tripura, that Dānava who remains there having seized all our offices. (52)
By you alone was fearlessness granted to him from the entire host of immortals;
therefore, having fallen into this distress, deliver us quickly from this peril. 53.
"We have come to you for refuge; this indeed is our boon.
Gaṇeśa said:
"I shall ward off all fear from you against that most terrible one."
This hymn composed by you shall be exceedingly pleasing to me, and it will become renowned as "The Destroyer of Distress" (Saṅkaṣṭanāśana). || 55 ||
This bestows all desires upon men who read it or hear it;
he who recites this at the three junctions of the day shall never encounter any distress. (56)
Brahmā said:
Having thus granted the boon to those gods while the sages and deities looked on, the omnipresent Lord of the universe vanished right there.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of Hymns," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1518 + 57 = 1575.
Chapter Forty-one, titled "The Arrival of Nārada," Vyāsa said:
O Four-faced One, tell me who am asking you: what was done by the Lord Gaṇeśa, the bestower of boons and the accomplisher of all things? || 1 ||
Brahmā said: Then the elephant-faced one, in the form of a Brahmin, went to Tripura;
that best of the twice-born beheld him seated upon a costly throne.
Having risen and paid his respects, he seated him on his own seat;
having honored him, he inquired: "O twice-born one, from where have you come? (3)
"O twice-born one, tell me who you are when I ask: what is your learning, what is your name, and what is your purpose? If you have the ability, we shall do it for you. (4)
The twice-born one said:
"O Daitya, we are those who take refuge in the evening; we are all-knowing and all-perceiving.
Wandering through the worlds at our own will, we move about with the desire for their welfare. (5)
Renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Kalādhara,
she has arrived at your abode, desiring to behold your majesty.
Having now beheld all these riches of yours, we are truly satisfied;
such wealth exists neither on Kailāsa, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor even in the world of Brahmā.
"The prosperity seen in you is certainly not like that which is found in the station of Śakra.
The Daitya said:
"O twice-born one, do you know that which is merely a name, or are you a mere vessel for a fraction [of knowledge]? (8)
Whatever riches exist in all the worlds, those of which you speak so highly—
if you know them, show me the most magnificent among them.
"O twice-born one, having seen you, I shall grant you whatever you desire, even my own life;
O sage, I do not recall ever speaking a falsehood, even in jest. (10)
Kalādhara said:
"O enemy of the gods, what would it matter to you if you saw the prosperity of others?
I am pleased with your humility; indeed, I shall grant you a portion. (11)
"O Daitya, remain steady there for a long time and enjoy yourself as you please within this triple city made of gold, silver, and iron, which stands ready for your arrows."
O Lord, it is impenetrable even by gods, gandharvas, humans, or serpents;
it bestows whatever object is desired, moves at will, grants all wishes, and is auspicious.
O Daitya, at some point in time, when Hara pierces him with a single arrow, then he shall meet his destruction.
Brahmā spoke these words:
"Having said this, he took up his bow and fixed an arrow between its ends;
he then fashioned the three cities, which resembled the three worlds."
It was filled with various beautiful mansions provided with long ponds and groves,
frequented by flocks of diverse birds, and was a celestial vehicle that grants all desires.
Deluded by the illusion, the Daitya who was stationed there rejoiced greatly;
shaking the three worlds, the Daitya roared like a thundercloud. 17.
Filled with pride and arrogance, thinking "there is none superior to me," he agitated the three worlds; then [the sage] spoke to that brahmin.
"Ask for what is difficult to obtain, O best of the twice-born; I shall grant that to you.
Having been addressed thus, the brahmin spoke to that Daitya, even though he was free from desire. (19)
The twice-born said:
I went to Kailāsa and beheld the supreme form of Gaṇeśa, which was perfectly worshipped by Śiva and which grants all desired objects. 20.
"Bring her to me and give her to me, O Lord of Asuras, if you have the power;
for such a form as hers has never been seen by me as I wander through the three worlds."
Therefore, O best of Daityas, my mind is attached to her;
having obtained her, O Lord of Asuras, I shall have fulfilled my purpose.
I shall spread your fame throughout the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile;
for there has been no donor superior to you in Tripura, who bestows whatever is desired.
The Daitya said:
"O Śaṅkara, I consider myself your servant and do not regard the gods as such;
having brought her, O best of the twice-born, I shall deliver that image. (24)
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, he reverently honored that Kalādhara;
he gave him ten villages, as well as cows, garments, and ornaments.
Abundant pearls, both of great value and others,
as well as gems, corals, and blankets of ranku-deer skin.
The Asura gave a hundred male and female slaves adorned with various ornaments,
as well as excellent horses with protective fenders, and chariots with golden axles and silver frames.
Having taken this which was given by force, Kalādhara departed for his own hermitage,
gladdening his wife and all the inhabitants of the hermitage.
Brahmā said:
Thus Nārada related the entire account to the gods;
they, in turn, awaited the appointed time as the days passed by.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Departure of Kalādharaga," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1575 + 29 = 1604.
Chapter Forty-Two, titled "Description of the Battle," ends here.
Vyāsa said:
What did that Daitya do when Kalādhara had departed? How was it that he brought and gave him this auspicious form of the Cintāmaṇi gem? (1)
O Four-faced One, explain all of this to me in detail;
listening to the pastimes of Gajānanī, I am not yet satiated even with this summary. || 2 ||
Brahmā said: O best of sages, I shall tell you everything that the Daitya did after he had departed; listen attentively, O sage. 3.
He dispatched two messengers to Śiva, who was staying on Mount Mandara, and instructed them:
"Go to Śiva and respectfully speak these words of mine."
O Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, there is in your house an auspicious image of the Cintāmaṇi jewel that grants all desires; bestow it upon the king of the Daityas through peaceful means alone.
Whether in the netherworld, in the heavenly realm, or again in the mortal world—
whatever was wonderful there, all that was brought by that Daitya from the depths to his own home.
"O Lord, let it be brought quickly; let us go to that one of great strength.
When you do not grant [it] through conciliation, then that Daitya will show his prowess. (7)
"He will seize her by force, and from that you shall suffer misery.
Having heard these words of the Daitya, the two went toward Śiva. 8.
The two of them spoke to Mahādeva regarding what they had been instructed by the king of the Daityas;
having heard these words of the messenger, the three-eyed Lord was overcome with wrath.
He spoke to the two messengers, saying, "I have forgiven your words as messengers;
otherwise, you would both be reduced to ashes like Kama—of this there is no doubt."
"What business have I with that Daitya, who has become as insignificant as a blade of grass to my Lord?
Let him come; let there be battle alone, for he desires to die in my presence. (11)
This form cannot be attained by him even in hundreds of births;
does the fire of universal destruction ever attain peace by the falling of a moth? || 12 ||
Is it possible for a mouse to cause the fall of Mount Meru by its own power?
Would the great ocean become dry simply by removing an incalculable amount of its water? (13)
Brahmā said:
Having heard the speech of Śaṅkara, the Daitya departed as he had come and reported to his master the words that had been uttered by Śambhu.
Having heard that, the Daitya, who was skilled in understanding the meaning of words, blazed up;
inflamed by the fire of anger, he seemed as if he were burning the three worlds.
And he commanded his fourfold army for battle;
the army suddenly set out toward Mount Mandara. 16.
It covered the surface of the earth like a boundless ocean,
with heaps of unsheathed weapons resembling many suns.
Roaring as terribly as a thundercloud and causing the mind of Death itself to tremble, the Daitya ascended his great chariot, which resembled a celestial vehicle (vimāna). 18.
Thereafter, desiring to slay Manovega, he approached Śambhu, who was adorned with a large gem-studded, beautiful armor, earrings, and armlets. 19.
Wearing a necklace of pearls, finger-rings, a golden girdle,
and a highly precious, shimmering crown inlaid with jewels.
At the sound of which the Harmanasa lake trembled;
that bow, quiver, tortoise-shell shield, and firm sword [he took]. 21.
The divine spear, which that bull among Daityas carried,
shone brilliantly as hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases sang and danced around it.
Bards and wandering minstrels also went before him with joy;
and Śaṅkara, having heard from the words of the messenger that the Daitya had arrived, [prepared for his reception].
Then Śūlapāṇi, having honored the elephant-faced god— who was endowed with innumerable powers, eager for battle, and drawn on by Time— [spoke].
Having bowed to him, circumambulated him, and placed his army at the forefront by force,
he— his eyes blazing with anger— departed from his own place for the field of battle.
Making the ten directions resound with the roar of "heroes," those warriors,
desiring to slay one another, advanced with their weapons.
The two armies, having closed their ranks and being thick with dust and darkness,
slaughtered one another at the head of the battle, devoid of knowledge of friend from foe.
A tumultuous battle ensued, in which nothing could be discerned;
the ground was drenched with the blood of slain elephants, horses, chariots, and heroes.
When the dust had subsided, the heroes fought individually against heroes;
some with spears, some with swords, and others with arrows sharpened on stone.
Some were slain with spears and fists, others with axes and clubs; there, among the fallen heroes, horses, and foot-soldiers, [the earth was covered].
A river of blood arose, carrying hair for its moss;
it had shields for its tortoises, swords for its fish, and heads for its lotuses and water-weeds.
With whirlpools of parasols, most terrible, carrying headless trunks like trees, it produced satisfaction for the heroes and caused joy to the vultures and jackals. 32.
Having seen the river, the powerful Giriśa went toward the Daitya;
the Daitya, mounted upon Tripura, also went before him, moving ever forward.
Then, seeing their leader engaged in combat, the other Daityas and followers of Śambhu fought one another in pairs without any confusion.
With various divine weapons, missiles, and even trees,
I shall describe their battles and names in brief.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning: 1604 + 35 = 1639.
Chapter Forty-three.
Brahmā said:
Then Giriśa and the leader of the Asuras fought in single combat;
Pracaṇḍa fought with Ṣaṇmukha, and Caṇḍa with Nandin.
The valiant Puṣpadanta also fought with Bhīmakāya,
while Bhr̥guṇḍī fought with Kālakūṭa, who was like a life-taking poison.
The two of great strength, Vīrabhadra and Vajradaṃṣṭra, fought;
and there, the powerful Indra also fought with the minister of the Daityas.
There, Jayanta, who was invincible in battle, fought with the powerful son of the Daityas;
meanwhile, the preceptor of the gods, the foremost among those skilled in weapons, fought with Kāvya.
Thus, the numerous duels between the gods and the Daityas cannot be described by me even in hundreds of years.
Chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors, elephant-riders with elephant-riders, horsemen with their equals, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers [engaged in combat].
They fought in that terrible battle, which resounded with the noise of various musical instruments and was filled with the sounds of neighing,
trumpeting, leonine roars, and the clatter of chariot rims.
And some fought with various forms of wrestling;
having cast aside their weapons in the encounter, they struck one another's limbs with their own limbs.
Then Pracaṇḍa struck the six-faced one with nine firm arrows, whetted on stone and released after being drawn back as far as his ear.
Having cut them down with straight-knotted arrows even before they could reach him,
Kārttikeya struck them with five shafts.
Fainting, the fierce Caṇḍa fell to the ground with his mind bewildered;
he was also struck by Nandin with five sharpened arrows.
He suddenly fell to the surface of the earth and swooned;
then, with a formidable body, he pierced Puṣpadanta with ten arrows.
In that battle, he cut them down with his sharp arrows;
and they too, having reached the surface of the earth, struck him with three [arrows] each.
Then the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra, filled with rage, struck Kālakūṭa and Bhṛguṇḍi there with five arrows.
Then Vajradaṃṣṭra struck him with four sharpened arrows;
having warded those off, he himself struck Vīrabhadra with three arrows.
Vīrabhadra swiftly cut them down with three arrows as they were still approaching;
he struck Vajradaṃṣṭra with force using three shafts.
Indra, too, struck down a minister of the Daityas with the fall of his thunderbolt;
then the son of the Daitya, raising a sharp sword, advanced.
Desiring to kill him as he was victorious while the heroes had fallen, [Kṛtavarman],
beholding him thus advancing, cut his sword with a feathered shaft.
Jayanta quickly struck the son of the Daitya with three arrows;
struck by them, he vomited blood and fell down overcome by fainting. 19.
Thus, when all the armies had been broken on every side,
he saw the Daityas, afflicted by the hosts of gods, intent on flight.
Some victorious Pramathas pursued him from behind;
thus it was while the gods were winning and their own army was fleeing.
The Asura, stationed in Tripura, came to the Lord himself;
having previously engaged in a battle with weapons, both of them would indeed fight with their life-force (asrta).
The Daitya discharged the Vārūṇa weapon, and a most terrible rain fell;
due to the abundance of mist, nothing could be discerned in the battle. || 23 ||
In some places, there was a tumultuous, terrible, and unassailable battle, fought by means of the light of lightning, which produced knowledge for both oneself and others.
Having observed that entire army afflicted by rain and wind,
and seeing his own troops fleeing in the ten directions out of fear of the falling rocks, [he spoke].
Giriśa swiftly released the Vāyavya weapon;
the great winds and massive clouds were shattered into fragments in the sky. || 26 ||
The army of the Daityas, tossed about by the wind in every direction,
lost their feathered arrows and the turbans of the heroes at a great distance.
