Some chariots, horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers fell down or were crushed;
uprooted creepers and trees covered the warriors. 28.
Drawing his bow back to his ear and seizing an arrow from a blade of grass, the Daitya likewise warded off that wind with a serpent-weapon (pannagāstra).
Chanting the mantra for the fire-weapon (anala-astra), he hurled it at Śiva’s army;
a shower of burning coals, capable of consuming everything, suddenly fell.
Afflicted by garlands of flames, they all thought it was the dissolution of the world;
from those blazing flames emerged a man who inspired great terror.
A massive-bodied being appeared, scraping the surface of the sky with his head;
his face was terrifying with its fangs, he let out a great roar, and he was tormented by hunger.
Licking his terrible tongue, which extended for a hundred yojanas,
he whirled the elephants about in battle by the force of the wind from his nostrils.
He devoured that army as the king of birds devours a serpent;
thus, the army of Bharga, though tormented by that man, was protected.
Having reached the back of Śiva, she cried out, "Protect me! Protect me!
Granting her fearlessness by saying, "Do not fear," he warded off the fire.
At that very moment, by the discharge of the Parjanya weapon,
the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain struck down that terrible being with a single arrow.
Then that man arose and devoured the soldiers of Śiva;
the Pramathas, overwhelmed by fear, fled away.
Stumbling, falling, and sighing, they trembled;
even Śiva, due to his lack of assistance, sought refuge in a cave.
Indeed, the heroes headed by Ṣaḍānana followed him closely;
meanwhile, the Daitya, having perceived Girijā alone on the mountain, desired to seize her.
Having abandoned the battlefield, he went to Kailāsa itself;
seeing him approaching from afar, the Daughter of the Mountain then trembled. 40.
The Daitya went to his father and said, "What indeed will he do with me?
Having heard her words, [the father] took her to a difficult-to-access dwelling. (41)
He established her, unknown to anyone else, in a state of fearlessness;
then that Daitya also, with the desire to seize her, went toward the golden mountain.
Having arrived, O best of beings, he did not see Girijā anywhere;
while wandering about, he beheld there a single, auspicious image of Cintāmaṇi.
Having immediately seized her— who was radiant like a thousand suns, adorned with various ornaments, and the most beautiful in the three worlds— he went to his own abode.
Surrounded by bards praising him with the sounds of various musical instruments,
the victorious and powerful one then went to Pātāla, being triumphant everywhere.
As that Daitya was walking away, the form of the cintāmaṇi then vanished from his hand; it was indeed like a marvel.
Considering that very [event] to be an ill omen, he re-entered that city,
extremely dejected and fallen into difficult anxiety.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the Section on Worship of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 43 ||
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 1639 + 47 = 1686.
Chapter Forty-four, titled "Description of Austerities," Vyāsa said:
What did Śambhu do after being defeated by Tripura?
How did he conquer that Daitya Tripura, who was so full of victory? || 1 ||
Brahmā said: Then Śambhu, having reflected in his mind,
fell into deep anxiety as he contemplated the surface of the earth deprived of Svāhā and Svadhā.
When will the gods dwell in their own abodes, freed from their fever? By what means might there be the defeat of the invincible one, so that we may have our residence back? 3.
While he was thus consumed by anxiety, Nārada, the best of sages,
arrived there by chance, having seen Śaṅkara and all the gods.
Seeing him, the god rejoiced as a mortal would upon obtaining nectar;
he honored him according to the prescribed rites once he had accepted the offered seat.
Embracing him, Śiva, who was deeply distressed by anxiety and seeking the welfare of the gods as well as the destruction of the Daitya, spoke to him thus: 6.
Śiva said:
"The Daitya has wrought a slaughter of all the gods by his prowess;
with their resolve shattered in battle, all the gods have fled."
"O Brahman, they have fled to the ten directions; I do not know who remains where.
Even my own weapons have been shattered by their missiles by the thousands. (8)
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Śiva, O best of sages, he spoke to him, considering the defeat of the Lord of the Three Worlds to be a supreme marvel. 9.
Nārada said: [Salutations] to the omniscient one, the lord of all sciences, the lord of all, the creator of all, the one with all faces, the destroyer of all, and the controller of everything. (10)
O Lord, who is capable of acting, not acting, or even acting otherwise;
who is endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, and who sports with the sixfold sovereign powers (*ṣaḍaiśvarya*).
O Lord, what need is there for me to speak to you, the best of all speakers, who as a sage wander incessantly through the three worlds, intent on singing? 12.
"In accordance with your words, I shall speak after deliberating.
Having said this and meditated for a moment, the sage spoke again to Śiva: || 13 ||
The Sage said:
Because you did not worship Gaṇeśa when you desired to go to war,
the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose eye is fire, has therefore met with defeat.
Now, first worship Vighneśa, the warder-off of obstacles;
having propitiated him and obtained his boon, go forth to battle with devotion.
"You shall defeat that Daitya; there is no need for hesitation here.
Brahmā said:
"In the past, the Lord was propitiated by him as well through great ascetic penance."
By him, the remover of the entire multitude of obstacles, a boon was granted to him:
"Except for Maheśvara, death shall not come to you from anyone. (17)
The Sage said:
"Therefore, O Lord of the Mountain, shatter these three cities that move at will with a single arrow; this is declared to be the means for victory. (18)
Having heard the means from the sage, Śiva attained incomparable joy;
and having heard the words previously spoken by the elephant-faced one, he spoke to that sage.
Śiva said:
"O Brahman, you have spoken the truth; by your words I have been reminded.
O sage, those two mantras were indeed previously taught to me. (20)
Those two, the six-syllabled and the single-syllabled [mantras], are the removers of all distress;
yet they were neither recited nor remembered by him whose mind was entirely absorbed in battle.
The elephant-faced god, the remover of all obstacles, has indeed not been remembered;
he is the cause of all, the creator, the protector, and the destroyer—Vināyaka. 22.
The sage said:
"Propitiate that Mahādeva, the elephant-faced one.
Brahmā said:
Having dismissed Nārada, the auspicious Lord departed for ascetic penance.
In the Daṇḍaka forest region, however, he sat in the lotus posture and muttered prayers,
having forcefully restrained his senses and concentrated on meditation.
Śaṅkara performed fierce penance for a hundred years;
then, from his lotus-like mouth, a supreme being emerged.
Five-faced and ten-armed, with the moon upon his forehead and the radiance of the moon,
he wears a garland of severed heads, is adorned with snakes, and is decorated with a crown and armlets.
Surpassing the radiance of fire, the sun, and the moon with his own light,
the ten-armed god, overwhelmed by that brilliance, beheld a fierce being standing before him.
Seeing Vināyaka with five faces and another Śiva with five mouths, the god reflected: "Have I become twofold? (28)
Or has this Tripura come here in my very form, another five-faced one among the thirty-three crores of gods? (29)
Or perhaps this is merely a dream that I have seen for a very long time;
or else, this elephant-faced one has come to grant me a boon.
"The god who removes all obstacles, whom I meditate upon day and night.
Brahmā said:
Having heard those words, the elephant-faced one spoke. (31)
This omnipresent Lord, the remover of obstacles, who was meditated upon as the inner witness, is he himself;
even the gods, sages, and the four-faced Brahmā do not know my true nature.
Not even the Vedas along with the Upaniṣads [know me], much less those who know the six systems of philosophy;
I am the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the entire universe.
"I am the Lord of the three qualities (guṇas) of all beings, from Brahmā down to the stationary and moving;
pleased by this austerity, I have come here to grant you a boon. (34)
"Choose boons, O Mahādeva, as many as you desire from me."
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of Austerities," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 1686 + 35 = 1721.
Chapter Forty-Five, titled "The Bestowal of Boons by Śiva.
The Sage said:
Then, when Vighneśa, the lord of gods and remover of obstacles, was pleased and desired to grant boons to Śarva, what did Sadāśiva choose? || 1 ||
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of Gaṇeśa, Śiva then spoke these words,
recollecting that elephant-faced one who is his own form and the bestower of boons.
Śiva said:
"O Lord, today my ten eyes are blessed by your worship; likewise, my arms are blessed. My five heads are blessed by your prostration, and my five faces are blessed by your hymn of praise."
Earth, water, air, and the quarters; fire, time, and that which consists of calculation (intellect);
ether, taste, form, as well as smell, touch, sound, mind, and the senses. 4.

Gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, humans, celestial rishis, and all the hosts of gods—Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Vasus, and the Sādhyas—all these, along with the moving and unmoving world, have been produced from you. 5.

O Lord of the qualities, you who are of undivided intellect, you create this entire universe from the quality of passion (rajas), you protect all this, and you withdraw it through the quality of darkness (tamas); you are eternal, effortless, and the witness of all actions.
Brahmā said:
Then, by the command of Śiva, I spoke to that god Gaṇeśa;
listen, O high-minded one, to the name I gave him. (7)
Your name is the primary seed-syllable among the matrices (mātṛkās), having the form of the syllable Om and being the very root of the Vedas;
since you are the Lord of the hosts here, let your name indeed be Gaṇeśa. 8.
When "Om" was thus uttered by the Lord of the Gaṇas, Śarva was pleased and granted boons:
"O Lord, whoever shall maintain mindfulness of you in all undertakings, until the end of his life, shall obtain freedom from obstacles. (9)
Without this [mantra], even a worm or an insect cannot achieve the fulfillment of their desires;
therefore, in every undertaking, one should employ your mantras—whether Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, or Saura. (10)

Whether in auspicious or inauspicious matters, whether pertaining to the Vedas or the world, you alone are to be worshipped first with diligent effort—O Lord, you who are the auspiciousness among all people, including the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and serpents. 11.
Therefore, O Lord, you are the embodiment of auspiciousness for him, since you are the bestower of blessings upon your own devotees;
whereas formerly, O Lord, you were not worshipped by that foremost of Daityas in battle because he had forgotten you.
Because of my failure to offer salutation, I have suffered that defeat; therefore, I have taken refuge at your feet.
O All-Powerful One, forgive my offense and grant me victory at the time of battle against all people. 13.
O Lord, let even those who do not worship you in any way—those dull-witted and impoverished ones—attain prosperity;
but those humans who worship you with devotion shall attain the perfection that bestows all goals. 14.
Ka said:
Having thus heard these words, the knower of the essence of all speech addressed these words to the Lord of the Mountain:
"O Lord of Umā, whenever you should grant me remembrance, at that time I shall come into your presence. (15)
O Maheśa, having invited that single arrow with the seed-syllable of my name, do you indeed reduce that Daitya to ashes by casting those three cities down upon us with its great brilliance. 16.

Then, with his mind fully satisfied by Śiva’s devotion, the Lord of the Gaṇas spoke a thousand of his own names to him who was properly prostrate, bestowing victory and granting the desires of people.
And he said to him: "Recite this at the time of battle, and you shall swiftly slay the Daityas.
By chanting this at the three junctions of the day, all desired objects are accomplished for men. (18)
Having heard those words of the elephant-faced one, Śiva honored him properly and rejoiced;
he installed Mahāgaṇeśa and quickly constructed a high, firm temple for him.
Having gratified the gods and the hosts of sages and perfected ones, and having bestowed gifts upon the foremost of the twice-born,
the Lord of the Mountain once again worshipped and paid homage to the boon-granting god Gaṇeśa.
He said to them all, "Let this Maṇipūra become renowned throughout the entire world.
Then, having been thus addressed by the Lord and all those [deities], the chief leaders of the Gaṇas vanished from sight.

When the assembly of sages, along with the Lord of the Gaṇas and his father-in-law, had vanished, Śarva too, accompanied by his own attendants, Gandharvas, hosts of Yakṣas, and celestial nymphs, returned to his own abode; and amidst supreme joy, he spoke to Girijā.
Having heard all those nectar-like words from the Lord of the Mountains, the gods, the lords of sages, and the masters of yoga rejoiced along with their wives;
and they considered Tripura as already destroyed and their own celestial abodes regained through the grace of Giriśa. 23.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Bestowing of Boons by Śiva," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 1721 + 23 = 1744.
Chapter Forty-Six, titled "The Narration of the Nectar-like Hymn of the Divine Thousand Names of the Illustrious Gaṇeśa," ends here.
Vyāsa said:
How did Gaṇeśa instruct that Thousand Names to Śiva? O you who are intent on showing grace to the world, tell this to me. (1)
Brahmā said: Thus, it is said that when the Lord, the enemy of Tripura, was striving to conquer the three cities,
he became indeed overwhelmed by obstacles due to his failure to worship Gaṇeśa.
Having mentally determined that cause of the obstacle,
he then worshipped Mahāgaṇapati with devotion according to the prescribed rite.
The Great Gaṇapati himself, being personally gratified by the worship of Śambhu, asked Aparājita for the means of pacifying obstacles.
It is the sole remover of all obstacles and the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
then he spoke this thousand names of himself to him. 5.

Of this great mantra, the *Śrīmad-Gaṇeśa-Divya-Sahasra-Nāmāmṛta-Stotra-Mālā*, Gaṇeśa is the seer (*ṛṣi*). The deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Mahāgaṇapati; the deity is also Śrī Svānandeśa Brahmaṇaspati. The meters (*chandas*) are of various kinds. The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is "GAM."

"Tuṇḍam" is the Śakti; "svāhā" is the Kīlaka. The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of pleasing the venerable Brahmaṇaspati (or Mahāgaṇapati) by means of the destruction of all obstacles during the recitation (japa). Now, the ritual placements (nyāsas):
To Gaṇeśvara and Gaṇakrīḍa, salutation with the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha). To Kumāraguru and Īśāna, salutation with the two index fingers (tarjanī).
To Brahmāṇḍakumbha and Citvyoma, salutation with the two middle fingers (madhyamā).
"To the one red and wearing red garments," homage with the two ring fingers;
"to the one served by all true gurus," homage with the two little fingers; "to the one whose obstacles are destroyed for those with true devotion," homage with the palms and backs of the hands.
Now follow the heart and other nyāsas:
"The metre is the body of the metre," *namaḥ* to the heart;
"Partless and stainless," *svāhā* to the head.
"O you whose play is creation, maintenance, and dissolution—vaṣaṭ to the tuft (śikhā).
"Knowledge, realization, and bliss—hūṃ to the armor (kavaca).
"Bearing the fruit of the eightfold yoga—vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (netratraya)."
"Anantaśaktisahita astrāya phaṭ"— thus is the binding of the directions (digbandha). Now, the meditation (dhyāna):
Seated upon a red lotus that shines like a young sprout rising from a sea of blood,
the three-eyed one holds in his arms a noose, a goad, an axe, and the gesture of granting fearlessness;
he is endowed with a spear, possesses the face of an elephant, has a vast belly, and is accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi.
I bow to the King of Obstacles, who is red in color, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, and who removes all fears.

"Salutation to the venerable Svānandeśa, who is accompanied by Śrī, Siddhi, and Buddhi; who bestows a gain of one hundred thousand; who is Brahmaṇaspati, together with his limbs (Aṅgas), his retinue (Parivāra), his Śaktis, his weapons (Āyudhas), his vehicles (Vāhanas), and his enclosures (Āvaraṇas).
Having thus performed mental worship with the five offerings (Pañcopacāra) using this name-mantra, one should recite [the following].
The illustrious Mahāgaṇapati said:
Of this great mantra, the *Śrīmahāgaṇapatidivyasahasranāmastotramālā*, Gaṇeśa is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Mahāgaṇapati is the deity (*devatā*); and the meters (*chandas*) are of various kinds.
Gaṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja). Tuṇḍa is the power (śakti). Svāhā is the pin (kīlaka).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of pleasing the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati by means of the destruction of all obstacles.
The illustrious Mahāgaṇapati said:
"Oṃ! He is the Lord of the Gaṇas, he who sports with the Gaṇas, the Master of the Gaṇas, the Sovereign of the Gaṇas."
He has a single tusk, a curved trunk, the face of an elephant, and a large belly.
Lambodara, Dhūmravarṇa, Vikaṭa, Vighnanāyaka, Sumukha, Durmukha, Buddha, Vighnarāja, and Gajānana—[these are the names of Gaṇeśa]. || 7 ||
Bhīma, Pramoda, Āmoda, Surānanda, Mahotkaṭa, Heramba, Śambara, Śambhu, Lambakarṇa, and Mahābala. || 8 ||
Nandana, Alampaṭa, Abhīru, Meghanāda, Gaṇañjaya, Vināyaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhīraśūra, and Varaprada. || 9 ||
Mahāgaṇapati, beloved of wisdom, the prompt bestower of grace,
dear to Rudra, the leader of the hosts, the son of Umā, and the destroyer of evil.
The Youth, the Teacher, the Son of Īśāna, the one whose vehicle is a mouse;
he who is fond of success, the Lord of Success, Success itself, and Siddhivināyaka.
Avighna, Tumbaru, Siṃhavāhana, Mohinīpriya, Kaṭaṅkaṭa, Rājaputra, Śākala, Sammita, and Amita—[these were his sons]. 12.
He is the source of the Kūṣmāṇḍa Sāman, the invincible, the subduer of the wicked, the victorious;
he is the lord of the earth, the lord of the world, the imperishable lord of all beings.
The creator of the universe, whose face is everywhere, whose form is the universe, the treasure-house, the radiant one;
the seer among seers, the bull, the friend of Brahman, the Lord of Brahman. 14.
The eldest king, the lord of treasures, beloved by the lords of treasures,
he dwells within the golden city and resides in the midst of the solar orb.

He who destroyed the waters of the ocean with the blow of his hand, who shattered the teeth of Pūṣan, who takes delight in the dalliance on Umā’s lap, who bestows liberation, and who protects the lineage. 16.
Wearing a crown, earrings, and necklaces, adorned with a forest garland, he is composed of mind;
having destroyed the fortune of the Daityas through his aversion to them, he has conquered the earth with the stamping of his feet.
Sadyojāta, wearing a girdle of gold and muñja grass, the remover of ill omens, the destroyer of bad dreams, the victorious, the virtuous, and the one established in sound. 18.
He is of beautiful form, the abode of all eyes, seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana);
he wears yellow garments, has broken teeth, and bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. 19.
He has variegated marks and dark teeth, a crescent moon on his forehead, and four arms;
he is the Lord of Yoga, situated upon the star Tāraka, a Puruṣa with ears like those of an elephant.
The sovereign of the hosts, the victorious and steadfast, the lord of elephants, the bearer of the banner;
the god of gods, the life-breath of Smara, the illuminator, and the pillar of wind.
Vipaścidvarada, Nādonnādabhinnabalāhaka, Varāharadana, Mṛtyujaya, and Vyāghrājināmbara. || 22 ||
He who wields the power of will, the protector of the gods, the crusher of the Daityas;
he who was born from the mouth of Śambhu, who is the fire of Śambhu’s wrath, and who arose from the smile of Śambhu.
He is the splendor of Śambhu, the remover of Śivā’s sorrow, the bringer of happiness to Gaurī;
he is born from the body of Umā, the source of Gaurī’s luster, and the one arisen from the celestial river.
He is the body of sacrifice, the great roar, the one with the stature of a mountain, and the one with the auspicious face;
he is the self of all, the self of all the gods, the head of Brahman, and the Veda as his ears.
The jar of the universe is his forehead, the ether of consciousness is his brow, and truth is the hair upon his head;
the birth, dissolution, and emergence of the world are his opening and closing of the eyes, while fire, sun, and moon are his gaze.

He has the Lord of Mountains as his single tusk, Dharma as his lower lip, and is strengthened by the Sāman chants; he has the planets and constellations for teeth, Vāṇī (Speech) for a tongue, and Vāsava (Indra) for a nose.

With his hand placed between his eyebrows, intoxicated by the pride of the knowledge of Brahman, with the principal mountain ranges as his shoulders, the moon and sun as his bell, and the Rudras as his neck; 28.

He whose hair is the rivers and streams, whose fingers are the serpents, whose nails are the stars, whose navel is the sky, whose heart is the ocean of milk, whose back is Mount Meru, and whose belly is the great ocean. 29.
With Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, and humans dwelling within his belly;
with the earth as his waist, creation as his phallus, the mountains as his thighs, and the oceans as his knees. || 30 ||
With his shanks reaching down to the netherworld, with the Sage as his heel, with Time as his big toe, and with the three Vedas as his body;
with the spheres of light as his fingers, he is as immovable as a tethered horse at its heart-peg.
The lotus-stamen of his head is a pleasure-lake for the sky of Śiva;
he is the fetter for the meditation of true devotees and is warded off by the waters of worship.
The son of Kaśyapa, a leader of hosts, a lord of the world, powerful,
illustrious, righteous, self-born, the foremost, and the sovereign of the first.
He is the lord of the island of the wish-fulfilling gem, whose dwelling is a grove of kalpa-trees;
he sits in the midst of a pavilion of jewels, resting upon a jeweled lion-throne.
He whose feet are bathed in intense head-oils, who is caressed by the crown of Jvālinī, whose glorious seat is gladdened by Nanda, and whose throne is adorned by Bhogadā. || 35 ||
He is the sacred seat (pīṭha) that grants all desires, the refuge for the seat of the throbbing Ugrā;
he is the crest-jewel of Tejovatī, adorned with Satyā and Nityā as his ear-ornaments.

He is the sacred seat (pīṭha) that destroys all obstacles, the refuge of the lotus of all powers (sarvaśakti), the support for the lotus-throne of the letters (lipipadmāsana), and the locus of the three abodes of fire (vahnidhāmatraya). || 37 ||
He had elevated forefeet, hidden ankles, and well-covered heels;
his shanks were fleshy, his knees were closely set, his thighs were thick, and his hips were prominent.
With a deep navel, a large belly, a broad chest, and long arms;
with thick shoulders, a neck marked by three folds like a conch-shell, protruding lips, and a long nose. (39)
His left upper tusk was broken, his right tusk was prominent, and he had large jaws; he possessed three short eyes, ears like winnowing baskets, and a thick, heavy head.
With the tip of his frontal protuberance shaped like a cluster of blossoms, wearing a crown of jewels, unrestrained, with a serpent-garland as a waist-band and a serpent as a sacred thread; 41.
He has a crest-ornament and bracelets made of millions of serpents; he wears necklaces and armlets of snakes;
his waist-band and belly-wrap are of serpents, and the king of serpents serves as his upper garment.
He is red, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands;
his eyes are red, his hands are red, and the sprouts of his lips are red.
He was white, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands;
he was radiant under a white parasol and fanned by white chowries.
Complete in all his limbs, marked with all the auspicious signs,
enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, and endowed with every beauty.
He is the most auspicious among all that is auspicious, the cause of all causes;
he is the sole doer of everything at all times, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the bearer of the Bījapūra fruit, and the holder of the mace.
He has a white body, bestows happiness upon the world, is the thread of progeny, and increases the lineage.
He wears a diadem, earrings, and necklaces; he is adorned with a forest garland and auspicious armlets.
He holds a sugarcane bow and a trident; he has a discus in his hand and bears a lotus; he carries a noose and holds a blue lotus; he bears a cluster of rice blossoms and possesses his own teeth. 48.
He wears the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī), is the self-controlled master who grants universal fearlessness with his single hand,
holds a rosary of beads, possesses the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and wields a mallet as a weapon.
Holding a full vessel, bearing a conch shell, and carrying a swarm of bees; holding a citron fruit, possessing a mango bud, and wielding an axe.
He who rains down jewels from golden jars situated upon lotuses;
the Lord of Bhāratī and Sundarī; he who is fond of Vināyaka and Rati. 51.
He is the most beloved of Mahālakṣmī, enchanting with Siddhalakṣmī;
he is the prior body of Ramā and Ramēśa, and the southern body of Umā and Maheśvara.
He whose left side is the great Boar (Varāha), who is the western limit of Rati and Kandarpa, who generates fragrance and joy, and who is the delighter of those who are already joyful. 53.
The glory of his flourishing prosperity, the promoter of supernatural powers and accomplishments,
the one with a gracious countenance who bestows favor, and the abode where beauty has blossomed forth.
He whose feet are resorted to by Madanāvatī; who has rendered Daurmukhya faceless; who destroys the sprouts of the prosperity of obstacles; and in whom the flow of joy is awakened by service. 55.
His feet crush those who create obstacles; he is honored by the power of Drāviṇī; (he is encompassed by Śakti);
his eyes are intensely serene; and his singular gaze is protected by Jvālinī. 56.
The deluder of the deluding goddess, the bestower of enjoyment, adorned with splendor;
possessing the beauty of the beloved face of a passionate woman, he presides over the earth. (Endowed with glory, the radiant one, the one-eyed lord.
He is the master of the great treasure-vessel Mahāśaṅkha, which is swollen with the pride of the earth. (He who is fond of treasures.)
He was the lord of the great treasure-lotus upon the crest of the earth, which bears the name of the Goddess.
He is to be served by all true gurus; he has the fire-crested one as his heart-abode;
he has Īśāna as his head and Devendra as his crest; he is the delight of the wind-god.
He possesses eyes of the finest quality, is an expert in the employment of divine weapons,
and delights in the protection provided by all the elephants of the quarters, such as Airāvata and others.
He is surrounded by the Vajra and other weapons, taking refuge in the fierce Gaṇas;
he is encircled by Jaya and Ajaya, bringing about both victory and non-victory.
His lotus feet are worshipped by Ajitā; he is adorned with Nityā and Anityā;
he takes delight in the company of playful women; and he is embellished by the beauty of Śauṇḍī.
He bestows infinite and endless bliss; he is the most auspicious among the auspicious;
he is served by the powers of will (icchā-śakti), knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and action (kriyā-śakti).
His feet were graced by the goddess Subhagā; he was the refuge of the most graceful;
he desired his beloveds; and he was fondly cherished in the amorous play of Mālinī.
He is the refuge of Sarasvatī, the delight of Gaurī, and the abode of Śrī;
his state is protected by his Guru, he is perfected in speech, and he is the lord of Vāgīśvarī.
He is the lover of Nalinī, who delights in Vāmā, and who is enchanting through Jyeṣṭhā;
his lotus-feet are sealed by Raudrī, he has "hum" as his seed-syllable, and he possesses exalted power.
He is the creator and protector of the universe and all else, possessing the power of Svāhā and accompanied by his *kīlaka*;
he has made his dwelling in the ocean of nectar, and his eyes roll with intoxication.
He is the host of those who partake of leavings, the Lord of the hosts of those who partake of leavings, and the leader of the Gaṇas;
he possesses perpetual perfection, is eternally devoted to Śiva, and is sky-clad.
He is without calamity, possessed of infinite vision, immeasurable, free from old age and death;
he is unturbid, the peerless warrior, indeed the infallible, the immortal, and the imperishable.
He is beyond reasoning, imperishable, unconquerable, without support, free from disease, and stainless;
he is the unfailing success, non-dual, non-terrible, and possesses immeasurable faces.
Formless, destroying the power of the oceans, the earth, and fire, characterized by the unmanifest;
he is the foundational pedestal, the support, yet devoid of both support and supported.
He whose banner is a rat, the fulfiller of hopes, the great charioteer with a rat,
who dwells in the midst of the sugarcane ocean, and who is eager for the eating of sugarcane.
Possessing an excellence surpassing that of sugarcane, he is attended by Sugarcane-Bow (Kāma). 73.
Possessing a splendor like that of the indragopa insect, with a luster equal to sapphire,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and as pure as the orb of the moon.
He who is fond of sacrificial fuel, the recipient of the *iḍā* oblation, the abode of *iḍā*, and the beloved of Indrā;
he who destroys the obstacles of the Ikṣvākus, and who desires the performance of one's duties.
He whose crown is Īśāna, who is Īśāna himself, the son of Īśāna,
the destroyer of calamities, the end-maker of the three types of craving, and entirely devoid of all worldly effort.
Upendra, the one whose crown bears the moon, who is fond of offerings of uṇḍeraka flowers, whose face is uplifted, who is lofty, and the noble leader of the gods. 77.

He is full of vigor, possessing the intoxication of heat; he is difficult to overcome through reasoning and counter-reasoning; he is the source of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas; and he is the promoter of prosperity and spiritual perfection.
He is easily attained by those with a straightforward mind; he is the liberator from the three debts.
He has destroyed the obstacles of his own devotees and has deprived the enemies of the gods of their power.
He who has lost his fortune for those whose worship is turned away, the destroyer of spider-webs and boils,
seated in the center of the seat of the letter *E*, with one foot serving as his throne.
The glory that has caused all demons to tremble, the refuge that has caused all other refuges to tremble;
a treasure-house of sovereignty, bestowing worldly and otherworldly prosperity.
He is the manifestation of the delight of the Airammada lake, his face resembling Airāvata;
he is denoted by the syllable Om, he is the syllable Om, he is the powerful lord of medicinal herbs.
A treasure-house of magnanimity, foremost in the removal of arrogance, and devoid of the sound of pride;
he was a goad for the gods and nāgas, and a goad for the enemies of the gods.
He is proclaimed in words ending with the visarga followed by 'aḥ';
he holds a water-pot, he is the cosmic eon (kalpa), he has matted hair, and his face is like that of a young elephant. 84.
The witness of karma, the performer of karma, the bestower of the fruits of both karma and its absence;
shaped like a kadamba bud, he is the leader of the hosts of kūṣmāṇḍas. 85.
The embodiment of compassion, Kapila, the expounder, the wearer of a waist-thread;
the dwarf, the lover of the sword, the one who dwells within the depths of the sword-blade, and the one as pure as the void. 86.

He whose abode is the horn of a bald man, who carries a skull-topped staff, who is difficult to approach, who is rich in virtues, who is profound, who dwells in the forest, and who is an ocean of the nectar of prose and verse. (87)
He who delights in prose-singing, the thundering roar, the first-born of the gods of song;
he who is devoted to secret conduct, the secret one, and who is described as the arrival of the secret.
He who dwells in the cave, who resides in the ocean of the cave, who is accessible through the Guru, and who is the Guru of Gurus;
he who wears a garland of bells and small bells, who is like a water-jar, and whose belly is like a jar. 89.
The letter Ṅa is expressed by the syllable Ṅa; he bears the trunk of the form of the letter Ṅa.
He is fierce, a friend of Caṇḍeśvara, the Lord of Caṇḍī, and possessed of fierce valor. || 90 ||
The Lord of the moving and the unmoving, the wish-fulfilling gem, ever eager for the act of tasting;
he whose form is the Vedic meters, who is the meter itself, who is difficult to perceive, and whose body is the meter.
The source of the universe, the witness of the universe, the lord of the universe, and that which consists of the universe;
he is the recitation, the one devoted to recitation, the object of recitation, and the Lord seated upon the lion-throne of the tongue. 92.
It was filled with bees humming with the sound of "jhalajjhalla" from their joyful buzzing,
while its jeweled anklets produced a resonant clanging with a loud, ringing "ṭaṅkāra" sound.
Residing within the sprouts of the two Ṭha letters, he is the sole bestower of perfection for all mantras;
he is Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍa, the lord of Ḍākinīs, the fierce Ḍāmara, and one who is fond of the ḍiṇḍima drum. || 94 ||
Delighted by the sound of the drum, the elephant-headed Vināyaka approached.
He is the supreme reality among all realities, the reality defined by the state of liberation;
he is situated within the stars, the Savior, and the destroyer of the stars.
The immovable pillar, the beloved of the pillar, the one who abides, the stationary and the moving world;
the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the giver, and the deluder of the Dānavas. 97.
Compassionate, possessing celestial power, the wielder of the rod of justice, the leader of punishment;
he who shatters clouds with the luster of his tusks, the destroyer of the elephant-like Daityas. 98.
With the tusks of his elephant firmly grasping the neck of the demon, he appeared like a divine horse;
the lord of wealth and grain, the blessed giver of riches, the sustainer of the earth. 99.
He is the object of meditation, manifest solely through meditation, meditation itself, and devoted to meditation;
he has the series of cosmic eggs as his girdle, with the natural resonance of sound as his roar. 100.
Nanda, the beloved of Nandī, the Sound, established in the midst of sound;
partless, stainless, eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, and free from affliction. 101.
The supreme ether, the supreme abode, the Supreme Self, the highest state;
higher than the high, the Lord of Creatures, the liberator from the bonds of creatures. 102.
He is perfect bliss, supreme bliss, the ancient Supreme Person;
his lotus eyes are serene, and he releases those who bow before him from ignorance.
Beyond the reach of valid means of knowledge and ordinary cognition, he is the dispeller of the suffering of those who bow before him;
he holds a fruit in his hand, is the lord of serpents, the sound of "phet," and is fond of molasses. 104.
He whose pair of feet is worshipped by Bāṇa, who delights in childhood play, whose feet are worshipped by Brahmā, who is a celibate student, and who is Bṛhaspati. 105.
The greatest of the great, devoted to Brahman, a friend of those who know Brahman, and dear to the knowers of Brahman;
possessing a vast roar and a preeminent cry, he has the series of cosmic eggs as his girdle.
Bharga is the one who bestows fortune with a mere glance of his eyebrows; he is auspicious and the remover of fear.
The Blessed One is easily attained through devotion; he is the bestower of prosperity and is adorned with ashes.
He is the capable one, the abode of beings, the bestower of enjoyments, and he whose sphere of activity is between the eyebrows;
he is the mantra, the lord of mantras, the master of mantras, and he who is delightful to those intoxicated with passion.
Wearing a girdle, moving with a slow gait, possessing an intelligent and lotus-like eye,
he was of great strength, great heroism, great vital power, and great mind.
He is the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the protector of sacrifice, and the bestower of the fruits of sacrifice;
he is the maker of glory, attainable through yoga, the master of ritual, and the lover of those who seek.
He is the essence, the lover of essence, the one who is to be tasted, the delighter, and the one worshipped by Rāvaṇa.
He is the protector who guards against demons, the one whose womb is a treasure, and the bestower of the happiness of sovereignty.
He is the object of perception, the bestower of the object of perception, the one who is to be perceived, he who abides in dissolution, and he who is fond of sweetmeat balls.
He was fond of dance, devoted to the art of dancing, a bestower of gain, and renowned throughout the world.
He is the most excellent, fire-faced, worthy of worship, and the object of the Vedānta.
The transformer, with eyes on all sides; the ordainer, with faces on all sides. || 113 ||
Vāmadeva, the leader of the universe, who warded off the thunderbolt of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
The support that restrains all bonds, the Lord of All, the all-pervading one. || 114 ||
He is the Lord of the hosts of Śambhu’s powers, attainable through the peace of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
The Teacher, whose abode is the crest of the flame, the refuge, the Lord of the mountain peaks.
He wears a garland of flowers from the six seasons; he is the support of the six and possesses the six syllables.
The physician for the cycle of existence, the omniscient one, the medicine among all medicines.
He whose play consists of creation, preservation, and dissolution; he who is the shatterer of the elephant of the gods.
With his great frontal globes smeared with vermilion, he is the bestower of the manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent. || 117 ||
He is the witness, the churning of the ocean, self-realized, and self-bestowing.
Independent, of true resolve, devoted to the singing of the Sāman, and happy. || 118 ||
He is the swan, the lord of the elephant-demoness, the invocation, and the consumer of offerings to gods and ancestors.
He is the sacrificial offering, the beloved of those who have offered oblations, joy itself, and that which resides within the heart-etching mantra.
The lord of the field, the sustainer of the earth, whose supreme goal is forgiveness.
He who brings swift security, whose bliss is peace, and who is a celestial tree for the earth-dwellers.
He is the bestower of Dharma, the giver of wealth, the granter of desires, and the increaser of good fortune.
He is the bestower of knowledge, the giver of prosperity, and the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It bestows beauty, grants heroic glory, and confers victory.
It brings all things under control, removes defects of the womb, and bestows sons and grandsons. || 122 ||
It bestows intelligence, confers fame, removes sorrow, and destroys misfortune.
The remover of sorrow, the destroyer of misfortune, the possessor of all powers. 123.
It causes the mouths of opponents to become paralyzed, pacifies an agitated mind, neutralizes the malevolent spells of others, and brings about the destruction of suffering. || 124 ||
A lava, a truṭi, a kalā, a kāṣṭhā, a nimeṣa, a tatpara, a kṣaṇa, a ghaṭī, a muhūrta, a prahara, day and night, and a full day-and-night (aharniśam). || 125 ||
The fortnight, the month, the solstice, the year, the yuga, the kalpa, the great dissolution;
the zodiac sign, the star, the lunar day, the yoga, the weekday, the karaṇa, and the degree. 126.
The Ascendant, the Hora, the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), Meru, the Seven Sages, and Dhruva; Rāhu, Saturn, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, the Moon, and the Sun. || 127 ||
Time, creation, maintenance, and the universe—whatever is stationary and whatever is moving;
earth, water, fire, wind, space, ego, primordial nature, and the individual soul. 128.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Rudra, Īśa, Śakti, Sadāśiva, the thirty gods, the ancestors, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras. || 129 ||
The Vidyādharas, spirits, humans, beasts, and birds;
the oceans, rivers, and mountains; the past, the future, and the source of existence—[all these are he]. 130.
Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala Yoga, the Purāṇas, Śruti, Smṛti, the Vedāṅgas, the conduct of the virtuous, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya; || 131 ||
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, Gāndharva, Kāvya-nāṭaka, Vaikhānasa, Bhāgavata, Sātvata, and Pāñcarātraka. || 132 ||
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Kālamukha, and Bhairava scriptures;
the Śākta, Vaināyaka, Saura, Jaina, and Ārhata compendiums. 133.

Existence and non-existence, the manifest and the unmanifest, the conscious and the unconscious, bondage and liberation, happiness and enjoyment, yoga and its absence, truth, the minute, and the great.
Svasti, huṃ, phaṭ, svadhā, svāhā, śrauṣaṭ, vauṣaṭ, vaṣaṭ, namaḥ;
knowledge, discernment, bliss, awakening, consciousness, tranquility, and self-restraint. || 135 ||
He is the support of the single syllable, devoted to the single syllable;
he possesses one-pointed intellect, is the sole hero, and assumes both singular and manifold forms.
He is of two forms, two-armed, and two-eyed; the protector of the island of elephants;
the son of two mothers, two-faced, beyond the pairs of opposites, and transcending duality. 137.
He who has three abodes, three hands, and three streams [of seed]; the bestower of the fruits of the three aims of life;
whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas); the origin of the three worlds; the Lord of the three powers (Śaktis); and the three-eyed one. 138.
He has four arms, four tusks, four selves, and four faces;
he consists of the fourfold means and is the refuge of the four castes and stages of life.
He who sets in motion the transformation of the fourfold activity of speech, who is pleased by the worship on the fourth lunar day, and who is born from the fourth lunar day. 140.

He whose self consists of five syllables, who is fivefold in nature, who has five faces, who performs the fivefold cosmic acts, who is the support of the five, who is of five colors, and who is devoted to the five syllables. 141.
He who is five palm trees high, who has five hands, who is permeated by the five *praṇavas*, whose manifestation consists of the five *Brahmas*, and who is warded off by five elephants. 142.
He who is fond of the five kinds of food, the one with five arrows, whose nature consists of the five Śivas;
whose seat is the hexagon, whose abode is the six cakras, and who pierces the six knots. 143.
He is the destroyer of the darkness of the six paths, the great lake of the six fingers,
the six-faced one, the brother of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), and he who is surrounded by the six powers.

He is the destroyer of the group of six enemies, the shatterer of the fear of the six waves; he is far beyond the six systems of logic, devoted to the six duties, and the refuge of the six tastes. 145.
He whose feet traverse the seven netherworlds, whose vast mandala encompasses the seven continents,
who is crowned by the seven worlds of the gods, and who bestows the boons of the seven suns.
He bestows the happiness of a kingdom with its seven constituents; he is adorned by the assembly of the seven ṛṣis;
he is the treasury of the seven meters; he is the seven officiating priests; and he is the substratum of the seven musical notes. 147.
The essence of the play of the seven oceans, served by the seven Mothers, intoxicated with the joy of the seven meters, and the lord of the seven-meter sacrifices. 148.

He whose form is to be meditated upon as the eightfold form, who is the cause consisting of the eight primordial natures (prakṛtis), who is the ground of the fruit of the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), and whose seat is an eight-petaled lotus. 149.
He is the glorious one enriched by the eight powers, the bestower of the eight sovereignities;
he possesses the splendor of the eight seats and sub-seats, and is surrounded by the eight Mothers.
He is served by the eight Bhairavas, worshipped by the eight Vasus, and assumes the eightfold form;
his form vibrates with eight wheels, and he is fond of the oblation of the eight substances. 151.
He who sits upon the throne of the nine serpents, the ruler of the nine treasures, the support of the city of nine gates, and whose abode is the nine gates. 152.
He is praised by the nine Nārāyaṇas, served by the nine Durgās, the great lord of the nine lords, and adorned by the nine serpents. 153.
His body is variegated with the nine gems; he bears the nine Śaktis upon his head;
he is the soul of the ten, possesses ten arms, and is saluted by the lords of the ten directions. 154.
He who consists of ten chapters, who possesses ten vital breaths, who is the restrainer of the ten sense organs;
he who is the great mantra of ten syllables, whose body pervades the ten directions. 155.
He is praised by the eleven great Rudras, he consists of eleven syllables, he possesses twelve staff-like arms, and his abode is at the end of the twelve. 156.
The Viśvedevas, divided into thirteen classes, are his presiding deities;
he is the fourteenfold Indra who grants boons and the sovereign lord of the fourteen Manus. 157.
Rich in the fourteen and other branches of knowledge, he is the lord of the fourteen worlds;
he embodies the fifteen-fold Sāman chants and is as stainless as the moon on its fifteenth day.
He resides in the sixteen supports, whose source is the sixteen vowels;
he dwells in the station at the end of the sixteen, and consists of the sixteen digits of the moon. (159)
He is the seventeenth of the seventeen arts, possessing seventeen syllables;
he is the lord of the eighteen islands and the author of the eighteen Purāṇas. 160.
He is known as the creator of the eighteen types of medicinal herbs;
he is skilled in the knowledge of the individual and collective aspects of the eighteen varieties of scripts.
The person (puruṣa) is the twenty-first, possessing twenty-one finger-like sprouts;
he is the essence of the twenty-four principles (tattvas), yet is designated as the twenty-fifth.
He is the lord of twenty-seven stars, the creator of twenty-seven yogas, the sovereign of thirty-two Bhairavas, and the great heart of thirty-four. 163.
He is the source of the thirty-six principles, his body consists of the thirty-eight kalās,
and he is the unobstructed mass of the forty-nine winds.
He is the array of fifty syllables, the embodiment of the fifty Rudras, the Lord of the fifty powers of Viṣṇu, and the abode of the fifty Mātṛkās. || 165 ||
He whose body consists of fifty-two lineages, who rests upon sixty-three syllables, who is the determiner of sixty-four letters, and who is the treasury of the sixty-four arts. 166.
He is worshipped by the host of sixty-four great Siddha Yoginīs;
he is the contemplation of Bhairava in the sixty-eight great sacred sites and fields (tīrtha-kṣetra). || 167 ||
The Lord consists of ninety-four mantras and is additionally endowed with ninety-six;
he is Śatānanda, Śatadhṛti, and Śatapatrāyatākṣaṇa. || 168 ||
Śatānīka, Śatamakha, he whose excellent weapon has a hundred edges, whose abode is the thousand-petaled lotus, and who is adorned with a thousand hoods. 169.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he is praised by a thousand names and possesses the power to take away the strength of a thousand eyes. 170.
Seated upon the throne provided by the king of serpents with ten thousand hoods,
he was attended by the hymns of a multitude of eighty-eight thousand great sages.
He is the support for the beloved of the lord of a hundred thousand; he consists of the mind of the lord of a hundred thousand;
he is pleased by four hundred thousand recitations; he is manifested by four hundred thousand. 172.
Abiding within the bodies of eighty-four lakhs of living beings,
he is resplendent like ten million suns and as pure as the rays of ten million moons.
He is the preeminent leader of seventy-five million Vināyakas,
and his limbs possess the splendor of being consecrated by seven crores of great mantras.
The soles of whose feet are bowed to by the thirty-three crores of the ranks of gods, who is indeed served by infinite deities and praised by infinite sages. 175.
He whose name is infinite, whose glory is infinite, who bestows infinite and infinite happiness;
he who is endowed with infinite power and is praised by infinite sages—
Oṃ, salutation to him who is praised by infinite sages!
"Oṃ! Thus has this thousand names of Vaināyaka been proclaimed. (176)
The man who recites this every day during the hour of Brahmā (brāhma-muhūrta) has all happiness pertaining to both this world and the next held within his very hand. 177.
Longevity, health, sovereignty, fortitude, heroism, strength, fame, intelligence, wisdom, constancy, splendor, good fortune, and beauty; || 178 ||
Truthfulness, compassion, forbearance, tranquility, courtesy, virtue, restraint over the world, universal consensus, and eloquence in debate; 179.
The wisdom of the assembly, magnanimity, profundity, and the splendor of sacred knowledge.
Elevation, noble lineage, virtuous conduct, majesty, heroism, and nobility—180.
Through the single recitation of this, there shall arise knowledge, discernment, faith, fortitude, superiority over all, and an increase in wealth and grain. (181)
The fourfold subjugation of men arises from the recitation of this [mantra].
Of the king, the royal consort, the prince, and the minister. || 182 ||
He for whose subjugation this is recited becomes his servant.
The effortless means for accomplishing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 183 ||
It removes the fear of śākinīs, ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and uragas.
It bestows the happiness of universal sovereignty and crushes all enemies. || 184 ||
It destroys all strife, causes the sprouting of burnt seeds, pacifies bad dreams, and gladdens the heart of an angry master. (185)
It is the means for accomplishing the six rites, the eight great siddhis, and knowledge of the three times; it is the pacification of the deeds of others and the crushing of enemy armies. 186.
On the field of battle, this alone brings victory to all.
It destroys the defect of total infertility and is the sole cause for the protection of the fetus. || 187 ||
Where this hymn to Gaṇapati is recited every day.
In that region, there shall be no famines, fears, or calamities.
Prosperity does not abandon that house where this hymn is recited.
Consumption, leprosy, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and cholera; || 189 ||
Gulma, splenomegaly, urinary calculi, dysentery, and great abdominal enlargement.
It cures cough, dyspnea, upward-moving wind (udāvarta), colic, and conditions arising from swelling and the like. || 190 ||
Headache, vomiting, hiccups, scrofula, and loss of appetite;
Fever produced by wind, bile, phlegm, combinations of two, or all three humors. || 191 ||
The adventitious [fevers] are difficult to treat, being either cold or hot, and occurring every day or at other intervals.
Thus, whether mentioned or unmentioned, [the causes] arising from diseases, humors, and so forth have been explained. || 192 ||
A single recitation of this hymn quickly pacifies everything.
It is perfected by a single recitation even for women, Śūdras, and outcasts. || 193 ||
Success is attained by even women, Śūdras, and outcasts through its recitation once;
this mantra of a thousand names should be recited for the attainment of auspiciousness.
One who possesses desires, reciting this hymn of Mahāgaṇapati, [attains their fulfillment]. || 194 ||
Having enjoyed all earthly pleasures here according to his desire.
With divine, delightful celestial vehicles that fulfill all desires. || 195 ||
In the abodes of Candra, Indu, Bhāskara, Upendra, Brahmā, Rudra, and the others.
Capable of assuming any form at will and moving according to his desire, he wanders here at his pleasure. || 196 ||
Having enjoyed desired pleasures together with his beloved kinsmen,
he became an attendant of Gaṇeśa and a dear friend of Mahāgaṇapati.
He is the source of bliss for Nandīśvara and others, and he is himself gladdened by all the hosts of attendants.
And by the grace of Śiva and Śivā, he was cherished as no different from their own son.
A devotee of Śiva whose desires were fulfilled once again by a boon from the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Remembering his past births and devoted to dharma, he is born as a sovereign ruler of the whole earth. || 199 ||
But one who is free from desire, constantly reciting with devotion and intent upon the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa), [attains success].
Having attained supreme perfection in yoga, he remained established in knowledge and dispassion. || 200 ||
In the consciousness of supreme bliss, where joy arises incessantly.
Beyond the universe, on the supreme shore, free from returning again. || 201 ||
Absorbed in the abode of Vaināyaka, he rejoices, eternally liberated.
The man who would worship me with a thousand names should thus honor me. || 202 ||
Kings come under his control and enemies fall into servitude;
all his mantras succeed, and all accomplishments are easily attained by him. (203)
This hymn is even more dear to me than the root mantra itself.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Nabhasya, which was my birthday. || 204 ||
One should perform worship and libation according to the rules with dūrvā grass and by name; endowed with devotion, one should especially offer oblations with the eight substances. || 205 ||
All his desired objects are accomplished here; of this there is no doubt.
This [mantra], when consecrated, recited, caused to be recited, heard, or taught, [yields these results]. || 206 ||
It has been explained, deliberated upon, meditated on, scrutinized, and rejoiced in.
It bestows all sovereignty upon everyone, both in this world and in the next. || 207 ||
Even for one who wanders according to their own will, he by whom this hymn is upheld is protected by the eighty million hosts born of Śiva.
One should worship the hymn written in a book as if it were a mantra;
there, Lakṣmī, the most excellent of all, dwells perpetually. (209)

One does not obtain through all gifts without exception, through all vows, through all sacred fords, or through all sacrifices, that fruit which is obtained instantly by the recollection of the Thousand Names of Gaṇeśa. (210)
That person who recites these thousand names every day when the sun is rising— at dawn, at midday, or in the evening— whether thrice a day or continuously,
shall become pre-eminent in sovereignty, masterful in speech, and spread far-reaching fame.
It destroys all obstacles, brings everything under one's control, and increases for a very long time through sons and grandsons. || 211 ||
Possessing nothing, with a single-minded focus, self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one should recite [the mantra] for four months, intent upon the worship of Gaṇeśa.
"Having utterly uprooted poverty, even that which persists for seven births, one obtains great fortune; such is the command of the Supreme Lord. (213)
Long life, freedom from disease, a family exceedingly pure, and riches that grant relief to the distressed;
eternal and stainless fame, ever-fresh speech, and a beauty that is truly auspicious;
virtuous sons and a beloved wife endowed with good qualities—whatever this may be, it is all the fruit of truth.
In the hand of whoever constantly recites this hymn to Gaṇapati, everything is held.
Oṃ! Gaṇañjaya, Gaṇapati, Heramba, Dharaṇīdhara, Mahāgaṇapati, the bestower of a hundred thousand [merits], and the one who swiftly grants grace. (215)

Amoghasiddhi is the immeasurable mantra, the wish-fulfilling jewel, and the treasure-trove; he is the auspicious one, the seed-syllable, the fulfiller of hopes, the granter of boons, and the auspicious one. 216.
Kāśyapa, Nandana, Vācasiddha, Ḍhuṇḍhi, and Vināyaka—by these twenty-one names, a man [is honored] here with these sweetmeats (modakas). 219.
If one desires my grace, one should offer a gift with devotion for a year to Vighnarāja; this is the truth for the attainment of desired goals. 218.
He who praises me with his mind fixed on me and intent on my worship is, by that very act, as if he had praised me with a thousand names; of this there is no doubt.
Homage, homage to you whose feet are worshipped by the best of gods; homage, homage to you whose self is incomparable auspiciousness;
homage, homage to you who alone achieve vast deeds; homage, homage to you whose face is like that of a young elephant calf. 220.
O Gaṇeśa, Īśa, Heramba, son of the two mothers, elephant-faced one;
O moon of the forehead, smoke-maker, sun, pot-bellied Vināyaka! 221.
O Brahmā, O single-tusked one, O Lord of Obstacles, O Viṣṇu, O Kapila, O you who are beyond attributes!
O Kālādya, O infinite bestower of perfection, protect me from the ocean of worldly existence! 222.

May he who is praised by the sound of clusters of small bells upon his feet, who has manifested a multitude of noble and traditional conducts, and whose cheeks are moistened by waves of rut-fluid—the one known by the name of King Gaṇapati—pacify all misfortune. 223.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Nectar-like Hymn of the Divine Thousand Names of Śrī Gaṇeśa," in the section on Devotion (Upāsanākhaṇḍa) of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Īśvara and Mahāgaṇapati. 46.
The cumulative total of verses from the beginning is 1744 + 223 = 1967.
Chapter forty-seven, titled "The Victory of Śiva," Vyāsa said:
When the Thousand Names had been completed and Gajānana was propitiated, what did Hara do next, O Brahmin? Tell me that. (1)
Brahmā said: By virtue of the boon granted by Gaṇeśa and through the instruction on the names, Śaṅkara was overjoyed; he danced and roared with a great sound. 2.
Having summoned his own hosts of gods, he signaled the time for battle;
and those gods, with great joy, went into the presence of Śiva.
Brahmā, Kubera, Indra, Agni, Vāyu, Soma, Varuṇa, and Aryaman, along with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Grahas, and Kinnaras—all having paid homage to Śiva, praised him. || 4 ||
The gods said:
"O Mahādeva, Lord of the World, Bestower of Joy to the World!
When shall we behold the great Daitya slain by you?"
"We have been deprived of our positions by that destroyer of the universe.
Brahmā said:
"Having heard these words of the gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow went forth with joy."
Meditating upon Gaṇeśa in his mind and having resolved to engage in battle,
he reached the palace with speed, accompanied by gods and Gandharvas.
Meanwhile, the spies reported the news to the Daitya:
"The Lord of Girijā has arrived with the army of the gods for battle. (8)
His armies equipped themselves with weapons, missiles, and armor;
and that great-sounding Daitya was adorned with the ornaments of war.
He delighted the heroes with abundant garments, garlands, and ornaments,
while he himself remained in Tripura as the warriors were stationed upon their various vehicles.
The great Daitya ascended, making the intermediate and main directions resound;
then a mighty battle took place between the two armies.
With various kinds of weapons and iron arrows capable of piercing the vital organs,
a torrent of blood arose that caused an obstruction on the path.
Struck by weapons, the warriors appeared like blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees;
and some, out of firm enmity, slew their enemies while still alive.
Some, seizing them by the hair, forcibly cut off the heads of the chariot-warriors as they fled, as well as those of horses and elephants.
The dust arising from the falling of his feet pervaded heaven and earth in an instant;
in that most terrible darkness, nothing whatsoever could be discerned. 15.
Then those various heroes,
having abandoned all hope for life and being resolved to die, waged that battle most fiercely.
When the dust had been laid by the wind, the dead gods were seen;
the army of the gods was scattered, while the army of the Daityas rejoiced.
Purandara, the wielder of the thunderbolt who delights in battle, arrived;
and upon merely beholding him with his hundred-edged weapon, the Daityas and Dānavas fled.
The wielder of the thunderbolt pulverized the asuras with his vajra-strikes;
they, however, lost their lives due to those fierce blows of the vajra.
Some had their legs broken, some their necks broken;
others had their bellies ripped open, and still others had their shoulders and arms severed.
Among those heroes—horses and chariot-warriors alike—their hopes were severed;
some had their broad chests pierced, while others had their shanks struck down.
Some fell with their ankles severed, while others fell from treachery;
from the falling blood of those slain, many rivers were produced.
Then, desiring to increase the enthusiasm of those heroes who were longing for victory,
the Asura of Tripura gradually began to roar and beheld them.
Seeing that his army had been slaughtered in many ways, he then approached Śakra to fight;
upon seeing Śakra, he said, "For what purpose do you wish to die? (24)
"Depart from battle alive; I shall not strike at your back, O Vāsava.
What power do you have to fight with me, O Lord of Śacī? (25)
Tell me, how will a goat fight with a lion?
Come and fight if you have the strength; if not, go as you please. (26)
When Śakra had spoken thus and stood firm,
the Daitya drew his bow, made it ready with a string, and rained down many arrows, striking the army of the gods.
From a single enchanted arrow, countless shafts issued forth;
crushing the gods and Gandharvas, they filled both heaven and earth.
Once more, a dense darkness arose from the mass of arrows, leaving no gaps between them.
By those arrows as well, those gods fell to the surface of the earth with their limbs mangled.

the great triple city, which could travel at will and was dependent upon a single arrow.
That which is devoid of the movement of Marut and is impenetrable by all the Nirjaras—

Joyfully he went to Kailāsa, the king of mountains, which was adorned;

"How did she manifest herself on that lunar day, and where was the king of the Daityas when he was consumed?

Brahmā said:
On the full moon day of the month of Bāhula, that great asura was burnt at evening;
indeed, that most terrible battle by day has already been described.

Because bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, and other such acts performed therein yield abundant merit,

A ghee lamp, an oil lamp, various auspicious food offerings,

Betel leaves mixed with cardamom, cloves, and saffron, as well as fruits such as rose-apple, mango, jackfruit, grapes, and plantains. || 16 ||

One should install the internal and external matrices (mātṛkās) according to the path of the Āgamas;

Then, having performed the installation of the mantra and likewise the installation of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa). || 20 ||
Having purified the materials for worship, one should then meditate upon the elephant-faced one—single-tusked, with ears like winnowing baskets, possessing an elephant's face, and four-armed. 21.
The god holds a noose and a goad, and with his hands he carries sweetmeats;

Come, O support of the world, honored by the foremost of gods and asuras;
O Lord of the helpless, omniscient one, worshipped by the celestial beings! 24.
"O Lord, this divine golden throne, adorned with various jewels, has been offered by me; please sit upon it. 25.

"This Madhuparka, filled with curd, honey, and clarified butter, contained in a bronze vessel and covered with another bronze one, has been brought by me for your worship; please accept it. (36)
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, please accept this well-perfumed water brought from all sacred fords by me at your request, so that you may bathe properly. (37)
"O Lord, accept this pair of red garments offered by me; they ward off the shame of the world, are priceless, and exceedingly fine. (38)
O God, Supreme Lord, please accept this silver sacred thread and this golden one adorned with jewels, which have been offered to you with devotion. 39.
At your command, I shall place many golden ornaments, set with various jewels, upon each of your limbs.
O Lord, I anoint you with the twelve limbs using the finest red sandalwood, blended with the eight fragrant substances; please show me your compassion. 41.
O Lord of the World, please accept these grains of rice mixed with red sandalwood paste for the sake of beauty upon my forehead; may you accept them. 42.
"O Supreme Lord, please accept the pāṭala, the karṇikāra, the bandhūka, the red lotus, the mogara, and the mālatī flower. (43)
"Accept this most enchanting garland, woven with various lotus flowers and sprouts, and adorned with bilva leaves. (44)
Please accept this ten-ingredient guggulu incense, which produces every fragrance and causes the destruction of all sins, offered by me. 45.
O Omniscient One, the supreme destroyer of darkness in all worlds;
accept this auspicious lamp, O God of gods; salutations be unto You. 46.
There was milk-rice mixed with sugar and combined with various kinds of cooked foods,

When you are satisfied, the entire world is satisfied; O Great Soul, eternally content, I offer this fragrant water for the sake of the final sipping (uttarāpośana). 53.
I give you water again for the purification of your face and hands, as well as sweet pomegranate, and [fruits such as] nimba, jambu, mango, jackfruit, and so forth. 54.
Grapes, the fruit of the plantain tree, ripe jujube, dates,
coconut, orange, citron, and likewise ginger.
"O Lord of Gods, please accept this urvāruka fruit;

"Take this beautiful sandalwood, auspicious for rubbing upon the hands and limbs, and this excellent powder prepared from various fragrant substances. (57)
