By your grace, various divine narratives have been heard by me.
"O father, I do not reach satiety, drinking you in like nectar;
now, O Lord, tell me of a vow that grants the fulfillment of all goals. (10)
Furthermore, through the performance of this [rite], the accomplishments (siddhis) come into the hands of practitioners;
indeed, they arise for those adepts by the grace of the Giver of Boons. || 11 ||
Śiva said:
Well asked by you, O Skanda, that which brings benefit to all!
Out of affection for you, I shall tell it, which bestows great success upon the earth. 12.
"O dear son, O son of the Kṛttikās, this vow, which is dear to Vināyaka, is the best among all vows; it is the means for accomplishing all human goals."
Without sacrifices, as well as without gifts, recitations, burnt offerings, and the like—this [rite], O Skanda, brings about all accomplishments and increases one's sons and grandsons. (14)
This most excellent vow quickly brings a king, a prince, or even his minister under one's control. 15.
By the power of this vow, a person is instantly liberated from great sins and minor misdeeds accumulated over many lifetimes. 16.
On this earth, such a man becomes a vessel for all accomplishments;
indeed, there is nothing on earth equal to this in bestowing pleasure upon Gaṇeśa. 17.
Skanda said: "O father, in which month does this most excellent vow take place? What is its procedure, and by whom was it practiced in the past? (18)
"Tell me all this, if you have compassion for me.
Śiva said:
"On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, having bathed, one should go to the house of a preceptor."
Having bowed down to that preceptor and subsequently honored him according to the prescribed rite, || 19 ||
Having properly gratified him with water for the feet, water for sipping, garments, and other most excellent ornaments, one should begin the vow according to his instruction.
"O Father, O Guru, the vow of Gaṇeśa brings about all accomplishments;
you alone, O Lord, are Śrī Gaṇeśa, the bestower of desired objects. (21)
Having been instructed in the vow by him, he should go with him to the bank of the Gaṅgā,
or to a lake or a natural pool, and there bathe according to the prescribed rule.
O Six-faced One, having bathed here with a paste of sesame seeds mixed with white mustard and the dhātrī fruit, one should always go home after performing this rite.
Having sat upon a pure seat and having worshipped Gaṇādhipa according to the path instructed by the Guru, one should thereafter commence the vow.
On the fourth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should fashion an image of Gaṇeśa out of clay and worship it daily until the fourth day of the month of Bhādra.
Abiding in the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), one should perform this supreme vow by means of fasting, eating a single meal, eating only at night, or eating food obtained unasked. || 26 ||
At the fourth period, being composed, he should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya);
eating it with sweet syllables, the devoted one should practice the vow.
O Six-faced One, [I shall describe] the Gāṇeśvarī Vidyā consisting of six syllables, or even that of two, four, or likewise a single syllable. || 28 ||
O Skanda, one should perform the recitation daily for either ten syllables, or twelve syllables, or even a hundred thousand (niyuta), or ten thousand (ayuta). || 29 ||
Or half of that, or half of that again, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) consisting of a tenth part,
while meditating upon the elephant-faced god day and night without weariness.
When the month of Proṣṭhapada has arrived, on the fourth lunar day, one should worship Gajānana with a golden image weighing one pala, or even half of that, or again half of that.
One should fashion [the deity] mounted upon a peacock or auspiciously seated upon a rat;
having constructed a small pavilion there, one should arrange a heap of grain.
Then one should place a pitcher made of gold, silver, or copper;
upon that, one should set a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper.
Then, having wrapped the water-pot together with its bowl in a pair of garments,
it should be provided with five types of sprouts and endowed with five jewels.
O Six-faced One, having first performed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā), one should install that Lord there with the root mantras, those declared in the Vedas, and those previously mentioned.
Having meditated upon the elephant-faced god and invoked him with supreme joy,
one should offer a seat, as well as water for the feet and water for sipping.
O Skanda, one should offer the *arghya* accompanied by jewels, perform the auspicious bath with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and bathe the Supreme Lord with well-perfumed waters;
one should likewise present a pair of red garments and an excellent sacred thread (*upavīta*). || 37 ||
One should adorn the Supreme Lord with various kinds of ornaments,
as well as with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, incense, lamps, and diverse offerings of food.
One should feed the Supreme Lord with cakes, flour-balls, sweets, rice, milk-pudding, and the like, along with the five nectars and various side dishes. || 39 ||
One should offer a fragrant unguent for massaging, fruit, and betel leaf;
one should give a golden sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), as well as an umbrella, a fan, and chowries.
Having offered the lustration rite (nīrājana) and the flower-offering accompanied by mantras, one should recite hymns;
then, having praised [the deity] with the Thousand Names, one should thereafter honor the Brahmins. 41.
Having kept a vigil at night with auspicious songs, dances, and other festivities, and having bathed at the clear dawn and performed the daily rites according to the rules; 42.
One should worship the deity as before, and then perform the fire sacrifice (homa);
having offered oblations with various kinds of liquids, one should perform the worship of the preceptor.
One should present that [gift] consisting of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, and so forth to the preceptor, and one should also bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) upon other Brahmins. 44.
Thereafter, one should feed one hundred and eight Brahmins,
or more if one has the means, or at least twenty-one.
One should give food along with milk-rice to the distressed, the blind, and the miserable;
and again, having received the most excellent blessing, one should bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 46.
Accompanied by friends and kinsmen, he himself should eat respectfully while observing silence. || 47 ||
Śiva said: Thus, O Skanda, has this auspicious vow of the Giver of Boons been described to you;
it bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men and grants the fruit of all desires. 48.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history:
in former times, there was a king named Kardama who was supremely devoted to dharma. 49.
He protected the earth as far as the ocean's edge by his own splendor;
by his virtues, the gods were captivated even as they remained constantly in their assembly hall.
Once, by the turn of fate, Bhṛgu went to his house;
then the king, rising up, received him with great respect.
Then, having been honored like a preceptor, the king spoke these words to that best of sages as he sat upon an excellent seat after his meal.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all truths, I ask something; please tell me that.
Who was I in my previous birth, and what meritorious deed was performed by me? (53)
By this [deed], such a kingdom has been obtained by me, with all its thorns removed— a kingdom never attained by other kings, nor will others ever attain.
"I am worthy of worship even by the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas;
O Sage, behold my wealth, which is equal to the riches of Kubera. (55)
That which is the jewel of the three worlds was brought here by its own splendor;
whatever object I desire, I behold it within this dwelling.
"O Lord, tell me by what deed was this attained?
O best among the virtuous, I desire to perform that merit once again. (57)
Bhṛgu said:
O best of kings, I shall tell you through the power of my concentration:
in a previous birth, you were a weak but pure Kṣatriya. (58)
For the sake of maintaining your family, you performed various kinds of work;
yet that work which was performed did not yield any fruit for you.
Afflicted by extremely harsh words from your wife and children,
you went into the dense forest without even asking your son and wife.
Wandering in all directions, you beheld Saubhari seated upon the Siddhāsana, attended by the foremost of sages.
O King, having seen that divine Saubhari and the other hosts of sages, they were teaching the great vidyā that destroys suffering to their disciples.
You fell prostrate on the ground like a staff and were greeted by them;
then you sat upon the seat shown to you by that sage.
Having obtained the opportunity, you respectfully questioned that divine being.
The Kṣatriya said:
"O Lord, O Sage, I am afflicted in many ways by the suffering of saṃsāra. (64)
Though severely struck by the word-arrows of his wife, children, and friends—
even toward these cruel relatives— his mind does not attain detachment.
O Sage, although I am severely afflicted by cold, heat, hunger, and thirst,
tell me some means for crossing this ocean of suffering.
Śiva said:
Having heard these words of his, Saubhari, filled with compassion,
reflected upon a means to destroy the king's suffering.
Then the sage spoke to that Kṣatriya, who was to be liberated from all sins:
"With a resolute mind, perform the vow which I shall describe. (68)
By the mere performance of which all suffering comes to an end;
it was practiced by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as by the Brahmarṣis. (69)
They were liberated from all sufferings and attained the unsurpassed perfection of Gaṇeśa, the giver of boons, who bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
The Kṣatriya said:
Who is this Gaṇeśa? What is his character, what is his form, and what is his nature?
What are his deeds, and how was he born? Tell me all of that.
If you are able to let me hear it, and if you would favor me by doing so.

The sage said: The virtuous declare that Lord of the Gaṇas to be that Brahman which is eternal, stainless, free from sorrow, whose nature is knowledge, which is the supreme reality, without beginning, middle, or end, and boundless.
Know him to be the Lord of the Gaṇas, from whom arises the syllable Om, from whom the Vedas and the world proceed, and by whom all this is pervaded. 73.
For his gratification, Brahmā, desiring to create the world,
performed a most difficult penance for a full hundred years.
Then the Creator, with a joyful mind, honored him who was pleased,
with various services, divine jewels, and likewise with fruits.
The Lord, being pleased, gave him two daughters, Siddhi and Buddhi, whom he had conceived in his mind; the omnipresent God also granted him a single-syllable mantra.
Then, having obtained his authority and being gratified by Viṣṇu in the past, Brahmā created the entire world by means of the six-syllabled mantra.
Having fashioned an image of Gaṇeśa according to the previously mentioned rite,
Hari performed the observances for one full year without any deficiency.
Having obtained the boon from Gaṇeśa, he indeed protected the world;
know Gaṇeśa to be of such a nature, as he is praised upon the earth. 79.
Worship with diligence Him who possesses manifold forms, who is without beginning, and who is the cause of all causes; you shall be liberated from all suffering.
The Kṣatriya said:
At what time should this unsurpassed vow be performed?
O best of sages, tell me now according to which procedure it is to be observed.
"At your word, I shall do this for the complete pacification of all suffering. || 81 ||
The Sage said:
One should begin the vow on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
and perform it with supreme devotion until the fourth day of the month of Bhādra.
One should daily worship the earthly Gaṇanāyaka with the sixteen types of offerings with devotion, and thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas. 82.
"O protector of the earth, perform this; you shall obtain all your desires.
Having heard this from him, O observer of noble vows, you undertook that vow.
When the vow was completed there in the circle of Saubhari’s hermitage, his house then became divine by the grace of Gaṇeśa. 84.
It was filled with divine men and women, accompanied by male and female servants, resounded with the chanting of the Vedas, and became crowded with herds of cattle. || 85 ||
Adorned with divine garments and endowed with various ornaments,
she stood waiting in amazement, accompanied by her children who were likewise adorned.
"When will my husband return?"—such was her constant anxiety;
meanwhile, you, having taken leave of the sage, departed for your own abode. 87.
Leaving that divine refuge and searching for his own home,
he was led to that palace by men dispatched by his wife.
Therefore, you too have come to know that power of the giver of boons;
by its power, you shall share in a kingdom in this birth.
Śiva said:
Having heard these words of Bhṛgu, King Kardama, overflowing with joy, performed everything exactly as it was enjoined by Bhṛgu. 90.

By the power of this vow, the king, possessing knowledge and dispassion, having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire and having established his sons in his own position, [attained liberation]. 91.
He has gone to the abode of Gāṇeśvara, from which one does not return again;
it is the fulfiller of all aims, O Skanda, the supreme vow among vows. 92.
Never before has there been such a vow, such a gift, or such sacred learning;
it accomplishes all goals, O Skanda—perform this vow if you so desire.
It was performed by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, by sages and men, as well as by Damayantī, King Nala, and Candrāṅgada. 94.
Having attained all their desires, they went to the station of Gaṇeśvara.
The Mountain said:
"Thus I have told you everything regarding this great vow, together with its history."
Meditate in your mind upon Gaṇanāyaka, the bestower of boons. || 95 ||
"O highly fortunate lady, by this vow you shall thereafter attain Śaṅkara;
it was told to you today out of affection—do not disclose this vow. (96)
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Himavat and Pārvatī," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa. || 51 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 2164 + 96 = 2260.
Chapter fifty-two, titled "The Description of Nala’s Vow," ends here.
Pārvatī said:
"O father, tell me: why was this done by Nala? Who is Nala?
Hearing his story brings peace to my mind. (1)
Himavat said:
"In ancient times, there was a great king named Nala among the Niṣadhas;
he was devoted to the Brahmins, a knower of the Vedas, heroic, generous, honorable, wealthy, and a sage."

He was a charioteer, a swordsman, an archer, a bowman, equipped with quivers, clad in armor, and possessed of great strength; he was skilled in weapons, honored by the gods, capable of traveling through the three worlds, and pure.
Even the remainder falls into silence when attempting to describe his virtues;
there is no counting the number of horses, elephants, and chariot-warriors likewise. 4.
Out of fear of him, even the gods led by Indra, along with the lords of the quarters, trembled— those who bear bows, those who wield weapons, and even those who carry the fire-weapon.
He whose wife was Damayantī, a temple of beauty—
she whom Brahmā created by subduing all [beings], repeatedly extracting the very essence.
Because she was fashioned by him with the thought, "She shall be celebrated as Damayantī," he bestowed upon her the beauty of all women residing in the three worlds.
Adorned with various ornaments and embellished with diverse jewels, her neck radiant with pearl necklaces, she was exceedingly beautiful and rich in excellent qualities.
In that city there was a great minister named Padmahasta, who was valiant,
equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect, and equal to Aṅgiras in statesmanship.
In loftiness he was like Mount Meru, and in profundity equal to the ocean;
once, that high-minded King Nala was seated there. (10)
Seated in the assembly hall in the midst of the circle of kings,
beautiful apsaras danced before him.
And bards, accompanied by hosts of Brahman-sages, praised him;
at that very time, however, Gautama approached the king.
Having risen and been respectfully seated upon his own throne by the king,
Nala, having been honored with supreme devotion, then questioned him.
Nala said:
"O Lord, O great sage, you have favored me with your sight;
today my birth, my kingdom, my father, my mother, my lineage, and my very life are [fulfilled]."
"O Great Sage, speak quickly the cause that makes your own scripture fruitful.
Gautama said:
"O King, I had a great desire to behold your majesty. (15)
The gods residing in heaven—Brahmā, Indra, Hari, and Śiva—praise you:
"You are blessed; though dwelling in the world of mortals, you are extolled by both mortals and gods."
Though I am eternally satisfied, I am gratified by beholding this worship and this splendor;
now, grant me leave, for I shall depart toward my own hermitage.
The king said:
O Brahmin, knower of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, originator of all scriptures, ocean of compassion, O sage, pause for a moment and sever my doubt. 18.
The sage said:
"Well asked, O great king! Out of affection for you, I have remained here;
for neither serpents, nor kings, nor gods ever transgressed your command. (19)
The king said: "O Brahmin, having beheld my own majesty, I am filled with wonder. By what merit or by what austerity did this come to pass for me? (20)
"Tell me truly, who was I in my previous birth?
The sage said:
"In a region beyond the Gauṇḍa country, in a city named Pippala..."
Formerly you were a Kṣatriya, poor yet wise and pure;
you were severely struck by the word-arrows of your wife, husband, and friends.
At night, having questioned none, you went out of despondency to the dense forest,
which was filled with trees and creepers, and inhabited by lions, tigers, elephants, and deer.
Then, as you wandered and wandered through the forest, you beheld an hermitage attended by lakes with cool waters and adorned with lotuses and other aquatic plants.
Having gone there to that sage Kauśika, a treasure-house of asceticism who resounds with the chanting of the Vedas, you should bow down to him with a spirit of devotion.
Uplifted by Kauśika, who is compassionate toward the wretched and the helpless, he, having learned of your suffering, uttered a blessing upon you. (26)
"The Lord of Gods, with the face of an elephant, shall be your bringer of auspiciousness;
having heard that gentle blessing, you have attained supreme joy. (27)
O King, you have propitiated that Brahmin, who is the means for fulfilling all desires, the destroyer of poverty, the auspicious bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 28.
Kauśika explained the worship of Gaṇeśa to you.
Kauśika said:
"O lord of men, observe the vow of Gaṇeśa for the duration of one month. (29)
Fashion an image of Gaṇeśa out of clay that is beautiful to behold;
perform the worship according to the previously mentioned rite, and listen to the narrative. 30.
"Day by day for the duration of a month, you shall then attain perfection.
The sage said:
"Having heard this, the king questioned Kauśika once again."
The king said:
"I do not know Gajānana; tell me of his true nature.
Having recognized that Lord of the gods of gods, I shall perform the supreme vow. (32)
The sage said:
When this question had been posed by him, the best of sages spoke concerning the one whose nature is ineffable and who is the very embodiment of the Supreme Brahman.
These forms of the nature of the *vaikārika* (the creative ego), fashioned by Gajānana, [appeared] to him. || 34 ||
Kauśika said:
He who is the creator of all worlds, the father, the mother, and the teacher of the universe;
he who is to be meditated upon by Brahmā, Indra, Śiva, and Viṣṇu—that one is Gajānana.
The sage said:
Having heard those words and having prostrated before the lord of sages,
you were then permitted by him and went to your own abode.
Beginning on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, he undertook this supreme vow,
fashioning an image of Gaṇeśa out of clay according to the prescribed injunctions.
Whether standing, speaking, remaining silent, walking, lying down, or eating, you attained unsurpassed perfection by meditating upon the elephant-faced god. 38.

Through the power of his vow, he was born illustrious, endowed with various elephants, chariots, horses, and the like, with abundant herds of cattle and accumulated wealth, and accompanied by male and female servants. (39)
You have bestowed all kinds of gifts for the gratification of the gods, and with joy you have constructed a magnificent temple for Gaṇeśa. 40.
Having enjoyed pleasures according to your desire, you met your end in due time;
you have now been born in the land of Niṣadha as a king named Nala. 41.
Therefore, O you who are worshipped by the people of the three worlds, prosperity is now firmly established in you;
please grant me leave, for that which was asked has been explained.
Himavat said:
When Gautama had thus departed, King Nala, having gained confidence from his words, undertook a vow after fashioning a most beautiful image. 43.
Having heard the story of Gaṇeśa and having worshipped him with devotion every day,
he obtained all his desires through the power of this vow.
"Thus, O maiden, has been told to you how Nala performed this vow;
it was the very same vow performed in a previous birth that was taught by Gautama. (45)
The full extent of whose power cannot be described by anyone.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nala Vow," in the Section on Devotion of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa. || 52 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 2260 + 46 = 2306.
Chapter fifty-three, titled "The Account of Candrāṅgada," in the [section on] 1.53; Himavat said:
Now I shall relate, O fair-faced one, how this was performed by King Candrāṅgada and his wife Indumatī.
In the region of Mālava, there was a famous city named Karṇa;
there dwelt a king named Candrāṅgada, who was possessed of exceeding prowess.
Endowed with the qualities of *aṇimā* and the rest, he was a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures;
a performer of sacrifices, a giver of gifts, a man of great wisdom, and one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
He has surpassed the divine Sudharmā assembly,
which steals away the brilliance of your eyes with its rays like those of sun-crystals.
O daughter, some of the exceedingly pure garments take on a variegated appearance due to their proximity to jeweled pillars, through the reflection of blue, red, and yellow hues.
She was most excellent and highly fortunate, devoted to the service of her husband,
virtuous in character, dedicated to her vows, and attentive to her mother-in-law and father-in-law.

Undistracted by household chores and devoted to the worship of deities and guests, she was renowned by the name Indumati and was beautiful in all her limbs. Although the king was himself of virtuous character, he was earnestly entreated by his ministers.
Abandon the extremely terrible sin of violence toward living beings.
Once, by the turn of fate, he went out to sport in the hunt within a forest filled with hyenas, boars, deer, and birds.
Clad in a blue tunic, with a blue turban as his upper garment,
he had bound on his finger-guards of iguana-skin and carried a small knife, a sword, and a shield.
Mounted swiftly upon a horse, the powerful one held a bow and arrows in his hands,
surrounded by such multitudes of heroes as well as ministers and servants.
Slaying deer and boars and sending them toward the city,
the king was seen wandering in the forest by the foremost of the Rākṣasas.
Upon seeing those Rākṣasas— who had mouths like caves, eyes like pits, gaping jaws, and who reached up to the sky— he trembled like one afflicted by a cold fever.
Upon seeing them, all the heroes and even the servants fled;
some went to the abode of Yama, while others fell to the ground in a swoon.
There, a certain cruel ogress, seeing that king who was exceedingly beautiful, embraced him and, deluded by passion, kissed him. (14)
Having placed his ministers upon her lap, she devoured the servants;
in the meantime, the king fled in haste. 15.
Sunk in the middle of the lake, he was no longer seen by the Rākṣasī;
held fast by the Nāga maidens, he was led to the palace in Pātāla.
Adorned by the Naga maidens with garments, ornaments, and decorations, those Naga maidens asked him, "From where have you come? (17)
"Who are you? To whom do you belong? What is your name? Speak the truth, O best of men!
Having heard these words of hers, the lord of men spoke to her. (18)
I am the powerful Candrāṅgada, son of Hemāṅgada;
my residence is in the city of Karṇa in the region of Mālava. 19.
Terrified by the fear of the rākṣasīs, he entered the great waters;
having been brought here by you, that which was asked has now been reported.
"All the worlds have been devoured by me while I was devoted to hunting;
it is only by the grace of the lake's water that I remain alive at present. (21)
Having heard these words, they then spoke again to the king.
They said:
"Become our husband here; everything you desire shall be accomplished.
For us, the daughters of the Nāgas, such enjoyment is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (23)
Having heard their words, that best of kings replied:
"O mothers, I have a vow of devotion to a single wife; how then could I abandon it?"
I shall declare to you the duties of kings born of the Lunar dynasty:
[the avoidance of] another's property, malice toward others, and likewise another's wife.
Gentle and virtuous kings do not desire to revile others;
they practice study, perform sacrifices, give gifts, and protect those who seek refuge. || 26 ||

Abstaining from prohibited conduct and the fulfillment of the purpose of injunctions—these are the duties for the three twice-born classes; however, for the Brahmin alone, there are the three beginning with officiating at sacrifices (yājana).
"Hospitality toward all castes is considered the highest duty.
Having heard these words of the king, all the daughters of the Nāgas [reflected]. || 28 ||
They reviled him, saying, "May you be separated from your wife in many ways!
Those women, distressed and overwhelmed by passion, bound him with iron fetters.
But the rākṣasī, having drunk water for that purpose,
ate the aquatic creatures found in that lake, yet she was still not fully satiated at that time.
The lotus-eyed queen,
seated upon her couch, heard this account from her own messenger, who had been spared by the Rākṣasī.
Hearing that the king had passed away, she fell to the ground in grief;
fanned by her female companions, she fell into a profound swoon.
Sprinkled with cool water by women weeping again and again,
she sat there sobbing, beating her chest, head, and face.
She lamented with piteous cries, saying, "O husband, my beloved!
Where has my lord of life gone, having abandoned me, his sweet-spoken wife? (34)
She was complete in all her limbs, humble, and intent on doing what was pleasing;
she was constantly devoted to her husband's welfare and always honored guests.
Where will my lord eat, or where will he go to sleep, having abandoned his golden bed covered with most precious rugs? (36)
"How will my beloved bathe, having abandoned the fragrant oil?
Who today, without him, will carry out the protection of the worlds? (37)
Who was the delighter of all people and of all the worlds, and who was the repository of virtues and the treasury of prowess?
Why has he, that storehouse of qualities, set this day? (38)
I behold all directions as empty without that Great-Souled One;
where shall I find happiness, and where will he go to find happiness? (39)
O Lord, for women of noble family, there is no happiness either in this world or in the next, other than that which comes from being with their own husbands, even if those husbands are lowly. 40.
"And who will provide protection for those who have come for refuge? Who will protect the distressed? Thus she spoke in many ways, wailing, miserable, and utterly distraught.
Having torn them off, she cast her ornaments far away;
she broke all her bracelets and fainted.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Candrāṅgada," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśa Purāṇa*.

Chapter fifty-four in the dialogue between Indumatī and Nārada.
Pārvatī said:
When she had fainted, what did the people do then?
Tell me that in detail, O father, for it brings joy to my heart. || 1 ||
Himavat said:
Then all the city-dwellers, skilled in various modes of speech,
wiped away their tears and composed themselves before the king’s wife.
The people said:
"O mother, arise! Do not grieve; set your mind on your son.
It is the tear of grief that burns the deceased; therefore, do what is beneficial for your husband."
"O lady of auspicious countenance, among mortals no one has ever been seen who lives for a long time,
just as people discard worn-out clothing and take up another."
In the same way, O blessed lady, even after casting off the body, a living being takes up another auspicious one;

One should meditate upon the One-Tusked Lord (Ekadanta), who assumes a body according to the desires of his devotees and bestows excellence upon gods and men. 15.
Thus Gajānana arrived for the purpose of seeing him, accompanied by Siddhi and Buddhi, just as he had been meditated upon by the serpent previously. 16.
Resembling a thousand suns, he pervaded the quarters of the sky with his radiance;
by his splendor, even Śeṣa became as if blind, overwhelmed.
Trembling, agitated by fear, his mind distracted and extremely distraught, he became composed after a mere moment and reflected thus in his heart: || 18 ||
What is this radiance that has arrived, resembling the fire of universal destruction? If it should burn all the worlds, it will surely consume me as well.
"How can auspiciousness arise when a virtuous deed is being performed?
Or rather, as Narada said, I shall behold the Lord of the Gaṇas. (20)
While he was thus consumed by anxiety, the elephant-faced one said to him:
"Do not fear, O you skilled in fallacious reasoning; I have arrived as the bestower of boons."
"Choose whatever resides in your heart that you meditate upon day and night;
I alone am the creator, protector, and destroyer of the universe, the Lord of all."
By your ascetic power, the moon, fire, the sun, and the stars shine;
though you are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, you have been gratified by my penance.
"I have manifested for the sake of granting boons and also for the benefit of the world;
therefore, you yourself choose from me whatever boons you desire in their entirety."
Śeṣa said:
"O Lord, I am overwhelmed by your splendor; I do not dare to look upon you or speak to you.
O sinless one, you have already bestowed your full and gentle grace upon me."
Ka said:
Thus entreated by him, the elephant-faced one, an ocean of compassion and lord of the gods, became possessed of gentle splendor, shining like ten million moons. 26.
Then Śeṣa, the lord of all, having bowed and offered praise, chose his boons:
"I salute the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God who is without beginning or end. (27)
I bow to the all-pervading Lord, the cause of the cause of the universe, whose nature is everything, the Sovereign of the universe, who is worshipped by the universe. 28.
I bow to the elephant-faced one, the leader of the Gaṇas, the powerful Lord of Garuḍa, the master of qualities, the one who transcends qualities, and the sovereign of the hosts. 29.
To the Lord who is the sovereign of the sciences, the God of gods, beloved by the deities,
dear to both spiritual perfection and worldly wisdom, the bestower of all accomplishments, and the giver of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I bow to the Lord Gaṇanāyaka, the remover of all obstacles.
Ka said:
Having thus praised the Lord of gods, the giver of boons, whose face is that of an elephant, [he spoke]. 31.
"Listen, O great sage, to those desires he chose.
Śeṣa said:
'Today my penance, knowledge, father, mother, and birth have become blessed.'"
This tongue of mine, which has begun to praise you—though it possesses many bodies, many eyes, and many heads—is truly blessed. (33)
My family and my character are blessed by the sight of Your pair of feet;
O You of unbroken valor, grant me unbroken devotion. 34.
O King of Obstacles, what indeed can be said regarding you, the Omniscient?
Because you have caused such immense pride to arise, my head has burst asunder. 35.
O Great Lord, by the grace of Nārada, your lotus feet were beheld by me when I was cast upon the surface of the earth by you in your great wrath;
now, O God, grant me preeminence throughout the three worlds.
Grant me unwavering proficiency and the power to sustain the earth upon my entire head;
grant me a place where I may behold you constantly.
Gaṇapati said: "If your head has been split tenfold, O Lord of Serpents, [grant] the presence of Śaṅkara, the preeminence of your lineage, and devotion to Śivā. 38.
Then you shall become renowned among people as the thousand-faced one, adorned with a thousand hoods, for as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars endure. (39)
By my grace, you shall possess firm strength to support the earth and a stable position upon the five-headed one who has five faces. 40.
"O best of serpents, you shall attain my constant proximity; O Śeṣa, whatever else you desire shall be fulfilled for you in its entirety. (41)
Ka said:
Having thus granted him boons, she indeed bound him within her own womb;
thus Gajānana received the name Vyālabaddhodara (He whose belly was bound by a serpent). 42.
The Lord placed his hand upon the head of Śeṣa to grant him fearlessness;
with joy, he himself revealed his own form as Virāṭ to Śeṣa.
With his voice he filled the sky, the earth, the intermediate quarters, and the cardinal directions;
for whom the earth was beneath his soles, the quarters were his ears, and the sun was his eye.
The herbs are his body hairs, the mountains are his nails;
the clouds are the water of his perspiration, and the four-faced Brahmā is his organ of generation.
He in whose belly is the entire world and the four oceans,
who has infinite mouths, who alone possesses infinite eyes, and who is the self-ruling Lord.
He is of infinite form and infinite power, possessed of extreme brilliance, such that thousands of cosmic eggs shine within a single pore of his skin. (47)
Seeing him in such a state, Śeṣa became as if bewildered with fear;
he again entreated Vighneśa, saying, "Be gracious."
Then that ten-armed god became mounted upon a lion;
the boon-bestowing god said, "Such a being has never been seen even by the gods."
"O Śeṣa, by my grace and through your good fortune, you have been seen by me today.
Your station shall remain immovable with me, even in Pātāla and even in Śiva’s realm.
Today, being well-pleased, I grant it to you, O Supporter of the Earth, as easily as one might give a flower. (50)
Śeṣa said:
"O Earth, you who support the earth upon your own head are known as 'Dharaṇīdhara' (Earth-bearer);
this name of mine is likewise famous and renowned throughout the world. (51)
"Remaining firm in this field, fulfill the desires of your devotees.
Brahmā said:
"Om," and having spoken thus to him, that Lord of Obstacles himself vanished.
The remaining [prince] also, having fashioned such an image, installed it with devotion;
he constructed a beautiful golden temple, enriched with many jewels. (53)
Bestow upon him this name, "Dharaṇīdhara" (Earth-Supporter);
for he, bearing the earth like a flower, has become the bed of Hari.
He became firmly established even as an ornament upon the navel-lotus of Vighnarāja.
Thus, O Vyāsa, has this wonderful majesty of the Lord of Obstacles been recounted to you. 55.
In the city of Pravāla, Gaṇeśa is renowned as Dharaṇīdhara;
for this very purpose was the propitiation of the Lord performed by Śeṣa. 56.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śeṣa," in the Section on Devotion (*Upāsanākhaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Ganeśapurāṇa*. 90.

Chapter Ninety-one.
Vyāsa said:
"O Lord, tell me another story of Gaṇeśa;
O Master, my mind becomes exceedingly eager as I listen. (1)
Brahmā said:
Once, when the dissolution had occurred, Gajānana commanded me:
"O Brahmā, by my command, perform indeed the manifold creation."
Then, from my heart, I conceived seven sons;
I shall tell you their names: Kaśyapa and Gautama, as well as [the others].
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, Atri, and Viśvāmitra—these seven were masters of all branches of knowledge. || 4 ||
"All of them said to me, 'O Brahmin, O Lord of the Gods, give us your command.
I, however, commanded Kaśyapa, for he is wise and superior among them. (5)
Then, commanded by me, "Perform my work, which is manifold creation," he replied to me, "So be it," and departed for the forest to practice austerities.
He recited the single-syllable mantra for a thousand divine years;
thereupon, the Lord Īśvara, whose face is an elephant, became pleased.
Four-armed, with eyes like lotuses, adorned with a great crown,
holding a noose and a goad, with a garland and a tusk in his hands, possessing beautiful armlets,
enriched with gold, gems, and jewels, and with a neck graced by a shimmering necklace of pearls.
With a belly like a serpent and a radiant halo shining like ten million suns,
his face was graced by a beautiful trunk and eyes that were wide open and gleaming.
Thus, the elephant-faced one appeared right before Kaśyapa,
his feet made resonant by the sounds of small bells and anklets.
Seeing that god, Kaśyapa, overflowing with joy, danced;
having bowed down, he worshipped him with various auspicious objects. || 11 ||
With palms joined in reverence and well-pleased, he spoke thus to the elephant-faced god:
"Blessed are my father and mother; blessed are my asceticism, knowledge, body, and sight."
Blessed is this earth, O father, and blessed are the trees and their fruits;
blessed is the single-syllable mantra by which the Lord of All has been beheld.
The elephant-faced one, whose nature is serene, is the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
wherein the four Vedas are rendered blunt and the Upanishads have become mute.
This which has been beheld by me, O Goddess, is beyond the range of mental speculations,
since from it these gods, headed by Agni, have manifested as the faces of Hara.
The seven netherworlds and the fourteen worlds—
in which all these find their dissolution— that very God has been beheld by me.
He who is devoid of qualities, without a presiding lord, inaccessible even to teachers, and formless—
He whom some know as Brahman, that very God has been beheld by me.
Ka said:
Thus satisfied by the nectar-like essence of those words, Gajānana spoke to Kaśyapa, who was bowing down and praising him with various hymns. 18.
Gaṇeśa said:
"O sage, I am now pleased with you because of your devotion, your hymn of praise, and your performance of rites;
choose from me whatever boon you desire in your heart. (19)
Kaśyapa said:
O Lord, grant me the power to create various kinds of beings, as well as devotion to Your lotus feet and the state of never forgetting them. 20.
"Grant me such a son, a delight to Kaśyapa by name, whom you may behold directly and whom I too may remember. (21)
Gaṇeśa said:
"O great sage, everything you desire shall be fulfilled from me quickly;
may my devotion never be forgotten by you, and I shall come to your side whenever you face distress. (22)
"By my grace, you shall perform a manifold creation.
Ka said:
"Having spoken thus, the divine sage vanished right there."
Kaśyapa also, filled with joy, then departed for his own abode.
Once, Kaśyapa was suddenly afflicted by a bodiless being;
finding no peace anywhere, he then went into the interior of his house.
He no longer remembered his daily, occasional, or optional rites, nor even meditation;
seeing him thus distraught, his fourteen wives [approached him]. 25.
Diti, Aditi, Danu, Kadrū, Vinatā, and others stood before him;
Kaśyapa enjoyed their company in turn within various chambers.
At the time thus described, Diti gave birth to numerous Daityas;
Aditi to the gods and Gandharvas; and Danu to the Dānavas.
Gradually, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas, as well as numerous wild and domestic animals, arrived there. || 28 ||
The earth, mountains, trees, oceans, rivers, and creepers; grains, minerals, gems, pearls, insects, and ants. || 29 ||
From them came the serpents and the flocks of birds; indeed, everything moving and stationary arose from them.
Having thus seen that manifold progeny born, he then [reflected].
The wise Kaśyapa rejoiced; having purified his debts and wealth and having observed the wheel of enemies subdued, he imparted various mantras.
To some he gave the sixteen-syllable mantra, and likewise the eighteen-syllable one;
to another he gave the single-syllable mantra, and to yet another the six-syllable one.
That bull among sages bestowed upon someone the five-syllabled, the eight-syllabled, and the twelve-syllabled mantra, as well as a great mantra.
One should continue performing the practice as long as the god is being beheld—the elephant-faced one, the support of all, the bestower of all perfections. (34)
When he had thus commanded them, they departed at that very moment;
they went to many places for the sake of austerity and then each recited his own mantra.
Whether sitting, eating, sleeping, or even while awake, they constantly remembered the elephant-faced Lord of Gods with undivided devotion. (36)
At the end of a thousand divine years, Gajānana, the ocean of compassion, being well-pleased, manifested himself before him in his manifold forms.
Whatever manner of god anyone had meditated upon, such a form appeared before him;
and before someone else, there stood one resembling a cloud, possessing eight great arms.
Before someone else, he appeared as the moon-colored, four-armed one;
before another, he was that six-armed Lord of the Gaṇas, deep red in hue.
He possesses a thousand eyes and as many arms;
though he appears in the form of a child, he shines as a youth and also as an old man.
With ten or twelve mighty arms, smoke-colored and of great splendor,
he possessed eighteen arms and was as radiant as ten million suns.
He is of the nature of light, possessing a massive body, riding upon the back of a rat;
he may also be mounted on a lion or a peacock, having the face of an elephant and many faces.
Having seen the god, they all, bowing with palms joined in reverence, joyfully praised the elephant-faced deity with devotion in many ways. 43.
All said:

"We bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa, from whom arise the infinite individual souls of infinite power, from whom proceed all qualities from the qualityless and immeasurable One, and from whom everything shines forth, eternally divided into the threefold distinction. (44)

Since from Him the entire world emerged—the All-Knowing One, the Lotus-Seated Lord, the All-Pervading Protector of the Universe—as well as Indra and the others, the hosts of Daityas, and human beings; therefore, we ever bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa. 45.

From whom fire and the sun arise, from whom existence, earth, and water proceed, from whom the oceans, the moon, the sky, and the wind come forth, and from whom all stationary and moving beings and the multitude of trees originate—we always bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa. 46.

From whom the Dānavas, Kinnaras, and hosts of Yakṣas come; from whom the Cāraṇas, elephants, and beasts of prey come; from whom the birds and insects, and from whom the plants come—we always bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa. 47.

We bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa, from whom comes the intellect that destroys ignorance, from whom the seeker of liberation attains prosperity that brings satisfaction to his devotees, from whom obstacles are destroyed, and from whom the accomplishment of all tasks always arises. 48.

From whom comes the attainment of sons, from whom the fulfillment of desired objects, and from whom manifold forms of devotion and knowledge arise; from whom come sorrow and delusion, and from whom desire itself ever proceeds—to that Gaṇeśa we bow and we worship. 49.
Since he possesses infinite power, that Śeṣa became the supporter of the earth and is capable of assuming manifold forms;
since the heavenly worlds indeed exist eternally in various ways through him, we bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa. 50.

We bow to and worship that Gaṇeśa, whose form is the Supreme Brahman, who consists of consciousness and bliss, and whom the words of the Vedas—stumbling with their minds—can never grasp, saying "not this, not this. 51.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Creation of Kaśyapa," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśapurāṇa.

Chapter Ninety-Two, titled "The Definition of the Name Gajānana," within the dialogue between Brahmā, Vyāsa, Bhṛgu, Soma, and Kāntā.
Ka said:
Having thus bowed to and praised Gajānana, they all spoke again to the Lord of the Gaṇas: "Today we are most blessed. (1)
O ancestors, our asceticism, charity, knowledge, and sacrifice are blessed;
today our very sight is blessed, for by it we have beheld the elephant-faced one.
Thus gratified by their words, which were like nectar, and by their praises,
the Elephant-faced One spoke while they listened, out of his profound majesty.
"Such a form as this has never been seen by me among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others— that form of mine which is now directly perceived by all, being devoid of qualities."
Highly pleased by this hymn of praise, I have come here to grant boons;
choose whatever you desire, indeed, everything that you wish for.
O Lord of Sages, having been addressed thus by that Vikaṭa,
they then chose from that elephant-faced one whatever was desired by each.
Because the boons granted by him are innumerable, they cannot be fully described even by four-faced Brahmās;
therefore, I have spoken of them in brief.
He granted each of those various boons that all had requested from the elephant-faced one.
Again he said to them all: "This hymn of praise is dear to me;
whoever recites it at the three junctions of the day shall become possessed of knowledge and blessed with sons."
One shall obtain longevity, health, sovereignty, fame, prosperity, victory, and success;
one shall attain all desired objects and, in the end, the supreme state.
Again, the Lord of the Gaṇas said: "A person should recite this hymn."
At the three junctions of the day, all his work shall be accomplished.
Whoever recites these eight auspicious verses eight times on the fourth lunar day for eight days shall attain the eight supernatural powers (siddhis). || 9 ||
Whoever recites this ten times every day for the duration of a month shall undoubtedly liberate from bondage that person imprisoned by the king. 10.
One desiring knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one seeking a son shall obtain a son;
indeed, one shall obtain every desired object by reciting it twenty-one times.
"The man who, devoted to Gajānana, shall recite [this] with supreme devotion.
Having spoken thus, the God then [disappeared] while everyone was looking on.
That elephant-faced one, the support of all, who possesses a beautiful countenance, vanished;
and they then fashioned an image of Gaṇeśa with a gracious face.
And having installed her in a magnificent palace constructed of jewels,
they gave her the very famous name Sumukhī.
Having worshipped and paid their respects, the gods departed for their respective abodes;
likewise, all those sages and worldly beings then returned to their various duties.
Some clearly gave her the name Ekadantī;
others, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras, established another supreme form for her.
Having worshipped her in many ways within an excellent golden palace,
they established for her the supreme name "Kapilā."
The Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, and Siddhas assumed other forms;
having established her in Mahālaya, they bowed to her and worshipped her. || 18 ||
They gave her the name Gajakarṇī, which was significant in its literal meaning;
by her power, they all ascended to heaven, seated in celestial chariots.
She was established by all human beings under the name Lambodarā,
while another supreme form was established by all the beasts of prey.
They worshipped her by the name Vikaṭā and departed for the forest;
likewise, the mountains and trees, having established another image and performed worship, [departed].
Having thus given them the name "Vighnanāśana" (Destroyers of Obstacles), they remained there on the earth;
and by his grace, those mountains and trees became renowned as such.
A form made of jewels and gold was established by all the flocks of birds;
it was worshipped and saluted by them under the name "Gaṇādhipa."
A single leader was appointed by all the serpent-bearers;
she whom they invoked was clearly known as Dhūmaketu.
A single auspicious image was installed by all the reservoirs of water;
it is worshipped with great festivals under the name Gaṇādhyakṣa.
By means of multitudes of worms, insects, and the like, as well as groups of trees and medicinal herbs, the supreme form was established, renowned as Bhālacandra. || 26 ||
By others who possess consciousness, another great image of Vaināyaka was worshipped with a spirit of devotion within the midst of a jeweled palace. || 27 ||
Renowned by the name Gajānana, she grants all desires to everyone;
they became famous throughout the three worlds, each according to their respective caste. 28.
"O Lord, by Your grace, they are happy and proficient in their respective duties;
I have the power to mention each of them by name. (29)
Having extracted the essence from the essence, this collection was composed as the "Thousand Names";
even from among those, twelve names were declared to be the very core of the essence.
Just as fourteen jewels were produced from the churning of the ocean,
so too, O Brahman, has your greatness been described to you in brief.
Śeṣa is not capable of describing it in detail, nor am I, nor even Hari;
[so too] the gods beginning with Indra, the living beings such as mosquitoes, and the yakṣas and rākṣasas.
In that regard, O son of Satyavatī, what need is there for me to calculate [the merit]?
Therefore, Gajānana is to be worshipped in all undertakings. 33.
He who does not worship the God of gods, the destroyer of obstacles—
that evil-souled one should be shunned from afar like a caṇḍāla.
The Sage said:
"Tell me the twelve names in their proper order;
by hearing or reciting them, everything shall proceed without obstacle. (35)
Brahmā said: Sumukha, Ekadanta, Kapila, Gajakarṇaka, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnanāśa, and Gaṇādhipa— || 36 ||
Dhūmraketu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Bhālacandra, and Gajānana—whosoever should recite or even hear these twelve names. || 37 ||
At the commencement of learning, at marriage, at entering or departing [a home],
as well as in battle or in times of distress, no obstacle shall arise for him.
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon the God who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a serene countenance. 39.
The giving away of ten million maidens, ten million sacrifices, and all vows, as well as all austerities, sacred fords, and shrines—[all these do not equal a sixteenth part of the merit of this]. 40.
Thousands of bhāras of gold, even the gifts of ten million, as well as the kṛcchra, taptakṛcchra, parāka, and induvrata penances—[all these do not equal the merit of this]. 41.
Even a hundredth part of the merit of these names is not attained by those [other acts].
Having risen in the morning, being pure and composed, one should recite these. (42)
The man who recites this with devotion—no obstacles shall come to that person;
all his undertakings will succeed, and in the end, he attains liberation. 43.
By the sight of him, the worlds and the gods become purified;
for this very reason, O Sage, there are the Sauras, Śāktas, Śaivas, and Vaiṣṇavas.
Having uttered the twelve names, they accomplish all their tasks;
even the attendants of Gaṇeśa perform them—what wonder is there in this? 45.
Indeed, O Brahman, the twelve effects are not accomplished without the utterance [of the breath]; therefore, one should utter that single [breath]. 46.
Whatever task is accomplished by the wicked and the nihilists, they too perform it by uttering the seed-syllable, even if out of ignorance. 47.
Thus, O Sage, your entire greatness has been described in brief;
the various fruits of worship have been set forth according to my understanding. 48.
As much as was told by Viṣṇu, that much has been described to you;
even he did not reach the end of this worship of Gaṇeśa.
"The greatness of Gaṇeśa’s name has not been fully known by him.
Bhṛgu said:
"Thus, O King, the wonderful greatness has been described to you by me. (50)
O King, this section on spiritual practice (Upāsanākhaṇḍa), which was imparted by the highly gracious Brahmā to Vyāsa, has been described by me. 51.
If you have faith in hearing it, then I shall describe another deed of Gaṇanātha as well, which destroys the sins of the beloved of Soma (the Moon). 52.
Sūta said: Thus, O great sages headed by Śaunaka, the worship of Gaṇeśa has been narrated to you, interspersed with various other stories. 53.
That which was uttered by Brahmā to the sage Vedavyāsa, and described by Bhṛgu to Somaka as the destroyer of sins; || 54 ||
Whoever should listen to this supreme Purāṇa of Gaṇeśa, having abandoned all calamities and having enjoyed manifold pleasures, (shall attain liberation). 55.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of both knowledge and realized wisdom, one attains supreme liberation through the grace of Gaṇeśa. || 56 ||
There is no returning for him again, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas;
he who causes [this] to be heard with great devotion shall partake of the fruit as described. 57.
Thus it was heard with supreme devotion by Somakānta as he received it.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Name Gajānana," in the Upāsanākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā, Vyāsa, Bhṛgu, and Somakānta.
May this be offered to the glorious Gajānana. I bow to the illustrious Śiva.
